articles.title: Estos son los 10 de países de América con más actividad cibernética: Colombia, México y Perú en la mira
articles.text:
El riesgo de sufrir un ciberataque se ha convertido en una preocupación para los países de América. Ante ello, el estudio Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026 identificó diferencias importantes entre los países de la región en cuanto a la actividad cibernética observada y los ataques de ransomware, una modalidad que secuestra datos o bloquea sistemas para exigir un pago.
De acuerdo con los registros de actividad vinculada a actores estatales recopilados por Microsoft entre el 1 de julio de 2025 y el 30 de junio de 2026, Estados Unidos concentró la mayor cantidad de eventos observados en América, con 531. Muy por detrás se ubicaron Brasil con 27 y Canadá con 26. El resto de los países incluidos en los datos registró cifras de un solo dígito.
Estos datos permiten elaborar un listado de diez países americanos con más registros de esta clase de actividad. Sin embargo, no deben interpretarse como una medición absoluta de la probabilidad de sufrir un ciberataque: el volumen observado no equivale al total de incidentes ocurridos ni permite establecer, por sí solo, qué país tiene las defensas más débiles.
El Top 10 de países de América según la actividad cibernética observada
Según los datos del informe, el listado queda conformado de la siguiente manera:
- Estados Unidos: 531 registros de actividad estatal observada.
- Brasil: 27.
- Canadá: 26.
- Chile: 9.
- Colombia: 9.
- México: 9.
- Perú: 7.
- Ecuador: 5.
- Argentina: 4.
- República Dominicana: 3.
Los registros de Chile, Colombia y México comparten la misma cifra, por lo que aparecen empatados en este indicador. El orden del listado sirve para organizar los datos publicados, pero no representa una clasificación definitiva de vulnerabilidad o de riesgo nacional.
La diferencia entre Estados Unidos y el resto de los países es considerable. No obstante, el número de eventos observados también depende del alcance de la actividad detectada y de los objetivos de los actores involucrados. Por esa razón, los datos deben analizarse junto con otros indicadores de seguridad digital.
El ransomware muestra otra dimensión de la amenaza
El informe también recoge cifras de ataques de ransomware, una modalidad en la que los delincuentes pueden cifrar archivos, interrumpir operaciones y amenazar con divulgar información robada si la víctima no paga.
En Estados Unidos, los registros de ransomware pasaron de 724 en 2025 a 1.087 en 2026, un incremento del 50%. Canadá también experimentó un aumento: pasó de 98 a 172 registros, lo que representa una subida del 76%. En Costa Rica, los casos reportados aumentaron de 23 a 32, un 39%.
Estas cifras corresponden a otro indicador y no deben mezclarse con los registros de actividad estatal para construir un único ranking. Además, Costa Rica aparece en los datos de ransomware citados, pero no forma parte de los diez países incluidos en la lista anterior de actividad estatal observada.
Microsoft también identificó diferencias entre las familias de ransomware detectadas. Qilin fue la más visible en sitios públicos donde los atacantes divulgan información de sus víctimas, mientras que Akira registró la mayor actividad en la telemetría de Microsoft Defender. Esto muestra que la amenaza puede manifestarse de distintas formas según la fuente utilizada para observarla.
Por qué América enfrenta mayores desafíos de ciberseguridad
El documento advierte que América Latina, junto con regiones como África y el sudeste asiático, registra una actividad creciente de ciberdelincuentes. Entre los factores señalados se encuentran la expansión de los servicios digitales y las diferencias en la madurez de las defensas de cada organización.
Los riesgos incluyen el robo de contraseñas y otras credenciales, los correos fraudulentos que buscan engañar a los usuarios, la explotación de aplicaciones expuestas a internet y los ataques contra dispositivos de acceso remoto, como redes privadas virtuales, cortafuegos y pasarelas de conexión. También pueden verse comprometidas las identidades digitales utilizadas para acceder a servicios en la nube.
La inteligencia artificial añade otra dimensión al problema: puede acelerar tareas de reconocimiento, elaboración de mensajes fraudulentos y automatización de ciertas etapas de un ataque. Al mismo tiempo, las organizaciones pueden utilizarla para detectar comportamientos sospechosos y reforzar sus mecanismos de defensa.
Qué significa el ranking para los usuarios y las empresas
La posición de un país en este listado no significa que todos sus habitantes o empresas tengan la misma probabilidad de ser atacados. El riesgo depende de factores como la información que se maneja, la exposición de los sistemas, la actualización de los programas y la capacidad de responder ante un incidente.
Microsoft recomienda priorizar la protección de las identidades digitales, acelerar la detección y respuesta ante amenazas y preparar mecanismos de recuperación para reducir el impacto de un ataque.
Para los usuarios, algunas medidas básicas siguen siendo relevantes: activar la autenticación multifactor, utilizar contraseñas únicas, desconfiar de enlaces inesperados y mantener actualizados los dispositivos. En las empresas, estas acciones deben complementarse con controles de acceso, copias de seguridad y planes de respuesta ante incidentes.
El Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026 ofrece señales para entender cómo evoluciona la amenaza en la región. Sus cifras permiten comparar indicadores específicos, pero no deben confundirse con una predicción exacta de qué países sufrirán más ciberataques en el futuro.

articles.title: Renault et EDF veulent réduire la facture d’électricité des Français grâce aux voitures électriques
articles.text:
Renault Group et EDF veulent que les propriétaires de voitures électriques paient moins cher leur électricité, simplement en laissant leur véhicule branché à la maison. Les deux groupes français ont signé un partenariat autour de la recharge bidirectionnelle, avec une première offre attendue d’ici l’été 2027.
Avec la recharge bidirectionnelle, ou V2G (vehicle-to-grid), l’électricité circule dans les deux sens entre la voiture et le réseau. Le propriétaire recharge sa batterie quand le courant est abondant et bon marché, et une partie de l’énergie stockée est réinjectée sur le réseau aux heures de forte demande. Renault a intégré cette technologie à la R5 E-Tech électrique dès sa présentation, en février 2024. Le constructeur et l’énergéticien annoncent désormais une économie sur la recharge équivalente à 10 000 kilomètres par an, au maximum. Le gain réel est fonction de la consommation du véhicule et du temps qu’il passe branché à domicile, d’après une note du communiqué commun des deux groupes. Pour tenir cette promesse, Renault confie à EDF l’installation des bornes et le pilotage de la recharge.
Une offre réservée aux maisons individuelles
Renault Group et EDF réservent leur future offre aux propriétaires de maisons individuelles. Ces clients pourront la souscrire chez les concessionnaires des trois marques du groupe, avec une borne posée par IZI by EDF et un service de pilotage de la recharge. IZI by EDF est le réseau d’installateurs de bornes du groupe EDF. À terme, les deux partenaires prévoient aussi d’utiliser l’énergie de la voiture pour alimenter certains appareils de la maison.
Il faut en effet davantage qu’une prise dans le garage pour renvoyer du courant vers le réseau. Pour profiter de l’offre V2G de Mobilize, filiale de Renault, commercialisée en France depuis octobre 2024, un propriétaire doit disposer d’un compteur Linky et d’une borne bidirectionnelle facturée 599 euros pose comprise. Il lui faut aussi l’accord d’Enedis pour injecter de l’électricité sur le réseau, ainsi qu’une attestation de conformité du Consuel, d’après la liste des conditions d’éligibilité au V2G établie par Mobilize. Les foyers équipés de panneaux solaires en autoconsommation partielle sont exclus du service.
Les locataires d’appartement ne peuvent donc pas, à ce stade, faire travailler la batterie de leur voiture. Chez Renault Group, l’argument mis en avant est d’abord celui du portefeuille. « Au-delà de l’innovation technologique, ce partenariat apporte une réponse concrète à deux enjeux majeurs pour les Français : le pouvoir d’achat et la transition énergétique », estime Jérôme Faton, vice-président chargé de l’expérience client et de l’énergie du groupe.
L’expérience d’EDF dans le pilotage de la recharge
Sur le volet logiciel, EDF apporte le savoir-faire de Dreev. Cette filiale d’EDF business services gère la recharge des véhicules branchés en fonction de la disponibilité et du prix de l’électricité, au sein du projet européen de bornes vehicle-to-grid EVVE, où EDF et Dreev comptaient, en octobre 2024, 250 bornes V2G en service, surtout en France et au Danemark, sur un objectif de 800. « Le groupe EDF dispose d’une solide expérience du pilotage intelligent, déployée auprès de plus de 100 000 clients en France et en Europe par notre filiale Dreev », souligne Christelle Vives, présidente d’EDF business services.
Pour EDF, ces milliers de batteries branchées le soir sont une source de flexibilité pour le réseau électrique. Le fournisseur peut puiser dans leur réserve aux heures de pointe, puis les recharger quand la production dépasse la demande, sans que le conducteur ait à intervenir.
Renault et EDF n’ont précisé ni le prix de la borne, ni le tarif auquel l’électricité réinjectée sera rémunérée. Le contrat Mobilize Power est opéré depuis 2024 par l’allemand The Mobility House, et les propriétaires de Renault électriques devront passer par lui pour revendre l’énergie de leur batterie jusqu’à l’arrivée de l’offre d’EDF, attendue d’ici l’été 2027.
La V2G permet à une voiture électrique non seulement de se recharger, mais aussi de renvoyer une partie de l’énergie de sa batterie vers le réseau électrique. Le principe consiste à charger quand l’électricité est abondante et moins chère, puis à réinjecter aux heures de forte demande, quand le réseau est sous tension. Pour l’utilisateur, l’intérêt se joue sur l’optimisation de la facture via des tarifs variables et/ou une rémunération de l’énergie injectée. Pour le réseau, ces batteries servent de réserve distribuée, utile pour lisser les pics de consommation et intégrer davantage d’énergies renouvelables. Cela suppose un pilotage automatisé pour respecter les besoins de mobilité (niveau de charge minimal, horaires de départ).
Une prise classique n’est pas conçue pour gérer un flux d’énergie sortant vers le réseau, ni pour piloter finement la puissance et la sécurité électrique. Une borne bidirectionnelle intègre de l’électronique de puissance (conversion AC/DC et souvent DC/AC), des protections et des fonctions de communication pour synchroniser l’injection avec les exigences du réseau. L’installation doit aussi garantir la conformité électrique (mise à la terre, protections différentielles, sections de câble, etc.), car on ajoute un générateur d’énergie derrière le compteur. Cette complexité explique la présence d’un installateur et d’une validation de conformité, surtout quand il y a injection sur le réseau public. Enfin, le pilotage doit pouvoir limiter ou couper instantanément l’injection en cas de contrainte réseau ou de sécurité.
Le compteur Linky sert de point de mesure communicant : il comptabilise précisément l’énergie consommée et, le cas échéant, l’énergie injectée, avec un suivi compatible avec des offres tarifaires dynamiques. L’accord d’Enedis est nécessaire car Enedis exploite le réseau de distribution : toute injection derrière le compteur doit être déclarée et encadrée pour éviter des risques sur le réseau local (tensions, protections, qualité de l’onde). L’attestation Consuel valide que l’installation électrique respecte les règles de sécurité en vigueur avant mise en service ou modification significative. Ces trois éléments structurent le cadre technique et réglementaire qui permet de “vendre” ou valoriser une injection d’électricité sans bricolage. Sans ce cadre, la V2G ne peut pas être opérée de façon fiable et conforme.

articles.title: NABARD-backed NABVENTURES raises Rs 450 Cr for second fund
articles.text:
NABARD-backed NABVENTURES raises Rs 450 Cr for second fund
NABARD’s venture capital arm has announced the first close of its second fund to back early- and growth-stage rural and agritech startups despite a broader funding slowdown in the sector.
NABVENTURES, the venture capital arm of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has achieved the first close of its second fund, securing Rs 450 crore in initial commitments.
The fund has a target corpus of Rs 1,500 crore, including a green-shoe option to accommodate additional investments. NABARD is the anchor investor in the fund, which will back early- to growth-stage technology startups focused on agriculture and rural development.
Established on April 23, 2018, as a wholly owned subsidiary of NABARD, NABVENTURES manages investments through its flagship Fund I and the specialised AgriSURE fund. The firm has invested in 23 companies across India's agritech and rural startup ecosystem. Its portfolio includes supply chain platform Unnati, farm-to-consumer brand Eggoz, snacking company Beyond Snack, and rural fintech startup Jai Kisan.
Earlier this year, aquaculture-focused agritech startup Aquapulse raised Rs 25 crore in an ongoing Series A round led by NABVENTURES and KisaanSay, with the investment made through the AgriSURE fund.
NABVENTURES Fund II will provide growth capital to companies using technology to address structural challenges across the agricultural value chain. Its focus areas include agritech, climate-smart solutions, supply chain and logistics, rural fintech, food and agribusiness, and other businesses driving rural transformation.
Announcing the First Close, Dr. Shaji Krishnan V, Chairman of NABARD stated, "The successful First Close of NABVENTURES Fund II at Rs 450 crore marks an important milestone in NABARD's continued commitment to fostering innovation across India's agriculture and rural economy. As the sector evolves, there is a growing need for scalable, technology-driven solutions that enhance productivity, strengthen value chains, improve farmers' incomes, and build resilient rural enterprises.”
“Through Fund II, we aim to partner with visionary entrepreneurs developing innovative solutions to address critical challenges across the agricultural ecosystem. Our focus is on supporting enterprises that deliver both strong commercial outcomes and meaningful social impact through sustainability, climate resilience, financial inclusion, and livelihood creation. By deepening support for the innovation ecosystem, NABARD seeks to accelerate the transformation of India's agriculture and rural economy, making it more resilient, competitive, and future-ready,” he added.
The deployment of fresh capital comes during an extended funding recalibration within India's agritech sector. Startups in the sector raised $202 million across 36 deals in 2025, reflecting a 25% decline from the $269 million recorded in 2024. The recent pullback contrasts sharply with the sector's peak investment activity in 2021 and 2022, when funding reached $728 million and $840 million, respectively. Market analysts attribute the slowdown to heightened investor scrutiny over capital-intensive operations, elevated customer acquisition costs, and monetization challenges among marketplace and logistics platforms.
The wider Indian venture ecosystem has reflected similar cautious sentiment. In the third quarter of 2026, total startup funding rose 5% year-over-year to $2.2 billion, even as deal volume fell 13% and the active investor pool contracted 24%.
Despite broader headwinds, established agritech operations continue to secure target capital. Farm machinery developer Balwaan Krishi raised $10.4 million in a Series B round in September, while B2B agri-supply chain platform Ninjacart secured $6 million in July. NABVENTURES' Rs 1,500 crore fund target signals institutional confidence in the long-term commercial potential of India's rural economy.""

articles.title: I tested MSI's Pro Max Edge AI+ mini PC and its offline AI is off the charts
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The processor may already be over a year old, yet combined with a powerful GPU, NPU and a stack of RAM, it has the raw power to comfortably run local AI. Standard mini PC performance is workstation-level, perfect for high-end creative and business use. As with the competition, the Pro Max Edge AI+ enables you to run LLMs fully offline and at speed, all made possible by the 128GB of unified memory, Strix Halo CPU and powerful integrated Radeon 8060S graphics. However, some other aspects feel dated, such as the slow 2.5GbE network; still, that local AI potential is impressive.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent local AI
- + Huge unified memory
- + Compact workstation design
Reasons to avoid
- - Older CPU
- - RAM can’t be upgraded further
- - Large power draw for a mini PC
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: 30-second review
The MSI Pro Max Edge AI+ is one of the most powerful mini workstations that I’ve tested, and proved to be a perfect tool for Creative application and running AI offline. Inside is the AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ 395, however, unlike previous machines of this size that I've looked at it's backed by Radeon 8060S graphics and, crucially for running local language models it comes with 128GB of unified memory.
This combination of high powered processers means that it was able to run surprisingly large local AI models all downloaded and managed within Lemonade. The most impressive task centered around sorting more than 2,600 images, generate images using the Flux and Qwen3 Coder models through Visual Studio Code and several other supporting apps. It was also able to generate a ten page website, although quite a bit of prompting was needed.
Performance for normal creative work, using Photoshop, Lightroom and Premiere Pro was equally impressive with the machine handling batches of Sony RAW files without issue. Pushing the abilities I checked out the performance editing 4K Canon EOS R5 C footage in Premiere Pro and once again that power of the Strix Halo took the edit in its stride.
There are of course some drawbacks such as the staggeringly high price at £5,999, then there the 2.5Gb Ethernet that just feels slow for a workstation of this level, and getting the most from local AI requires plenty of setup and experimentation, but then that's just how things are with AI at the moment.
But once configured, that’s where the Pro Max Edge AI+ starts to make sense. If you need private, completely offline AI for coding, image organisation or other long-running workloads, there’s an enormous amount of processing power packed into this relatively compact machine.
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? From $5,499
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Directly from MSI
The MSI Pro Max Edge AI+ is available from the MSI website for $5,499 (US); €5,299; £5,999. It’s also widely available from most online retailers.
- Value: 4 / 5
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Specs
CPU: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 16-core / 32-thread Zen 5
GPU: AMD Radeon 8060S integrated graphics
NPU: AMD XDNA NPU, up to 50 TOPS
RAM: 128GB LPDDR5X-8000 unified memory
Maximum GPU memory allocation: Up to 96GB
Storage: 2TB M.2 2280 NVMe PCIe Gen 4 x4 SSD
Rear ports: 2x USB 2.0 Type-A, 1x USB 10Gbps Type-A, 1x USB 40Gbps Type-C with DisplayPort 2.0 Alt Mode and 15W PD output, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x DisplayPort 1.4a, 1x RJ45 Ethernet, 1x 3.5mm audio combo jack
Networking: 2.5Gb Ethernet
Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi 7
Operating system: Windows 11 Pro
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Design
The first impressions of this mini PC are impressive. It arrives with a slightly larger form factor than I’m used to for a mini PC, but then again, this has one of the Strix Halo CPUs inside, and that’s matched with an equally impressive integrated GPU and NPU.
What marks this new machine out, despite its rather ageing CPU, is the fact that it’s been fully optimised to run LLMs with 128GB of unified RAM soldered to the motherboard and AMD Radeon 8060S integrated graphics.
The machine is by no means large at 197.5 x 188.4 x 94.5mm, and while heavier than most mini PCs, it comes in at just 2.9kg, so if you need it, it’s still perfectly portable. On the portability, I was pleased to see that the power supply is integrated into the form factor, so there’s no power brick to lug around with the machine itself.
This means it’s equally at home on your desktop or, if you’re a creative and you do need to take your machine with you, then it’s still relatively portable.
Around the body, there are plenty of ports and connectivity options, which are given space due to that larger form factor. Size-wise, it sits somewhere in the middle of a mini PC and mini tower.
On the front, you have two USB Type-A ports offering 10Gbps and one USB4 port with 40Gbps. This also supports DisplayPort 2.0 and 15W USB power output.
Alongside this USB port is a full-sized SD 4.0 UHS-II card reader that will appeal to creatives, along with a 3.5mm audio jack. The other addition on the front is a performance mode switch that you can use to quickly adapt between Performance and Eco modes.
At the rear, you have a further two USB 2.0 Type-A ports and a USB 3.2 10Gbps Type-A port, a USB Type-C port that offers 40Gbps, and again this supports DisplayPort 2.0 and 15W USB Type-C power output. The USB ports are joined by HDMI 2.1 with HDR and up to 4K 60Hz, DisplayPort 1.4, a 2.5GbE RJ45 Ethernet port and a further 3.5mm audio combo jack.
On the exterior, that pretty much rounds everything up, but inside you have two M.2 NVMe slots, one filled with a 2TB M.2 NVMe PCIe Gen 4 x4 SSD. The onboard RAM is soldered on and can’t be upgraded, but that is enough to run LLMs and many of the major creative applications with AI features.
On the design and build, it’s a shame that there is no OCuLink port for connecting out to an eGPU; even with the USB4 port, the fact that the RJ45 port is limited to just 2.5GbE is a disappointment. I would have expected that a machine of this price would have at least 5GbE, if not 10GbE. When it comes to the overall quality and design, it’s both aesthetically pleasing and exceptionally well made, as you’d expect at this price point.
- Design: 4.5 / 5
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Features
As of 1 October 2026, this machine has just hit the shelves. Yet one of the headline features, the Strix Halo Ryzen AI Max+ 395, is already over a year old. This CPU features an integrated Radeon 8060S GPU and an NPU, alongside 128GB of unified LPDDR5X-8000 RAM, which enables the ultrafast processing required by many of the AI features to really push through.
That CPU, while a little older than some of the latest AI mini PCs that we’re seeing, enables the machine to be well balanced when it comes to performance, although this is still an expensive option. That CPU offers 16 cores and 32 threads with AMD’s Strix Halo Zen 5 architecture.
This is joined by the equally impressive AMD Radeon 8060S integrated graphics and integrated AMD XDNA NPU, which offers up to 50 TOPS of AI processing. This means that with all of those processors combined, there’s 126 TOPS of potential within this one small machine.
Storage capacity is catered for with two M.2 slots, each NVMe PCIe Gen 4 x4, and my review sample arrived with a 2TB module. Across the machine, there’s a decent array of ports both front and back, and it’s great to see that it features a USB4 port on both the front and back. If you do need to connect ultra-fast storage, this is perfectly possible. These ports also support DisplayPort 2.0 and 15W power output, which again is extremely handy.
On starting up the machine, it’s pre-installed with Windows 11 Pro, and MSI has included its management software, which enables you to activate certain AI features, as well as security and settings options to adjust the machine’s performance.
One of the features that I mentioned in the design section is the fact that the power supply is integrated, and this offers 300W of power, which is needed by these AI-enhanced processors to handle all of that processing.
Wi-Fi 7 supplies the wireless connectivity, which is now becoming the standard, although Wi-Fi 8 has just started to emerge on some devices. It also features a UHS-II SD card reader, again great to see, and a single LAN port at the back, which is 2.5GbE. This is a little disappointing on a machine of this price and performance. I would have expected a minimum of 5GbE and preferably 10GbE.
- Features: 4 / 5
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Performance
Crystal Disk Mark Read: 6122.48
Crystal Disk Mark Write: 5827.92
Geekbench 7 CPU Multi: 21905
Geekbench 7 CPU Single: 2672
Geekbench 7 GPU: 96251
PC Mark Overall: 9990
Cinebench 2026 CPU Multi (Threads): 6932
Cinebench 2026 CPU Single (Threads): 457
Fire Strike Overall: 25009
Fire Strike Graphics: 28653
Fire Strike Physics: 29422
Fire Strike Combined: 11480
Time Spy Overall: 10777
Time Spy Graphics: 10972
Time Spy CPU: 9792
Wild Life Overall: 65611
Steel Nomad Overall: 2158
Windows Experience Overall: 8.8
Procyon: 1125
Getting into the performance of the machine, the initial setup is as straightforward as ever. Windows 11 Pro is relatively straightforward, and once you plug the machine in and connect up all the peripherals, it’s just a case of running through the final steps, connecting it online, and within about 10 to 20 minutes, the machine will be up and running, ready for you to install whichever software you want.
In this test, I’ve run a wide variety of different applications, starting off with the basics of Microsoft Office to test productivity. I’ve also installed the Adobe Creative Suite, with a focus on Adobe Photoshop, Lightroom and Premiere Pro, and alongside that, to start some of the AI testing, I’ve also installed DaVinci Resolve.
As this machine is very much focused on AI, especially with that Strix Halo processor, I’ve also installed Lemonade to manage the local LLMs and downloaded and installed a good variety of different options, including Flux, Qwen 3 and Qwen 2.5 releases, to enable a variety of different tasks that I’d later test the machine with.
Starting out with general computer use, Microsoft Office and Windows run smoothly, as you would imagine on a machine of this price and power. Microsoft Word, PowerPoint and Excel can all easily be opened at the same time, with images, data and content being transferred from one to the other without any noticeable slowdown or hesitation.
Copying and pasting images is straightforward, and as I opened multiple windows over the week of testing in the Edge browser, there was no issue or slowdown. It also proved that the Wi-Fi 7 connection to my Wi-Fi 6 hub was exceptionally solid.
Progressing on from Microsoft Office, I loaded up a few apps from the Adobe Creative Suite and, using Adobe Bridge, checked through a couple of thousand images, both JPEG and RAW, that were shot on the Sony A7 IV. Again, here you really see that processor and the Radeon 8060S GPU handle the rendering of thumbnails exceptionally quickly.
Unlike on many smaller mini PCs, there is really very little time needed for each new thumbnail to render, enabling me to quickly scroll from top to bottom through the images without having to wait to see what each file contains. Selecting a batch of images and then opening them in Adobe Camera Raw once again just showed how powerful this machine was.
While I was dealing with large Sony RAW files, and a decent quantity at a time, there was absolutely no slowdown on either individual or batch adjustments. Then, opening those up into Adobe Photoshop was equally fluid, with only a few seconds needed between ACR and the Photoshop workspace for each of the 50 images to fully load.
Even with my desktop workstation, which is a relatively powerful machine and also features 128GB of RAM and a decent GPU, what up to this point I’ve always felt was pretty fluid now seemed relatively slow in comparison. As I then switched over to Lightroom to quickly check and enhance another batch of files, it was again apparent that image editing on this machine was well below what it was capable of doing.
Even with generative expand and image generation, render times were a few seconds rather than up to a minute, which is what I have experienced with other small mini PCs. The real show of power came when I loaded up Adobe Premiere Pro and went to work on a 4K video edit using C-Log footage from the Canon EOS R5 C.
Again, it was as if I was just editing 1080p video shot on a mobile phone, and the machine could handle cuts and edits of the five-minute video without too much issue from over an hour’s worth of footage.
The only consideration here was that the footage was being imported from an external Thunderbolt 4 drive, and here I was a little disappointed that I couldn’t connect my NAS to the system so that I could network edit due to the limited speed of the 2.5GbE network port on the back. Instead, I had to rely on a traditional external SSD for storage, although there is thankfully an additional internal M.2 slot which would take additional internal storage if required.
Still, the video editing potential is there, and it’s impressively fast, but this led me directly to checking out the machine’s AI potential, and this is where things really started to develop.
To test AI performance, more specifically local AI performance, I first installed Lemonade and then, through that, downloaded a variety of different LLMs and models for different tasks.
These included Qwen 2.5-VL-7B-Instruct-GGUF, which is a vision model and was used to inspect and recognise images. I used this in combination with ExifTool to organise and label a variety of files for website creation.
I fell back on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF, and this was absolutely superb for coding HTML and CSS Grid for the test. While this took quite a bit of additional configuration, especially training it to use Grid formats rather than straight HTML, and connecting it through Visual Studio Code, I was again impressed by just how simply it all tied together.
The biggest task that I put the machine through was file organisation, and this is a task that I’ve always put off. Even after a few months of using various different techniques to sort the images, it’s always good when one of these machines comes in so that I can start to pick up from where I last left off.
While they automate the process, it’s still relatively slow. Here I fed in over 2,634 images and used GPT-OSS-20B-NPU to really put the machine through its paces. Not only was it able to recognise the images, but it started to sort them at a relative speed, although I did fall back onto Qwen 2.5-VL-7B-Instruct-GGUF in order to complete the task, and not all images were recognised. Checking the content of those images, they were mostly nondescript or under or overexposed, so the subject wasn’t recognisable in any way.
Taking time to set up the machine is something that I found all the way along when using AI machines: they’re not ready to use out of the box, and there is a certain learning curve needed in order to configure the LLMs in a way that works for you. While they do run offline, as all tests were carried out in this review, I did utilise online AI at points to select the different models for the different tasks that I had in mind.
One of the next tests that I ran was to create a quick static website that I could then update on a regular basis. For this, I first loaded Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF through Lemonade. I also opened Visual Studio Code and installed the Continue extension. I created a folder with all the assets that I wanted for my project, including Word documents that I converted into plain text and images that were reformatted into JPEGs.
In Visual Studio Code, I was then able to use the Continue AI chat window, connect the model that I wanted and put in the prompt to create a 3D printer review website with a variety of different sections. I also uploaded some general design ideas so that it had a good plan of what it was going to create. I’d already pre-designed the look and layout using CSS Grid, as I like the speed of pure static HTML rather than a more standard CMS site. I then hit Enter and let the local model do its thing.
One of the first things that I noticed was that, within Visual Studio Code, I would have to accept file creation for each file that it generated. In this review, I haven’t yet found a workaround for this so that it can just create the files without prompting.
But checking out the HTML, it was exceptionally clean, if a little textbook, and the final result was pretty good, although there were a few minor rendering issues with the JavaScript that I hadn’t wanted it to create. For some reason, none of the images that I had given it had been included in the design, so essentially it was just CSS layout and review text.
Again, going back in and re-editing, it started to slowly develop the website into what I wanted, and this really starts to show you the power of localised AI and what’s possible. By the time the whole process was finished, the server session recorded 152,937 input tokens for what was essentially a 10-page website and processed 24,639 output tokens, which were generated across 51 requests.
To actually complete the site, I would consider around 200 requests realistic. The final response generated 406 tokens at 47.85 tokens per second, equivalent to approximately 8.5 seconds of generation, with a time to first token of 1.99 seconds, which is pretty much on par with some of the online models that I use. The entire process, which involved a little to and fro from prompts and letting the machine work through the task, was an hour.
As I went through further models and further experiments with the localised AI, I was increasingly impressed by what it was capable of doing, with the most useful application being the file sorting. I have run file sorting with some of the other AI models and been impressed, but here things seemed to take a bit of a step up, with the power of the GPU and CPU taking on most of the processing.
Quickly checking which processors were in use showed that there was no NPU involvement in the sorting process, as I was using the Qwen 2.5-VL-7B-Instruct-GGUF model. However, it did appear that there were spikes of NPU use during the processing.
When selecting the models, if you do want to make full use of that NPU, then you select an NPU-compatible model, but this varies per task, and new models are being released all the time that you can download and experiment with. This is where most of the time with AI comes in, as you do need to experiment a great deal to make the most of these machines and their AI potential.
For most users, however, if you’re just using Copilot or the built-in AI behind Photoshop or Premiere Pro, then the potential is also there, and that does fall back onto the processor and NPU, with more improvements arriving over time. The final AI test was to incorporate AI into DaVinci Resolve for some video editing.
While I’ve only just started to experiment on this front, the way that DaVinci and the AI model interact on this machine is slightly eerie and impressive, with some pretty decent rough cuts of three-channel video straight off the bat. I’m hoping that, with a bit more experimentation, I’ll get usable edits, but even in these early stages of experimentation, the potential of this machine is apparent.
While other lesser machines are able to do many of these tasks, what makes it different here is the absolute speed at which the hardware is able to cope. Because of the 128GB of onboard memory, it doesn’t stall or run out of steam partway through a task. In the final task, really just for a bit of fun, I loaded in Flux-2-Klein-9B-GGUF for some generative image creation.
Here, I asked it to create a picture of a Labrador in the New Forest in spring, summer, autumn and winter. I was able to create each of those images in less than a minute. The Flux model is a little limited in what you can actually do with it, but I was able to load a portrait of myself into the system, then use that to generate a picture of myself and a Labrador in the New Forest. This was again entertaining and surprisingly good for something that runs offline.
However, there were some of the issues that you always get with even the online models, such as extra arms and fingers where you weren’t expecting them. Still, this is fully offline AI running without any cloud server intervention.
- Performance: 4.5 / 5
MSI PRO MAX Edge AI+: Final verdict
The MSI Pro Max Edge AI+ is an impressive mini PC, although slightly larger than the small box-like machines that I usually look at, but even with a processor that is over a year old, when it is combined with the integrated Radeon 8060S GPU and NPU, it already offers impressive power.
But then, when you add in 128GB of unified RAM, a fast SSD and plenty of connectivity options, you have a machine that is finally capable of running LLMs locally. The one point about any machine like this is that they’re not simple plug-and-play systems when it comes to the AI potential.
Setting up the local language models in the way that you want to use them does take time, and for anyone just getting into local AI, expect to put aside at least a week to fully experiment with each of the models and what they can do, as well as the different model types that utilise the CPU and GPU and those that really make use of the NPU.
Once you’ve done that and you know exactly what you want to do, then it takes another day to fully set up the machine to do exactly what you want from scratch. After testing several of these machines, I now jot down the models that I need to install in order to run these tests, and even then I’m looking at a good half-day to download all of that content.
But then, once it’s set up, the potential is massive. Unlike lesser machines with less RAM and without these AI-enhanced CPUs, you can actually run proper localised language models, and the output they produce is also exceptionally good.
When you spend time not only making sure that all the downloads are there and available for them, but also training them so that they produce the style of content that you want, they become even more powerful. Personally, I found the best way to use this is to run a combination of cloud AI to help prompt the local AI into getting exactly what you want, use the paid tokens for the knowledge and the local AI for the heavy local work.
It all takes time, but compared with just a few months ago, the leap forward is massive and, really, while this machine is expensive, it does offer true offline AI if you want it.
Should I buy the MSI Pro Max Edge AI+?
| Value | Strix Halo power with the usual pricing | 4 | 
| Design | Stylish design that gives space for cooling | 4.5 | 
| Features | 128GB unified-memory enable the power to run local LLMs | 4 | 
| Performance | Powerful GPU just gives this machine the edge over some close compitition | 4.5 | 
| Overall | Incredibly powerful workstation in a compact form | 4 | 
Buy it if...
You want offline AI
Running some of the commands that I utilised in this test would cost a substantial amount if using a cloud-based option. However, here, while that process is time-consuming, there’s no additional cost.
You have long-running tasks.
The file sorting for the 2,500 images was lengthy, and that’s just the start of it, so having a machine that I can leave running in the background sorting out images is extremely appealing.
Don't buy it if...
You just need a powerful machine.
There are plenty of machines as powerful as this for general work, but without that massive AI potential, that you can buy for a far lower price.
You don’t really need local AI.
The idea of local AI is good, but for the majority of people, the free or minimum-tier options available from the major players will offer you far more than you get from this machine.
It’s only when you start to customise things that this becomes viable.
For more professional-grade desktops, we've tested the best business computers and the best mini PCs.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.

articles.title: Cuáles fueron los primeros celulares comerciales de la historia: top 6 de Nokia 1100 al primer Motorola
articles.text:
Hubo una época en la que hablar por teléfono en plena calle parecía una escena de ciencia ficción. Hoy, los celulares permiten trabajar, estudiar, tomar fotografías y acceder a internet desde cualquier lugar, pero la historia de estos dispositivos comenzó con equipos voluminosos, costosos y con una autonomía limitada.
En poco más de cuatro décadas, la industria pasó de teléfonos que apenas permitían conversar durante media hora a los smartphones que concentran buena parte de la vida digital.
El primer celular portátil comercial fue el Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, que llegó al mercado estadounidense en 1983. Su desarrollo había comenzado años antes: en 1973, el ingeniero, Martin Cooper, realizó una llamada desde un teléfono móvil experimental.
Este dispositivo comercial pesaba cerca de 800 gramos, medía unos 25 centímetros de alto sin contar la antena y costaba alrededor de 4.000 dólares. Su batería necesitaba aproximadamente diez horas de carga para ofrecer hasta 30 minutos de conversación.
Aquel avance fue posible gracias al despliegue de las primeras redes celulares comerciales. Japón puso en marcha una red en 1979 y los países nórdicos inauguraron el sistema NMT en 1981. Desde entonces, fabricantes como Motorola, Nokia y Siemens compitieron por reducir el tamaño de los equipos y ampliar sus funciones.
Seis celulares que marcaron la historia de la telefonía
Estos seis dispositivos muestran algunos de los principales cambios que transformaron la telefonía móvil, desde los primeros modelos portátiles hasta la llegada de los smartphones modernos.
1. Motorola DynaTAC 8000X (1983)
Fue el primer teléfono celular portátil comercial y uno de los símbolos tecnológicos de los años ochenta. Su elevado precio y sus dimensiones lo convertían en un producto reservado principalmente para empresarios y usuarios con alto poder adquisitivo. Aunque sus prestaciones eran limitadas, permitió imaginar un futuro en el que las llamadas ya no dependieran de una línea fija.
2. Motorola MicroTAC (1989)
Motorola presentó el MicroTAC como una alternativa más compacta que sus modelos anteriores. Su diseño incorporaba una pieza plegable sobre el teclado que protegía los botones y se extendía hacia la zona del micrófono. Este formato anticipó una tendencia que cobraría fuerza durante los años noventa: fabricar teléfonos cada vez más pequeños y fáciles de transportar.
3. IBM Simon (1994)
Considerado uno de los precursores de los teléfonos inteligentes, el IBM Simon combinaba funciones de telefonía con herramientas digitales. Contaba con una pantalla táctil monocromática, calendario, agenda, bloc de notas y correo electrónico. Su precio elevado y su disponibilidad limitada impidieron que alcanzara una adopción masiva, pero anticipó varias características que hoy son habituales en los smartphones.
4. Motorola StarTAC (1996)
El StarTAC popularizó el diseño plegable tipo concha, que permitía reducir el tamaño del teléfono al cerrarlo. Pesaba alrededor de 88 gramos en algunas versiones y se convirtió en un referente de portabilidad. Su formato influyó en numerosos modelos posteriores, cuando los fabricantes buscaban combinar comodidad, diseño y facilidad de uso.
5. Nokia 3310 (2000)
El Nokia 3310 se convirtió en uno de los celulares más recordados de su época por su resistencia, su batería duradera y la posibilidad de personalizarlo con carcasas intercambiables. También ganó popularidad gracias a juegos como Snake, conocido en español como la culebrita. Su éxito ayudó a consolidar el celular como un producto de consumo masivo.
6. Nokia 1100 (2003)
Con un diseño sencillo, una linterna integrada y un precio accesible, el Nokia 1100 llegó a mercados de todo el mundo, incluidos países donde el costo de los teléfonos era una barrera importante. Vendió alrededor de 250 millones de unidades, una cifra que lo convirtió en uno de los modelos más vendidos de la historia. Su éxito demostró que no era necesario tener funciones avanzadas para conquistar a millones de usuarios.
El cambio que abrió la era de los smartphones
En 2007, Apple presentó el primer iPhone, un dispositivo que combinó teléfono, reproductor multimedia y navegación por internet en una pantalla táctil capacitiva. Aunque no fue el primer equipo con pantalla táctil, su interfaz y su diseño contribuyeron a transformar las expectativas de los consumidores.
La evolución posterior incorporó cámaras avanzadas, aplicaciones, conexión permanente a internet y sistemas operativos cada vez más completos. Así, el celular dejó de ser una herramienta dedicada principalmente a las llamadas para convertirse en una plataforma digital que acompaña a las personas durante todo el día.

articles.title: Un satellite soviétique "mort" vient de se désintégrer en orbite : pourquoi les experts s’inquiètent
articles.text:
Un satellite mis en orbite par la défunte URSS vient de se désintégrer en orbite autour de la Terre. Et il n'est pas le seul ces derniers temps.
L'espace au-dessus de nos têtes est de plus en plus encombré par rapport à l'époque de la conquête spatiale des années 60. Mais s'ils peuvent apporter de plus en plus de services à l'humanité, à l'image de Starlink, cet encombrement rend les systèmes plus fragiles, surtout si les débris s'accumulent. Et c'est un problème que l'on pourrait bientôt voir surgir vu la tendance actuelle.
Le satellite de l'époque soviétique Meteor 2-7 s'est désintégré en orbite basse
En mai 1981, l'Union soviétique lançait dans l'espace un satellite météorologique militaire et civil du nom de Meteor 2-7. Un engin spatial qui a eu le temps de remplir sa tâche, et qui était depuis longtemps. Et ce 5 octobre dernier, il a subi une désintégration en orbite basse (la deuxième de son histoire).
C'est la société de surveillance spatiale LeoLabs qui a annoncé cet événement. Elle dit avoir détecté des dizaines de fragments au niveau du satellite. Meteor 2-7 se situait à environ 850 kilomètres au dessus de la Terre, dans une région dense en débris orbitaux.
Le dernier d'une série qui dure depuis plusieurs mois
Et ce n'est malheureusement pas un événement isolé. « Il s'agit du dernier d'une série d'événements observés au cours des six derniers mois. Pris dans leur ensemble, ils révèlent une tendance préoccupante pour la sûreté et la sécurité spatiales, et soulignent la nécessité absolue d'une surveillance continue » explique ainsi LeoLabs dans un message posté sur X.
Parmi les engin spatiaux qui se sont désintégrés récemment, on retrouve un satellite espion américain USA 32 (septembre 2026) ou bien le corps d'une fusée chinois (août 2026). Un satellite Starlink s'était lui aussi fragmenté il ya quelques mois.
La multiplication des satellites dans l'espace entraîne de manière générale une croissance des potentiels débris qui pourront se retrouver là-haut, mettant en danger non seulement les satellites en fonction, mais aussi les missions habitées. On se rappelle ainsi qu'au mois de novembre dernier, trois taïkonautes s'étaient retrouvés coincés dans leur station spatiale Tiangong à cause de débris ayant abîmé le vaisseau destiné à assurer leur retour sur Terre.

articles.title: FBI Arrests Another ShinyHunters Suspect Reportedly Involved in Its Jobs Portal Hack
articles.text:
The FBI has arrested another suspected co-conspirator of ShinyHunters, FBI Director Kash Patel said on October 9 in a post on X.
ShinyHunters is the extortion group that said in September it had breached the FBI's jobs portal and stolen sensitive data on almost all FBI agents and job applicants. The FBI has not named the suspect, and no charges have been made public.
The suspect is a Canadian citizen who was arrested in Pennsylvania, according to The New York Times and CBS News. Both cited unnamed sources.
The Times reported that the arrest was made on suspicion of involvement in the theft of FBI data. A law enforcement source told CBS News that the suspect is believed to have been directly involved in the hack.
An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the Times report, CBS News said. Patel's post does not say whether the suspect took part in the breach. It calls ShinyHunters "the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident."
Patel also wrote that the FBI will keep working with its partners "to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate." Other suspected co-conspirators are still free, the law enforcement source told CBS News.
Earlier Arrests in the Netherlands and Jordan
Reuters counts the new arrest as the third made public since news of the breach broke in late September. The FBI said in a statement Reuters reported on October 3 that it had "already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects."
| Where | When | Made public by | Suspect | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Netherlands | September 15 | Dutch police and the FBI | A 24-year-old Amsterdam man. Identified to Reuters and CBS News as Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police have not named him. | 
| Jordan | September 29, according to Reuters' sources | Reuters, citing unnamed sources. Jordanian state media also quoted an official who confirmed an arrest and gave no name, The National reported . | Named by Reuters' sources as Saif al-Din Khader. | 
| Pennsylvania, according to The New York Times and CBS News | In the week it was announced, according to CBS News | FBI Director Kash Patel | Not named. A Canadian citizen, according to the same two outlets. | 
The man arrested in the Netherlands was taken into custody a week before ShinyHunters announced the FBI breach on September 22. The Dutch police statement, published in Dutch, does not mention the FBI or its jobs portal.
The FBI said in a video statement that he is one of the group's alleged leaders and that Dutch police made the arrest under Dutch law with FBI support. ShinyHunters told The Hacker News that he has no association with the group.
Khader, the suspect detained in Jordan, is cooperating with the FBI, according to Reuters, which cited people familiar with the matter.
The FBI has not said whether the new arrest resulted from that cooperation.
What Was Stolen and How the FBI Says It Happened
A sample of the data that ShinyHunters shared contained extensive personal information on FBI employees, details of sensitive job roles, and psychiatric and medical information, a Reuters analysis found. An internal FBI notice confirmed that hackers obtained employee information, a source told CBS News.
The FBI's review has so far found that the breach resulted from a security failure on a platform managed by an outside organization. It happened after "a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform," Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told Reuters on October 5. The FBI has removed the contractor.
The FBI did not name the platform or the organization. Two sources told Reuters they are PeopleSoft, Oracle's human resources software, and Accenture. Accenture told Reuters it was "proud to support the mission of the FBI" and did not answer the news agency's questions about the contractor.
ShinyHunters said it targeted the FBI over an advisory from May that it says makes false claims about the group. The advisory describes ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group that specializes in large-scale data breaches and extortion.
The FBI alleges that the group has breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments since last year.

articles.title: NVIDIA fonce vers les 6 000 milliards de dollars : le danger ne vient pas de là où on l'attend
articles.text:
L’explosion des investissements dans l’intelligence artificielle continue de propulser NVIDIA vers des sommets jamais atteints en Bourse. Le fabricant de puces semble pourtant arriver à un point où ses plus gros clients pourraient aussi devenir ses concurrents les plus gênants.
NVIDIA n’est plus très loin d’un territoire où aucune entreprise n’a encore posé le pied. Sa capitalisation a frôlé les 5 800 milliards de dollars début octobre avant de revenir autour de 5 550 milliards le 8 octobre. À ce rythme, le cap symbolique des 6 000 milliards n’a plus rien d’inimaginable, même si le parcours reste loin d’être parfaitement linéaire.
Après 3 000, 4 000 puis 5 000 milliards, le prochain record est en vue
Apple avait été la première entreprise à franchir les 3 000 milliards de dollars de valorisation en janvier 2022. NVIDIA a depuis accéléré la cadence en atteignant les 4 000 milliards le 9 juillet 2025, puis les 5 000 milliards le 29 octobre suivant.
Cette envolée repose d’abord sur une réalité très concrète. Les géants du cloud et de l’IA continuent d’engloutir des sommes considérables dans leurs centres de données, où les puces Blackwell occupent une place centrale. Le chiffre d’affaires trimestriel de NVIDIA a ainsi plus que doublé sur un an pour atteindre 96,2 milliards de dollars.
Le groupe dispose également d’une énorme capacité de rachat de ses propres actions avec une enveloppe encore disponible de 235 milliards de dollars. De quoi offrir un soutien supplémentaire au cours lorsque les conditions s’y prêtent.
NVIDIA ne compte évidemment pas s’arrêter à Blackwell. La génération Rubin doit prendre le relais alors que l’inférence et les agents IA réclament toujours davantage de puissance de calcul. Plus loin se profilent aussi la robotique et la conduite autonome, deux marchés encore modestes face aux centres de données, mais susceptibles de devenir de nouveaux moteurs de croissance.
Le plus gros danger pourrait venir de ses meilleurs clients
La concurrence traditionnelle n’a toutefois pas disparu. AMD pousse sa gamme Instinct et tente de grignoter une partie du marché des accélérateurs pour l’IA.
La menace la plus intéressante vient cependant des entreprises qui achètent aujourd’hui les GPU NVIDIA par dizaines de milliers. Google développe ses propres TPU, Amazon ses puces Trainium et d’autres géants technologiques cherchent eux aussi à concevoir davantage de composants en interne. Chaque calcul effectué sur une puce maison est potentiellement un calcul et une entrée d’argent qui échappent à NVIDIA.
Une autre limite pourrait être beaucoup plus terre à terre. Construire des centres de données demande des capitaux immenses, mais aussi suffisamment d’électricité pour les alimenter. NVIDIA reconnaît elle-même que les contraintes de financement et d’infrastructure peuvent ralentir certains projets.
Les GPU dédiés à l’IA combinent un très grand parallélisme et des unités de calcul spécialisées (tensor cores) qui accélèrent surtout les opérations de matrice, au cœur du deep learning. Blackwell et ses successeurs visent autant l’entraînement (phase coûteuse pour créer un modèle) que l’inférence (phase de production pour exécuter le modèle), avec des gains sur la performance par watt et la bande passante mémoire. L’enjeu se déplace de plus en plus vers l’inférence à grande échelle, car les usages agents IA multiplient les requêtes et les coûts d’exécution. Chaque nouvelle génération cherche aussi à mieux exploiter le calcul distribué entre plusieurs GPU via des interconnexions très rapides, pour éviter que le réseau ou la mémoire ne deviennent le goulot d’étranglement.
Quand un acteur du cloud conçoit ses propres accélérateurs, il cherche à optimiser le coût total (achat, énergie, refroidissement) et à adapter le matériel à ses charges de travail. Ces puces “maison” peuvent être étroitement intégrées au logiciel interne et aux services cloud, ce qui améliore l’efficacité pour certains modèles ou scénarios. Si une part croissante de l’entraînement ou de l’inférence bascule sur TPU/Trainium, cela diminue mécaniquement la demande de GPU NVIDIA sur ces volumes. En pratique, le basculement dépend de la maturité de l’écosystème logiciel (compilateurs, bibliothèques, frameworks) et de la capacité de production, deux facteurs qui déterminent la vitesse à laquelle un hyperscaler peut vraiment substituer des GPU.
Un rachat d’actions consiste pour une entreprise à utiliser sa trésorerie pour racheter ses propres titres sur le marché, puis à les annuler ou les conserver. En réduisant le nombre d’actions en circulation, cela peut augmenter mécaniquement le bénéfice par action (EPS) si les profits restent constants, ce qui soutient parfois le cours. Ces programmes peuvent aussi servir de coussin en cas de volatilité, car ils ajoutent un acheteur important et régulier. En contrepartie, l’argent consacré aux rachats n’est pas investi ailleurs (R&D, capacités industrielles, acquisitions), et l’effet dépend fortement du prix de rachat et du contexte de marché.

articles.title: Qué empresas lideraban la venta de celulares al inicio del negocio: quiénes eran los Apple y Samsung de la época
articles.text:
Durante las décadas de 1980 y 1990, mucho antes de que Apple y Samsung se convirtieran en protagonistas del mercado de los teléfonos inteligentes, otras compañías dominaban la industria de la telefonía móvil.
Motorola, Nokia y Ericsson fueron algunas de las marcas que definieron esa etapa, con equipos que marcaron el paso de los primeros celulares comerciales a dispositivos más compactos, accesibles y preparados para las redes digitales.
Motorola fue una de las grandes pioneras del sector, mientras que Nokia terminó por convertirse en el principal fabricante mundial de teléfonos móviles a finales de los años noventa. Ericsson, por su parte, tuvo un papel relevante tanto en el desarrollo de dispositivos como en la infraestructura que permitió expandir las comunicaciones inalámbricas.
La comparación con Apple y Samsung ayuda a entender la evolución del negocio, aunque el mercado de aquella época era diferente al actual: los celulares se utilizaban principalmente para llamar y enviar mensajes, y el diseño, la autonomía de la batería, la cobertura y la resistencia eran factores decisivos para los compradores.
Motorola, la compañía que abrió el camino
La historia del teléfono móvil comercial está estrechamente vinculada con Motorola, empresa estadounidense que presentó en 1983 el DynaTAC 8000X. El dispositivo, de gran tamaño en comparación con los celulares actuales, pesaba cerca de 800 gramos y ofrecía una autonomía limitada. Su precio de lanzamiento rondaba los 4.000 dólares, por lo que estaba lejos de ser un producto accesible para la mayoría de los consumidores.
Aun así, el DynaTAC 8000X representó un hito: permitió realizar llamadas sin depender de una conexión telefónica fija. Durante los años siguientes, Motorola continuó desarrollando equipos que contribuyeron a definir el diseño de los celulares.
En 1989 presentó el MicroTAC, un modelo compacto para los estándares de la época que incorporaba una pieza abatible sobre el teclado. En 1996 llegó el StarTAC, uno de los primeros teléfonos plegables de gran popularidad comercial. Su tamaño reducido y su diseño lo convirtieron en un dispositivo emblemático de la segunda mitad de los noventa.
Motorola fue una marca de referencia durante los primeros años de la telefonía móvil, aunque el crecimiento de nuevos fabricantes y la expansión de las redes digitales modificaron progresivamente el equilibrio de fuerzas.
Nokia conquistó el mercado mundial
Si Motorola ayudó a establecer el negocio, Nokia fue la empresa que consiguió llevar los celulares a una escala masiva. La compañía finlandesa, que originalmente se dedicaba a otras actividades industriales, se convirtió en un actor central de las telecomunicaciones durante los años noventa.
En 1998, Nokia superó a Motorola y pasó a ocupar el primer puesto mundial en ventas de teléfonos móviles. Su crecimiento estuvo relacionado con la expansión de las redes GSM, la variedad de modelos y una oferta que abarcaba distintos segmentos de precios.
La marca se hizo conocida por fabricar dispositivos resistentes, con baterías de larga duración y funciones sencillas de utilizar. Modelos como el Nokia 3210 y el Nokia 3310 alcanzaron una amplia popularidad y se convirtieron en referencias de una época en la que el celular comenzaba a ser un objeto cotidiano.
El dominio de Nokia continuó durante la década siguiente. En su momento de mayor participación, alrededor de 2007, la compañía concentró cerca del 40% del mercado mundial de teléfonos móviles, según estimaciones históricas de la industria. Esa posición la convirtió en el fabricante dominante justo cuando el sector estaba a punto de experimentar una transformación profunda.
Ericsson y los otros fabricantes que competían por el mercado
La sueca Ericsson fue otro de los nombres importantes de la telefonía móvil. Además de fabricar teléfonos, desarrolló infraestructura de telecomunicaciones y participó en la evolución de los estándares digitales que permitieron conectar a millones de usuarios.
Su trayectoria estuvo vinculada con GSM, una tecnología que facilitó la expansión de las redes móviles en Europa y otros mercados. En 2001, Ericsson y Sony formaron una empresa conjunta para fabricar teléfonos bajo la marca Sony Ericsson, que posteriormente ganó notoriedad con equipos orientados a la música y la fotografía.
El mercado también contaba con otros fabricantes relevantes. Siemens, de Alemania, destacó con productos como el S10, presentado en 1998 y reconocido por incorporar una pantalla a color. Panasonic y Alcatel también comercializaron teléfonos populares en distintos mercados, mientras que empresas como Samsung comenzaron a ampliar su presencia internacional.
La llegada del iPhone cambió las reglas
El lanzamiento del iPhone en 2007 modificó las expectativas sobre lo que podía hacer un teléfono. La pantalla multitáctil, la navegación por internet y la integración de aplicaciones impulsaron un modelo de negocio distinto al de los celulares tradicionales. La expansión de Android, presentado en 2008, aceleró esa transformación.
Nokia y Motorola tuvieron dificultades para adaptarse al nuevo escenario, mientras que Ericsson dejó de competir como fabricante independiente de celulares tras la evolución de su alianza con Sony. Samsung, por su parte, consiguió consolidar su posición con una amplia gama de teléfonos inteligentes.
Así, las empresas que habían definido la primera etapa de la telefonía móvil cedieron protagonismo a nuevos líderes. El cambio no fue inmediato ni respondió a una sola causa, pero mostró que, en tecnología, la experiencia acumulada no garantiza el liderazgo cuando las reglas del mercado cambian.

articles.title: Nvidia RTX Spark AI laptops hit pre-order — here are 3 I recommend
articles.text:
Pre-orders open for Nvidia’s RTX Spark workstations — and these are the 3 local AI laptops I’d buy for business
The most expensive configurations will set you back $7,000
Running AI locally is becoming an increasingly attractive option for small businesses that want more control over their data, predictable computing costs, and the ability to experiment with the technology without relying on cloud services. Nvidia's new RTX Spark laptops could make that easier, combining powerful processors, Blackwell graphics, and large amounts of unified memory in portable computers.
Pre-orders are now open, with the first models scheduled to ship on October 16. Prices start at $2,599.99, although more powerful configurations can cost considerably more.
There are models from all of the major manufacturers, including Microsoft, Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell, but for small businesses looking to run local AI models and develop applications, these are the three laptops I'd recommend.
My top 3 RTX Spark laptops for AI
Microsoft's 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra is one of the least expensive ways to get Nvidia's new RTX Spark hardware, with pre-orders starting at $2,599.99. The Surface Laptop Ultra is available with up to 128GB of unified memory.
I'd consider the entry-level model for a small business exploring internal AI assistants, document analysis, coding tools, and other relatively modest local AI applications.
HP's 16-inch laptop features a 3K OLED touchscreen and can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory.
HP's 24GB and 32GB versions use a smaller RTX Spark chip, while configurations with 48GB or more feature the full 20-core Grace CPU and 6,144-core Blackwell GPU.
For more demanding AI projects, I'd look closely at the 64GB or 128GB versions rather than just choosing the cheapest model.
The Asus ProArt P16 is a good choice for small businesses that combine AI development with creative work. It features a 16-inch display and offers up to 128GB of unified memory and 2TB of storage.
Why RTX Spark makes sense for small businesses
One of the main attractions of running AI locally is the ability to process information without sending every request to a cloud-based service, which could be handy for anyone working with confidential documents, proprietary code, customer information, internal research, and so on.
Nvidia's RTX Spark platform combines a Grace CPU with a Blackwell GPU, with unified memory configurations ranging from 24GB to 128GB. The full chip includes a 20-core CPU and 6,144-core GPU, while the lower-end version has an 18-core CPU and 5,120-core GPU.
The memory configuration is particularly important for local AI, since larger models can require much more memory than conventional business applications. That said, memory capacity alone doesn't guarantee performance. The size of the model, its precision, software compatibility, and available GPU resources all affect how well it runs.
For a small business taking its first steps into local AI, I'd start by looking at the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, which is one of the more affordable RTX Spark options.
If your business needs more memory for larger models, HP's OmniBook Ultra 16 is worth considering, particularly in its 64GB and 128GB configurations.
For companies combining AI development with video editing, image generation, and other creative applications, the Asus ProArt P16 offers another option.
The new RTX Spark laptops are scheduled to start shipping on October 16, with pre-orders available through Best Buy and other manufacturers.

Wayne Williams is a freelancer writing news for TechRadar Pro. He has been writing about computers, technology, and the web for 30 years. In that time he wrote for most of the UK’s PC magazines, and launched, edited and published a number of them too.

articles.title: P7 DarkSword iOS Exploit Kit Adds Crypto Wallet Data Theft and Remote Commands
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unseen variant of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit called P7 DarkSword.
"Compared with the variants we usually observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and adds two way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said in a new report published Thursday.
The name "P7" is a nod to the threat actor's use of the "p7_" variable prefix in changes made to the original DarkSword code.
DarkSword was first publicly documented earlier this March by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), iVerify, and Lookout, detailing its ability to target iPhones running iOS versions between iOS 18.4 and 18.7. The kit was detected in the wild in November 2025.
The toolkit is engineered to chain multiple iOS vulnerabilities to escape the browser sandbox, escalate to kernel privileges, and inject the main payload into SpringBoard, the iOS process that handles app launches and the home screen. The exploit chain is assessed to be a commercial product that somehow landed in a second-hand market, from where it was acquired by financially motivated operators and other threat actors since late 2025.
The exploit kit has been put to use in attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine by multiple threat actors, including a Turkish commercial surveillance vendor named PARS Defense via a fake Snapchat-themed website and a Russia-aligned threat actor called Star Blizzard (aka COLDRIVER) using fake invitation lures.
In August 2026, attack surface management platform Censys detailed a campaign mounted by an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor that involved targeting Apple iOS devices with the exploit kit, in addition to serving an Apple ID decoy sign-in page.
As recently as last month, iVerify said it observed "multiple unsuccessful, likely LLM-assisted attempts to update the framework to support iOS 26.x," fueled by the leak of the exploit kit shortly after its public disclosure. These variants, the mobile security company added, are focused on stability, stealth, and quality of stolen data.
P7 DarkSword represents an evolution in these aspects by eliminating debug logging over HTTP requests and syslog and using browser localStorage to prevent re-exploitation. Unlike prior variants that copied and exfiltrated the keychain database to process on the attacker's infrastructure, the new version extracts keychain data into JSON on the phone prior to exfiltration.
"The implant is injected into the SpringBoard process, which handles all communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said.
The latest iteration is equipped to poll for commands every 15 seconds, send a "heartbeat" message, send a list of installed applications, and transmit iCloud Keychain information and data from applications like Apple Notes, Photos, and cryptocurrency wallets.
The response to the periodic tasking poll contains commands to be executed on the victim's phone. This includes -
- execute_command, to execute operating system commands like ls, dir, cat, mkdir, rm, echo, ps, memdump, ipconfig, netstat, and whoami, among others
- ls, to list directory contents
- download, to read a file from the device and upload it to the C2 server
- photos, to upload photo files from "/var/mobile/Media/DCIM"
- apps, to enumerate app containers and extract bundle IDs
- exec, to execute arbitrary JavaScript directly inside the implant runtime
- file_upload, to recursively scan one or more paths and upload matching files
- basic_info, to send device metadata to the C2 server
- disk_scan, to recursively scan the filesystem starting from "/,", record metadata for files, directories, and symlinks, and upload the information in the form of a report
- ios_app_data, to find app sandbox and app-group containers for requested bundle IDs and upload selected app files
- wallet_scan, to scan for installed wallet apps
- wallet_extract, to extract wallet-related data for imToken wallet app
- memo_scan, to upload Apple Notes databases
- photo_scan, to upload photos from Apple Photos
- sleep, to modify the beacon polling interval
- exit, to halt the beacon loop and stop the implant
The disclosure comes as Censys said it identified open directories on five hosts carrying components related to DarkSword and Coruna, another iOS exploit kit uncovered this year as weaponized in attacks aimed at iPhone models running iOS versions between 13.0 and 17.2.1.
"Coruna is the companion payload kit the same ecosystem distributes," Censys said. "Its stages run inside the victim's browser session after DarkSword's exploit stages land, and its wallet-harvesting modules steal crypto recovery phrases, balances, and keystore data from iOS apps. Operators run DarkSword and Coruna together against their own C2 infrastructure."
The five hosts are listed below -
- 43.134.165[.]205, which serves DS-Fusion v1.0 (aka DarkSword Fusion), a combined package that includes both DarkSword and Coruna in a single bundle
- 166.88.95[.]90, which operates as a C2 server of the implant and has recorded two real Chinese iOS devices (183.154.173[.]30 and 182.239.114[.]223) polling a beacon page every three seconds for several hours on September 6, 2026
- 23.148.212[.]237, which serves as an analysis workspace that shows the operator developing exploit chains for iOS 26 (such as for CVE-2026-31001), which are not covered by DarkSword or Coruna.
- 47.102.192[.]23, which serves as a staging host for the Coruna kit
- 156.239.230[.]120, which exposes the entire C2 platform and has been observed polling a device on September 15, 2026
An analysis of the production server's exploit registry has revealed that the DarkSword exploit kit comprises two CVE identifiers not previously documented -
- CVE-2025-24201, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the WebKit engine that could allow an attacker to break out of the Web Content sandbox (Fixed in iOS 18.3.2 and iPadOS 18.3.2)
- CVE-2025-31200, a memory corruption vulnerability in the Core Audio framework that allows code execution when processing an audio stream in a maliciously crafted media file (Fixed in iOS 18.4.1 and iPadOS 18.4.1)
It's suspected that the open-directory cluster and the 156.239.230[.]120 platform are run by a Chinese-speaking threat actor with an aim to conduct cryptocurrency wallet theft. That said, exactly who is behind is unknown.
"The platform runs a Chinese-speaking exploitation-as-a-service operation," Censys researcher Aidan Holland said. "The admin panel exposes an agent/reseller model, and a copy of the production server recovered 11 victim recovery phrases, 179 device loot directories, and a 75-account control-plane roster."
Censys said it also detected a separate China-based operator running the same kit in the wild against its own C2 server at "66ds[.]lol," while including a new cryptocurrency wallet target (BitKeep) not present in the open-directory set. The findings once again highlight the proliferation of the kit among financially motivated actors.
"The operator behind it sits on Tencent and Shenyang hosting, tied to the operator through a unique self-signed certificate authority," Censys said.
