articles.title: Tesla renames 'Full Self-Driving' to 'Tesla Assisted Driving' in Europe | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”
It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company.
Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.
Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.”
In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!”
Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.
Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.
But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.

articles.title: Mistral’s new Large 4 trails some Chinese open models in independent tests
articles.text:
Independent tests rank Mistral’s new trillion-parameter Large 4 the best AI model outside the U.S. and China — but Chinese open-weights still overcome Europe's best efforts
Its best result is a cyber test, but it falls behind on the index.
Mistral launched its trillion-parameter Large 4 (ML4) model this week, saying it “pushes the frontier of open-weight performance.” Artificial Analysis (AA), an independent AI benchmarking firm, ranked Mistral's Large 4 as the best model available from outside the U.S. and China in its index. The mixture-of-experts model, trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs, scored its personal best in AA’s CyberGym-E2E-AA end-to-end cybersecurity measure, although several Chinese open models beat it overall.
ML4 scored 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, which AA says makes it the “most intelligent model from outside the US and China." At least five Chinese open models scored higher on the index: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) at 39, GLM-5.3-Flash at 42, Kimi K3 (max) at 44, GLM-5.3 (max) at 45, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 46. While MiMo-V2.6-Pro is comparable in total size to ML4, GLM-5.3-Flash is about one-third the size at 320B parameters total and 18B versus ML4’s 49B–52B active. Unlike the rest, ML4 isn’t open yet: Mistral says its weights are due “by the end of the month.”
| Mistral Large 4 vs. Chinese open models on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index (Oct. 6) |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model | Index score | Parameters, total / active | Cost per index task | Weights | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Pro | 46 | 1.0T / 42B | $0.13 | Open | 
| Z.ai GLM-5.3 (max) | 45 | 753B / 40B | $2.01 | Open | 
| Moonshot Kimi K3 (max) | 44 | 2.8T / 104B | $2.00 | Open | 
| Z.ai GLM-5.3-Flash | 42 | 320B / 18B | $0.25 | Open | 
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) | 39 | 552B / 16B | $0.27 | Open | 
| Mistral Large 4 Preview | 38 | 1.05T / 49B–52B | $1.13 ($0.57 at launch pricing) | Due by end of October | 
| DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 (max) | 36 | 1.6T / 49B | $0.67 | Open | 
Cost is a different story. ML4 comes in at $1.13 per AA task at list price, or $0.57 at the 50% discounted launch price. This compares to $0.13 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and $0.25 for GLM-5.3-Flash. Although comparatively expensive, ML4 scored what AA calls its “strongest result” and Mistral calls “the highest of any model” with an 81.7% score on CyberGym-E2E-AA, compared with GLM-5.3-Flash’s 74%, from a model whose post-training run Mistral claims is “still in flight.”
While the score is impressive, it is only one of three tests in the Cyber Index; ML4 only scores 16% in DeepsecBench-AA and 51% in CWE-Bench-AA. However, AA’s projection is that, once the weights ship, it “will rank among the top three open weights models on the Cyber Index.” This leaves the door open for ML4 to apply to narrower tasks.
| Mistral Large 4 on Artificial Analysis' Cyber Index and its three tests (Oct. 6) |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model | Cyber Index | CWE-Bench-AA | DeepsecBench-AA | CyberGym-E2E-AA | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grok 4.7 (xhigh) | 56 | 68% | 27% | 74% | 
| Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Pro | 56 | 63% | 26% | 79% | 
| OpenAI GPT-6 Luna (max) | 53 | 57% | 24% | 78% | 
| Z.ai GLM-5.3-Flash | 50 | 56% | 20% | 74% | 
| Mistral Large 4 Preview | 50 | 51% | 16% | 82% | 
| OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (max; declined some tasks) | 33 | 63% | 37% | 0% | 
| Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback; declined some tasks) | 29 | 58% | 27% | 1% | 
Mistral bets on this, saying ML4 is “state-of-the-art among open models” on enterprise workloads such as “cybersecurity, finance and law,” and that in visual grounding, where its 1.6B-parameter vision encoder comes in, it can go as far as “surpassing even frontier closed models.” On AA’s Cyber Index, Mistral says, ML4 ranks “among the top five models globally,” and it solves 93% of Cybench, a set of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions.
CEO Arthur Mensch went further in Abu Dhabi, saying the model is “above the Chinese models on certain aspects, including cyber,” Reuters reported. Mistral’s other figures include DeepSWE v1.1 at 61.7%, Coding Agent Index at 49.8%, AutomationBench at 59.9%, and Dense 200 at 42%; AA’s own chart puts ML4 at 27% on Terminal-Bench 4.0.
ML4 does, in fact, beat OpenAI’s closed GPT-6 Luna (max) on CyberGym-E2E-AA, but Luna matches ML4’s 38 on AA’s index at about one-sixteenth of the cost per task ($0.07). Mistral says frontier models such as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra “score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task,” and AA’s chart marks both as declining some tasks on safety grounds.
Outside of that test, Mistral says ML4 also beats DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max on the Coding Agent Index; per AA, it is cheaper than the latter. Overall, AA’s index-vs.-cost chart puts ML4 below the Pareto line and just outside the “Most attractive quadrant.”
The cost comes from needing 200 million output tokens to run AA’s index, against a median of 81 million. As for speed, ML4 generated 116.1 tokens per second, with 1.46 seconds to the first token. This puts ML4 at about 33% faster than its tier median and 2.6x faster to the first token. AA’s speed is measured on Mistral’s own API, which Mistral says runs on the same hardware the model used for training.
ML4 was “trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe,” the company said. This is up from 3,000 Nvidia H200s used to train Large 3, released last year, which was smaller at 675B total parameters with 41B active. The training occurred over “roughly two months,” as reported by VentureBeat.
Mistral raised a €3 billion Series D in what the company calls “the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company” in its post. Mistral Compute has planned for 18,000 Grace Blackwell chips, as announced with Nvidia last year. Mistral says it is “significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters,” and that ML4 will become the base for “a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models.” The model’s open weights, once released, will be able to run on a private cloud or on-premises.
The weights, architecture details, and additional benchmarks are expected before the end of October. Artificial Analysis lists the preview as proprietary until the weights arrive. Once it does, the model may be re-scored, and Mistral’s claims will be held to task. For the first two weeks following release, ML4 can be used via API at a discounted rate.
While European models still have a lot to prove, based on previous performance and ML4’s showing with an 8-point gap versus a similar-size Chinese model that’s also a lot less expensive, Mistral has demonstrated resolve and produced a model with, at least, niche application, as the basis to eventually close that gap.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: La nueva búsqueda de Windows 11 cambia por completo la forma de usar tu PC
articles.text:
Tras años de ser el hazmerreír del sistema operativo, la búsqueda de Windows 11 está lista para recibir un cambio definitivo. Microsoft comenzó a abrir el acceso al nuevo sistema de búsqueda que debutará en los próximos meses para todos los usuarios. La versión más reciente ya está disponible y resuelve muchos de los problemas que ha acarreado esta función durante años.
Microsoft avisó que los usuarios del programa Insider ya pueden probar la búsqueda renovada de Windows 11. De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, esta versión se ha reconstruido sobre WinUI 3 y las pruebas iniciales muestran mejoras notables en rendimiento y consumo de memoria. Los usuarios ya no tendrán que lidiar con la búsqueda lenta y cargada de resultados que no le interesan a nadie.
Ahora, cuando escribas en el recuadro de búsqueda, la interfaz mostrará un listado de archivos, carpetas o funciones relacionadas que se actualizan a medida que tecleas. La nueva búsqueda de Windows 11 incluye vistas previas de documentos de Word, presentaciones de PowerPoint o imágenes. También existen tarjetas con elementos visuales cuando preguntes por el clima o por alguna atracción mundial, por ejemplo: "¿Qué altura tiene la Torre Eiffel?".
Lo mejor que le ha pasado a Windows 11 en años
Un agregado interesante son las acciones en línea, que te permiten completar tareas sin tener que abrir otra aplicación. Puedes escribir frases como "cambiar a modo oscuro", "enciende el Bluetooth" o "activa la luz nocturna" para ejecutar la acción sin tener que entrar al menú Configuración. También es posible silenciar el sonido, reducir el brillo de la pantalla, minimizar todas tus ventanas o reordenarlas en el escritorio con una instrucción de texto.
Microsoft mencionó que están comenzando con las acciones más usadas y seguirán añadiendo otras conforme pase el tiempo. La tecnológica confirmó que la nueva búsqueda de Windows 11 también permitirá realizar acciones en el móvil, siempre y cuando lo tengas conectado a través de la aplicación Enlace a Windows.
“Esta nueva experiencia de búsqueda de Windows está diseñada para la velocidad”, dijo la compañía. “Está construido sobre WinUI 3 y forma parte de nuestra inversión más amplia en modernizar nuestras experiencias principales de Windows”.
Cómo activar el nuevo buscador de Windows antes de que llegue a todos
Si quieres probar la nueva experiencia de búsqueda en Windows, lo primero que necesitas es inscribirte en el programa Insider. Esta característica solo está disponible en la compilación 26340.9616 del canal Experimental o en la 28120.3181 si tienes la versión 26H1. Para acceder a ella debes ir a Configuración > Windows Update > Windows Insider > Funciones experimentales (o feature flags), en donde encontrarás "Nueva Experiencia de Búsqueda de Windows". Es probable que el interruptor no aparezca, ya que el despliegue es gradual.
Un punto en contra es que la búsqueda solo se puede usar en inglés en su versión inicial. Microsoft la actualizará al español y otros idiomas en versiones posteriores, pero si quieres usarla ahora, tendrás que acostumbrarte a cambiar los ajustes del ordenador en inglés ("switch to dark mode", "minimize all my windows", etc.).
Esta actualización también incluye otras mejoras y funciones, como un widget que muestra el porcentaje de batería de tu portátil y dispositivos conectados. El Administrador de Tareas amplía la agrupación de procesos para que las aplicaciones combinen procesos en segundo plano separados en una categoría unificada. También se actualiza la experiencia del PIN de seguridad, vista previa de fuentes en el Explorador de archivos y más.

articles.title: Rwanda’s Entelon is building AI for organisations still running on paper - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Rwandan startup Entelon is building AI products and custom systems that take over the slow, manual work many African organisations still depend on.
Founded in Kigali in August 2025 by Alain Barsime Shema and Don Durkheim, Entelon has developed a suite of products spanning health, research, education, customer experience and travel, alongside custom AI systems built for individual organisations.
“Entelon makes AI work for African businesses and institutions. We build AI products and custom AI systems that take over the slow, manual work organisations still run on, like paper forms, hand grading, unanalysed phone calls, and data entry, so their people can focus on decisions,” Durkheim, the startup’s co-founder and president, told Disrupt Africa.
“We build for how organisations here actually operate: the languages their people speak, the tools they already use, and the infrastructure they have.”
The startup’s products include Mamora AI, a community wellbeing platform built for HDI Rwanda, through which residents report symptoms and conditions in their community to help detect disease outbreaks early. Its research product, Visko, turns existing questionnaires into live digital surveys.
“Upload any questionnaire, whether a PDF, Word file or a photo of paper, and AI turns it into a live digital survey. During interviews, it transcribes answers and automatically fills the form. The interview ends, and the clean dataset already exists,” Durkheim said.
Entelon’s education product, Klok AI, reads students’ handwritten exam answers and suggests marks step by step, while the teacher keeps control of every grade. Phibram, meanwhile, listens to every call in a call centre and turns conversations into a continuous picture of service quality, while HeyRwanda is a companion app for visitors covering discovery, navigation, voice translation and payments.
“Alongside the products, we build custom systems for organisations: voice agents, AI agents tailored to each team, workflow automation and data analysis,” said Durkheim.
The startup also conducts its own research where existing tools fall short.
“We trained our own text-to-speech model on roughly 500 hours of Kinyarwanda audio and are co-developing a Kinyarwanda LLM, so our voice products work for people global tools don’t serve,” Durkheim said.
He said Entelon was addressing a gap left by global AI products.
“AI tools are built for organisations that already run on clean digital systems. Most African institutions don’t. They run on paper forms, manual data entry, phone calls, and spreadsheets, often across several languages,” he said. “Global AI products assume a starting point these organisations haven’t reached, so they never get adopted.”
“We start from where organisations actually are. Visko accepts the questionnaire a research team already has, even a photo of a paper form. Klok AI works with handwritten exams. Phibram works with the calls a bank or hotline already receives.”
Durkheim said demand was concrete.
“Rwanda’s central bank requires regulated financial institutions to run customer satisfaction surveys, and banks need a way to hear what customers actually say on the phone. Research organisations spend weeks building digital forms by hand before collecting a single answer. Teachers spend nights grading by hand,” he said.
The startup is bootstrapped, funded by revenue from custom AI work and product contracts, and is already seeing traction.
“Across our products and custom systems, Entelon handles over 1,000 AI interactions a day,” said Durkheim. “Mamora AI is our clearest signal. It reaches over 500 users through more than 30 community health workers, and they have filed over 1,200 reports since launch.”
Visko is in commercial use by research organisations and NGOs for market research, while Klok AI and Phibram are in conversations with institutional buyers in education and banking.
Entelon makes money from two revenue streams.
“Organisations pay us to build and maintain voice agents, AI agents, and automation for their operations,” Durkheim said. “Visko charges per questionnaire, per project, or through enterprise contracts. Phibram is billed on usage credits.”
The startup is currently focused on its home market, but has its eye on expansion.
“Rwanda is the right place to start: small enough to reach decision-makers directly, and digital-first enough that institutions are actively looking for better tools,” said Durkheim.
“Expansion follows the products. Visko, Phibram and Klok AI solve problems that exist in research organisations, banks and schools across Africa. East Africa is next, with each product entering where we can land a first anchor customer.”

articles.title: 3,10 % brut pendant un an : combien rapporte réellement le livret boosté Bfor+ de BforBank ?
articles.text:
Un apport pour une maison, une nouvelle voiture ou les études supérieures d’un enfant : l’épargne est un excellent moyen de donner vie à ses projets, ou simplement de se constituer un matelas de sécurité en cas de coup dur.
Reste que le temps que l’épargne soit suffisante ou que l’opportunité se présente, il n’est pas évident de choisir où placer son argent. Entre les plafonds, la faible rémunération et le problème de la disponibilité, trouver le placement le plus pertinent pour faire fructifier ses économies demande du temps et des connaissances.
C’est pour faciliter cette démarche que BforBank, la banque en ligne du groupe Crédit Agricole, a conçu le livret d’épargne Bfor+. Jusqu’au 2 novembre, ce livret profite d’une offre de bienvenue avec un taux brut garanti de 3,10 % pendant un an, pour un dépôt maximum de 200 000 €. Rémunératrice et protégée jusqu’à 100 000 € par la garantie des dépôts : la somme versée travaille tout en restant toujours à portée.
3,10 % brut pendant 12 mois : ce que la durée change
Le gros avantage de cette offre Bfor+ tient à la durée de son taux boosté : les 3,10 % brut sont garantis pendant 12 mois pleins. Face à une offre comparable, par exemple boostée à 5 % durant 3 mois avant de passer à un taux plus classique de 1,20 %, le livret Bfor+ rapporte sur un an 44,2 % d’intérêts bruts en plus :
| Taux première année | 5 % pendant 3 mois, puis 1,20 % | 3,10 % pendant 12 mois | Avantage de l’offre à 3,10 % | 
| Taux moyen annuel brut | 2,15 % | 3,10 % | +0,95 point | 
| Intérêts bruts pour 10 000 € placés | 215 € | 310 € | +95 € (+44,2 %) | 
Le plafond total du livret est fixé à 4 millions d’euros, mais le taux boosté de 3,10 % brut ne s’applique qu’aux premiers 200 000 € placés sur le compte. Une fois ce montant dépassé, la rémunération du surplus revient au taux annuel standard brut, actuellement fixé à 1,20 % par BforBank et susceptible d’évoluer.
Tous les intérêts sont soumis, par défaut, aux prélèvements fiscaux et sociaux. Il s’agit du prélèvement forfaitaire unique (PFU), aussi appelé flat tax, fixé à 31,4 % en 2026 : 12,8 % d’impôt sur le revenu et 18,6 % de prélèvements sociaux. Même après impôts, soit environ 2,13 % net, le livret Bfor+ rapporte donc davantage pendant un an que le Livret A, rémunéré à 1,7 % net depuis le 1ᵉʳ août 2026. Ce dernier est exonéré d’impôts, mais ses versements sont plafonnés à 22 950 €.
À taux et fiscalité constants, pour le cas d’un placement de 10 000 € rémunérés pendant une année complète, le livret Bfor+ offre environ 212,66 € d’intérêts nets, contre 170 € pour le Livret A.
Une épargne toujours disponible en cas de besoin
La rémunération n’est pas le seul avantage de ce livret Bfor+. Contrairement à d’autres types de placements, tout ou partie de la somme placée reste disponible à tout moment en cas de besoin. Si le projet se concrétise plus tôt que prévu ou change de cap, versements et retraits se font gratuitement par virement.
BforBank n’applique d’ailleurs aucun frais pour l’ouverture, la gestion ou la fermeture du compte. Le livret doit conserver un solde minimal de 10 €, qui correspond également au montant minimal de chaque versement ou retrait pour le livret d’épargne Bfor+. Les intérêts sont calculés par quinzaine et versés sur le livret le 31 décembre de chaque année, ou au moment de la clôture.
En cas de défaillance de BforBank, les dépôts éligibles sont couverts par le Fonds de garantie des dépôts et de résolution (FGDR), jusqu’à 100 000 € par personne et par établissement. Ce plafond englobe le livret Bfor+ et les autres dépôts éligibles du client chez BforBank, notamment son compte courant.
Comment bénéficier de l’offre Bfor+ ?
Ce taux boosté à 3,10 % pendant un an est réservé à la première ouverture d’un compte sur livret Bfor+ entre le 1ᵉʳ octobre et le 2 novembre 2026 inclus, par une personne physique majeure capable. Le livret est réservé à un usage non professionnel et sert à financer des projets personnels, comme un mariage, l’achat d’un bien ou une épargne de précaution.
Pour en profiter, tout se passe dans l’application BforBank : ouverture d’un compte courant (pièce d’identité et justificatif de domicile à l’appui), puis du livret Bfor+, activé par un premier versement de 10 € minimum. La demande doit être faite au plus tard le 2 novembre 2026 pour obtenir le taux de 3,10 %.
L’offre est limitée à un livret par détenteur, même s’il est possible d’en ouvrir plusieurs à taux standard pour différencier plusieurs projets. Le délai de rétractation est de 14 jours, ce qui laisse le temps de découvrir la facilité d’usage de l’application BforBank, qui permet de gérer ses comptes – compte courant, livrets, etc. – et de contacter le service client par chat ou téléphone.
Le livret Bfor+ a reçu le Label Excellence Épargne 2026, décerné par les Dossiers de l’Épargne, après une première distinction en 2024. Dans la catégorie des livrets d’épargne, une cinquantaine de contrats sont étudiés : l’évaluation repose à 90 % sur les taux standards et à 10 % sur la souplesse du produit, notamment l’accessibilité des fonds et la facilité d’utilisation. Cette distinction porte donc sur les caractéristiques du livret, au-delà de son offre de bienvenue.

articles.title: Le Roborock F25 Steam utilise la vapeur pour décoller les taches tenaces
articles.text:
On connaît les nettoyeurs vapeur, destinés à l’entretien des moquettes et des textiles d’ameublement. Mais quand la vapeur s’invite au sein d’un aspirateur-balai laveur, son utilité peut s’avérer un peu plus floue. La marque Roborock donne une réponse très concrète avec son F25 Steam, l’une des nouveautés de sa gamme d’aspirateurs-laveurs.
L’utilité d’un aspirateur-balai qui passe la serpillière en même temps qu’il aspire est plutôt évidente : cela permet de réaliser deux tâches ménagères en une, sans trop se fatiguer et en gagnant du temps. L’autre avantage est de pouvoir aussi bien ramasser de la poussière et des débris solides que des dégâts liquides, comme une boisson ou un pot de sauce renversé.
Là où la situation peut se compliquer, c’est quand la tache a eu le temps de sécher, ou quand elle est huileuse. Dans ce cas, utiliser un aspirateur-laveur peut ne pas suffire à en venir à bout. La solution la plus adaptée est d’utiliser soit de l’eau chaude, soit de la vapeur pour vraiment tout nettoyer.
La vapeur, une alliée face aux taches les plus tenaces
Roborock fait partie des constructeurs qui cherchent à innover constamment avec leurs appareils. Depuis deux ans, la marque étoffe sa gamme d’aspirateurs-balais laveurs F25 avec des nouveautés régulières, destinées à répondre à des besoins de plus en plus pointus. Et avec le Roborock F25 Steam, actuellement disponible pour 420 € au lieu de 589 € sur son site, elle associe le pouvoir de la vapeur à la combinaison, déjà éprouvée, du lavage et de l’aspiration.
Le Roborock F25 Steam embarque donc une technologie qui porte le nom de VaporFlow. Lorsqu’elle est activée, l’appareil chauffe l’eau jusqu’à 180°C dans son module interne, puis diffuse la vapeur sur toute la largeur de nettoyage. Roborock précise que sa température atteint environ 99°C à la sortie de la buse avant de redescendre sous les 70°C lorsqu’elle entre en contact avec le sol. Cela permet d’utiliser la vapeur pour décoller efficacement les saletés incrustées, sans prendre le risque d’abîmer votre revêtement, y compris s’il est en bois massif.
Le mode vapeur est prêt à fonctionner en une soixantaine de secondes et son autonomie est d’environ 20 minutes. Une durée plus réduite que lorsque VaporFlow est désactivée, mais qui s’avère suffisante pour vous attaquer quotidiennement aux taches les plus grasses et tenaces. On peut également noter que Roborock revendique une élimination des bactéries et allergènes de l’ordre de 99,9 % : de quoi associer concrètement la propreté à l’hygiène des sols.
Le Roborock F25 Steam, bien plus qu’un nettoyeur vapeur
La vapeur peut donc s’avérer redoutable face aux sols sales. Mais si le Roborock F25 Steam ne proposait que ce mode, ce ne serait pas un aspirateur-laveur de nouvelle génération ! En réalité, l’appareil associe la fonction VaporFlow à un rouleau-brosse qui réalise 450 rotations par minute et exerce une pression de nettoyage de 33 N. Ce dispositif frotte le sol afin de détacher les résidus, tandis que la puissance d’aspiration de 25 000 Pa récupère les déchets secs, les liquides et l’eau sale.
La conception FlatReach du F25 Steam lui permet, quant à elle, de s’incliner complètement afin de passer sous les meubles bas. En d’autres termes, même lorsqu’il n’exploite pas le potentiel de la vapeur, cet aspirateur-balai laveur se montre tout de même efficace pour nettoyer partout.
Enfin, une fois le sol nettoyé, le Roborock F25 Steam retrouve sa station de chargement. Celle-ci lance un cycle d’autonettoyage à la vapeur destiné à retirer les saletés présentes dans le rouleau. Un autoséchage à l’air chaud à 95°C prend ensuite le relais afin de ne pas laisser l’occasion aux mauvaises odeurs de s’installer.
Roborock F25 : des aspirateurs-laveurs pour tous les foyers
Roborock cherche à proposer des aspirateurs-laveurs les plus complets et polyvalents possibles. Cependant, la marque le sait : la vapeur n’est pas indispensable dans tous les foyers. C’est pourquoi la gamme F25 comprend des modèles aux positionnements différents, qui vont du F25, le plus simple pour nettoyer et aspirer, au F25 Ultra, qui associe la vapeur à un nettoyage des sols à l’eau chaude.
Entre ces deux modèles, on trouve une déclinaison d’une dizaine de références, dont le Roborock F25 Steam constitue une solution complète et équilibrée. Si vous désirez découvrir le reste de la gamme F25, elle vous attend sur le site de Roborock.

articles.title: Ein KI-Film bei den Oscars? Dieser generierte Animationsfilm will sich die Auszeichnung holen
articles.text:
Ein KI-Film bei den Oscars? Dieser generierte Animationsfilm will sich die Auszeichnung holen
Eigentlich sollte der Film Gods Don’t Give Gifts im Oktober 2026 in Kinos in den USA erscheinen. Jetzt haben die Verantwortlichen dahinter eine Verschiebung angekündigt. Der KI-generierte Film soll erst am 4. Dezember 2026 auf Leinwänden gezeigt werden. Der Grund: Damit bewegt sich Gods Don’t Give Gifts näher an der Award-Season für Filme und der Bekanntgabe der Oscar-Nominierten für 2027.
Dieser KI-Film will zu den Oscars
Passend zu der Ankündigung der Verschiebung und den Oscar-Ambitionen haben Gossip Goblin und Fable, die beiden verantwortlichen Studios hinter dem KI‑generierten Film, einen Trailer veröffentlicht. Bei Gods Don’t Give Gifts handelt es sich um eine Anthologie, bestehend aus vier animierten Kurzfilmen. Allesamt spielen im Universum von Gossip Goblin, dem Youtube-Kanal von Zack London. Der studierte Bildhauer und Anthropologe veröffentlicht auf dem Kanal seit mehr als zwei Jahren kurze KI-generierte Clips einer dystopischen Welt und konnte damit mehr als 1,5 Millionen Abonnent:innen gewinnen.
In Gods Don’t Give Gifts dreht sich alles um den „zweiten Kreislauf der Menschheit“, wobei es im Gossip-Goblin-Universum insgesamt 13 solcher Kreisläufe gibt, wie Variety berichtet. In der gezeigten Welt ist der Tod nicht mehr das Ende. Körper können ersetzt und mit bestehenden Erinnerungen ausgestattet werden. Auf dem Planeten Niiro Cradle ist „Bewusstsein deshalb zum primären Objekt der Kontrolle, des Handels und der Modifikation“ geworden.
Wie es auf der Webseite zum KI-Film heißt, „upgradet sich die Menschheit Stück für Stück“, um sich von der „Schwäche des Fleisches“ zu befreien. Doch der Übergang verläuft alles andere als problemlos: „In Hinterhof-Shops werden Jailbreak-Modifikationen für Körper angeboten, Priester beteuern den Verlust der menschlichen Seele. Und Schuldner werden in Tierkörper verfrachtet.“
Wie stehen die Chancen für den KI-Film?
Mit dem Release des KI-Films soll auch eine besondere Kampagne starten. Laut Fable und Gossip Goblin soll es spezielle Vorstellungen für Mitglieder der Oscar-Academy geben. Zudem werden auch weitere Kritiker:innen vor dem eigentlichen Kinostart eingeladen, um sich ein Bild von Gods Don’t Give Gifts machen zu können. Im Anschluss soll der Film als Anwärter auf den Oscar für den besten animierten Film angemeldet werden.
Edward Saatchi, CEO von Fable, sagte dazu: „Fünf Jahre lang war die Frage: Wann wird ein KI-Film einen Oscar gewinnen? Gods Don’t Give Gifts ist der erste Film, der eine Chance auf eine Nominierung hat, und danach kann alles passieren.“ Wie auf der Website von Gossip Goblin betont wird, werden die Geschichten des Studios von Menschen erdacht und geschrieben. KI sei nur ein „Multiplikator“.
Aktuell hat die Academy nur ein Verbot für KI-Inhalte verhängt, wenn Schauspieler:innen oder Drehbücher KI-generiert werden. Grundsätzlich könnte Gods Don’t Give Gifts also zugelassen werden. Ob das bei möglichen Anwärtern auf den Animations-Oscar wie Toy Story 5 (Pixar) sowie den von Kritiker:innen und Zuschauer:innen gefeierten Hoppers (Pixar) oder Die vergessene Insel (Dreamworks Animation) realistisch ist, bleibt bis zu den ersten Kritiken des KI-Films abzuwarten.

articles.title: Ce drone de frappe français revendique 2 000 km de portée sans GPS, et un premier pays s'y intéresse déjà
articles.text:
Entre le Shahed, bon marché mais facile à abattre, et le Tomahawk, redoutable mais cher et rare, Harmattan AI veut se faire une place. La start-up française a présenté mardi 6 octobre IRIFI, un drone de frappe qui revendique 2 000 kilomètres de portée et se passe de GPS.
Un drone pour la frappe en profondeur
Harmattan AI le destine aux missions loin du front contre des cibles comme des dépôts, des sites industriels, des aérodromes, des postes de commandement ou des centres logistiques. Dans son communiqué, la firme précise qu’IRIFI embarque une charge utile non divulguée et se tire depuis un lanceur mobile en conteneur, pour un déploiement « rapide, agile et à grande échelle ». L’idée est de saturer les défenses par le nombre, ce que les missiles classiques ne peuvent pas faire.
Son PDG, Mouad M’Ghari, résume cette logique : « Le Shahed est bon marché et facile à produire en masse, mais il est imprécis et facile à abattre. Les Tomahawk et les Storm Shadow sont des concentrés de technologie très résistants, mais ils sont chers et produits en très petit nombre. » Selon lui, « l’autonomie fondée sur l’IA permet désormais de combiner le meilleur des deux mondes ».
Comment fonctionne-t-il ?
Tout se décide avant le lancement : des officiers choisissent les cibles et règlent les paramètres de la mission. Ensuite, selon l’entreprise, plus aucun contrôle humain n’intervient. Pour s’orienter, le drone ignore le GPS et ses équivalents, trop exposés au brouillage, et un guidage visuel prend le relais à l’approche de la cible.
Harmattan AI annonce un vol sous la détection radar et une précision au mètre. Un seul commandant, aidé d’une IA qui trie des images satellites, pourrait lancer des dizaines de frappes. Pour l’instant, la société ne donne ni le prix du drone, ni la nature de sa charge, ni de date de mise en service.
La société met en avant le principe « autonomie dans l’exécution, autorité humaine sur l’action létale ». Le choix des cibles reste validé par un humain, mais avant le lancement. Côté portée, elle est annoncée à 2 000 km et cette distance équivaut presque à deux fois la traversée de la France métropolitaine, du nord au sud. Impressionnant certes, mais cela ne suffit pas à faire d’IRIFI un cas à part puisque le Shahed-136 revendique déjà une portée de 2 500 km.
Ce qui peut permettre à IRIFI de se distinguer sur les champs de bataille modernes, c’est sa navigation sans signal satellite, qui lui permet de résister au brouillage électronique.
Une lettre d’intention avec le Maroc
Dès le lendemain de la présentation, l’Administration de la défense nationale marocaine et la filiale marocaine de Harmattan AI ont signé une lettre d’intention pour acquérir, développer et produire IRIFI dans le royaume, à l’ouverture du Marrakech Air Show. Harmattan AI affirme que les briques technologiques critiques du système seront développées et produites sur place, par des équipes essentiellement marocaines. L’accord prolonge un partenariat signé en juin 2026, qui prévoit l’ouverture d’un centre de R&D de l’entreprise à Rabat.
Il ne s’agit toutefois que d’une lettre d’intention, pas d’un contrat de livraison, et le système est encore au stade du développement.
Une start-up qui monte vite
Créée en 2024, Harmattan AI est la première licorne française de la défense, avec une valorisation supérieure à un milliard d’euros. Elle a levé 200 millions de dollars lors d’un tour mené par Dassault Aviation, avec qui elle travaille sur le programme NAMIB. En juin, l’armée française lui a commandé 5 000 microdrones Delco, à livrer au plus tard début 2027.

articles.title: How to keep AI agents within their permissions
articles.text:
Written by: Ido Shlomo Co-Founder and CTO of Token Security
AI agents should do more on their own. Who has the time or attention span to approve every command? And watching agents do the work they’re asked to do is mind-numbingly boring.
But agents do need boundaries, especially in corporate environments. Without a clear limit on what they can do, agentic flows tend to use all available access.
Here's a real-world example: A developer asks their agent to figure out why a nightly export job is failing. The team's rule for agents is simple: they work through read-only roles. But the developer also holds admin for on-call work, and both profiles sit in the same ~/.aws/config.
The agent hits AccessDenied when it tries to rerun the job, so it switches to the admin profile, assumes the role, and runs aws s3 rm against the production bucket to clear out the half-written export first.
The credential is valid. The developer may assume admin privileges, and the admin can delete S3 objects. AWS checks the signature, not who is holding the key, so as far as AWS knows, the developer did this. The violation is that an agent used a role that agents aren't allowed to use. Unlike intent, you can check that on every request.
Who’s to blame? The developer who shouldn’t have handed the agent their credentials and let it auto-approve actions? The harness maker? That’s the wrong question. Again, agents should do more on their own, speaking both as a developer and as a manager of developers who work with AI.
Instead of assigning blame, we need to know where this deletion attempt can actually be stopped. There are several possible enforcement points, and each depends on what the control can see, what it can block, and whether the agent has another path to the same action.
We want autonomy with limits we can actually enforce
First, we need to scope the problem. There’s constant pressure to expand agentic access, and usually, the reason makes sense in isolation. A task gets stuck, for example. Or there’s a new integration for a service that holds some of the organizational context.
The result is always the same: the next task starts with more access than the previous one.
A second source of pressure is the agent itself. Agents look for new credentials when the ones they have are blocked, without asking the human in charge whether they can have that access.
This behavior is agnostic to the source of the instructions. A malicious prompt injection can cause overreach attempts, but so can mistaken assumptions during an authorized task.
Valid Key, Wrong Hands
AWS checks the signature, not who holds the key. When an agent grabs an admin profile, the request appears to come from the developer.
Token Security maps every agent to its owner, identities, and permissions, so your controls block actions outside the assigned task and allow the rest to run.
See where it stops
Be specific about what you are enforcing
Agents use tool calls to retrieve data or take action, so that’s where the enforcement matters most. That said, "control tool calls" is a very coarse rule. What if the tool is a shell that can run an SDK? It can also be a browser with an authenticated session. When you allow the tool, you also allow what’s behind it.
To properly understand what’s happening, we need the operation, its arguments, the account and resource accessed, and the identity in use. For data operations, we also need to understand what the output is and where this output is routed.
There’s a lot that goes into a proper decision about the validity of an action.
In most agent harnesses, local commands, file operations, skills, and delegation are also tool calls. They matter because of where they lead. For example, reading ~/.aws/config is how the agent finds an admin profile to use.
So enforcement at the tool call is critical, and so is deciding on the action inside it.
Where enforcement can happen
Some of the damage can be prevented through reasoning checks that assess a plan or action against the task at hand. But this is a probabilistic control, and some malicious instructions will pass through. There’s no good alternative to having proper mitigation controls that can stop an action.
| Method | What it’s useful for | What I would check before relying on it | Risk it removes | Autonomy cost | 
| Managed agent settings | Restricting tools, permissions, approval modes, and allowed integrations close to the agent. | Which clients honor the settings? Can a user, project, or agent override them? Model and effort settings can attempt to restrict access, but they’re behavioral choices by nature. | Broad when the app enforces it; little for behavioral settings | Low, except approval modes, which cost the most | 
| Runtime hooks | Checking a supported operation before it runs, with context from the agent's session. | Can the user or agent change or disable it? Does it cover alternate tools and subagents? Does it block before execution, including on errors and timeouts? | Per operation, for the events it sees | Low if automated, high if it asks a person | 
| Gateways | Inspecting and blocking the requests routed through them, with a shared policy across connected agents. | Which traffic do they actually see: model requests, MCP tools, direct APIs, or network traffic? Can the agent reach the same system another way? | High for routed traffic, none for the rest | Low, since only the blocked call stops | 
| Sandboxes | Limiting the files, processes, network routes, and credentials available to an agent. | What can the agent still do inside those limits? Are reachable services restricted to the right account and operations, or just an allowed domain? | Caps reach, not what happens inside | Medium, as tasks needing outside access break | 
| Endpoint enforcement | Governing local agent use through endpoint software or the EDR that’s already deployed. | Can it stop a particular operation, or only a process or host? What is visible inside containers or VMs? Which hosted agents sit outside its reach? | Local agents only | High if it kills a process or host | 
| Credential and target-service authorization | Reducing the authority granted to an agent and enforcing access at the system that holds the resource. | Are credentials specific to the agent and task? Are there alternate credentials? Can the service distinguish the agent from the person or shared account behind it? | High, wherever the request comes from | Medium, as narrow access stalls tasks and sends agents looking for more | 
| API-based management | Changing agent settings, removing permissions, revoking credentials or sessions, and disabling access where platforms expose those actions. | When does the change take effect? What happens to existing sessions and cached tokens? Is it the prevention of future access or a response after the action? | Mostly after the action | None until it fires | 
These methods overlap and complement each other. A hook that calls a policy service and a gateway that consults an identity graph do a better job because the enforcement and decision points are in the locations best suited to them.
This table is far from exhaustive, and there are more considerations for some of these methods. Take managed settings, for example. Model and effort settings are behavioral in nature, but with some harnesses, permissions are much more than a prompt saying “please don’t flip out”.
In Claude Code, for example, permission rules are enforced by the application itself, and managed settings can restrict user overrides. In that case, control lives in a settings file, but that doesn’t make it less effective.
With hooks, the basic premise depends entirely on their placement in the execution chain. You can’t stop an event that’s already happened, and failure behavior varies by hook types and events.
Gateways have their own complexities, as they must base their authorization decisions on what they see. Look at AWS AgentCore, which demonstrates policy checks for connected tools. Note which calls it sees.
Sandboxes and scoped credentials solve different problems. Proper isolation can remove access capabilities, whereas a scoped credential limits what happens after access is granted. See Cloudflare's sandbox authentication design, which shows a way to add credentials outside the sandbox, so the agent doesn't need to possess the secret. Its operations, though, will still require authorization.
Apply the same policy to a hosted agent
Consider a support agent that’s asked to summarize open cases. Its connector uses a service account built for agents that edit and close cases. The agent decides that some cases look resolved and tries to close them.
Again, the capability comes with the credential, and the agent is within its grant. The place where the action is disallowed is the agent’s approved read-only policy.
To enforce it, the policy must be something a control can check, such as: “This agent may read cases, and any call that edits or closes one is denied, regardless of the service account it holds.”
If that agent lives in a hosted environment, an endpoint control on the employee’s laptop might have no opportunity to stop the action, since it’s all server-side.
Here, you’ll need cooperation from the SaaS platform’s own controls, rely on a tool gateway, or have a narrower service identity. And again, it depends on what the platform exposes and where the calls run.
Which brings us to coverage gaps in our controls. There’s no one perfect control here. Hooks aren’t better than endpoint enforcement, which isn’t better than a sandbox. It’s all about what you deploy and where.
| Method | Coding agent on a laptop | Support agent in a SaaS platform | 
| Managed agent settings | Works if the client honors them | Only what the vendor exposes | 
| Runtime hooks | On the events the runtime exposes | Only if the platform offers hooks | 
| Sandboxes | Limit files, network, and credentials | The agent runs on the vendor's servers | 
| Endpoint enforcement | In reach | Out of reach | 
| Gateways | Catch the admin calls, if AWS traffic routes through them | A tool gateway in front of the connector | 
| Credential and target-service authorization | Keep admin out of the agent's reach | A read-only service account for summaries | 
| API-based management | Revoke the session after the fact | Disable the connector after the fact | 
Two methods can stop both of these examples before the action reaches the target: a gateway that sees the relevant traffic and credential scoping at the target. The other methods depend more heavily on where the agent runs and what the runtime exposes.
Above all, you want the agent to keep working within its approved policy. Read-only is not complete. It can still expose sensitive data, depending on where the output goes. Anthropic's containment analysis explains why.
Choose what’s practical, then test the ways around your control
You’ll likely be deciding what’s practical based on your deployment. Managed settings require supported clients and central administration, for example. And you won’t have hooks without a runtime that exposes the right events. Gateways force you to route traffic through them, and endpoint controls mandate software installation and maintenance.
None of these is free. The controls introduce trade-offs, require maintenance, and must account for an ever-growing volume of AI-driven work.
Take the AWS example from the beginning of the article. Blocking the literal command is a start, but what if the same request comes through an SDK? With a different credential? Through delegation?
The security requirement to block deletion remains the same, but there are many different paths to it.
Then there’s the question of value, and you have to consider it as much as the control capabilities. How much delay do the controls add? How often does someone need to unblock a false positive? Are we reducing risk or introducing problems?
SACR's ARISE report centers on runtime intervention, delegated authority, and action-level decisions. This should be brought down to a concrete request, a policy, and evidence of what happened when the agent tried it.
A short guide, based on where your agents run and what you control there:
| Where your agents run | What you usually control | Start with | Then add | 
| Developer laptops and IDEs | The endpoint, agent settings, local credential files | Managed settings, plus hooks where the client supports them | A gateway for cloud API traffic, and endpoint enforcement for clients you can't configure | 
| Your own cloud, CI or containers | The runtime, network egress, and workload identity | A sandbox and per-agent workload credentials | A gateway on egress | 
| SaaS platforms | Connector credentials and the platform's admin settings | A narrow service identity per agent | Platform controls through the API, and a tool gateway in front of connectors, where the platform allows it | 
It probably isn’t one or the other. Instead, most organizations have all of the above, mixed together, with controls spread around different teams as well. Across these environments, the one common denominator is identity. So start with credential scoping at the target, as this dictates the reach wherever the agent is running. Then, add one policy source that every enforcement point reads from.
Do this, and you’re in a good starting position.
Where Token fits
At Token Security, we are building around the identity intelligence graph and the decisions it can support across the different enforcement points. Our current focus spans agent settings, gateways, endpoint enforcement, and APIs into identity and agent platforms.
The broader vision is to build or connect to the enforcement capability the customer needs. We don't need to build everything ourselves.
The graph connects an agent to its owner, the identities it consumes, the permissions associated with those identities, and the resources it can access. That’s the kind of context that policy engines can use to decide what an agent may do, rather than assuming that the credential's full authority is appropriate.
In a recent gateway demo, we demonstrated this exact idea: same developer, same session, and the agent’s call is denied on admin and allowed on readonly. Other controls can enforce read-only access, too.
Supplying the right identity context and applying the policy across the different places agents work is paramount, yet complex, as this process requires reliable attribution. If we cannot distinguish the agent's request from a human using the same credentials, the graph doesn't magically fix it.
What about baselines? Keep in mind that past behavior can only be used as an input, not the policy itself. The fact that an agent usually just reads data does not prove that a write is forbidden. That’s the job of the rule that pins agents to readonly. Missing or stale context also requires an explicit decision, as with hook timeouts.
I want an agent to complete the investigation or the support summary without requiring approval for every step. I also want to know exactly where an action outside that task will stop. That's what I would ask of every enforcement method, including Token Security.

articles.title: Se sigue buscando al vecino de Salamanca que colocó una piscina de 2 metros cúbicos en el patio de luces de su comunidad de vecinos
articles.text:
Dicen que el calor agudiza el ingenio. A finales de mayo, con un episodio de temperaturas excepcionalmente altas para esas fechas, en plena ola de calor, alguien en Salamanca debió de pensar que un patio de luces era un sitio estupendo para montar una piscina. Lo que no tenía a mano, al parecer, era un aparejador. Cuatro meses después, el Ayuntamiento sigue sin encontrar al autor de la idea y ha tenido que recurrir al Boletín Oficial del Estado, que viene a ser como gritar su nombre por la ventana, pero con un distintivo bastante más severo.
Expediente que hace aguas. Los hechos, según recogimos en Decoesfera y Xataka Smart Home, arrancan el 28 de mayo. Ese día Urbanismo recibe el aviso de que hay una piscina en un inmueble de la calle Camelias, en el barrio de Garrido. El edificio es de 1967, tiene cuatro plantas más bajo y, según el expediente, ningún espacio común libre. La piscina estaba en un patio interior compartido por varias comunidades, y fue la de los portales de Fernández Nieto 6-8 la que dio la voz de alarma.
Las cuentas son sencillas. Dos metros cúbicos son 2.000 litros, y 2.000 litros de agua pesan unos 2.000 kilos. Sumemos depuradora, patas, lona y demás aparatos y tenemos 2.100 kg, más o menos lo que pesan un par de utilitarios pequeños. Con la diferencia de que un coche no salpica. Para quien prefiera medidas domésticas, son unas diez bañeras llenas hasta el borde, sin patito de goma que amortigüe el asunto.
Xataka precisa que era una piscina portátil, y ahí está la trampa: portátil lo es hasta que se llena. OKDiario la describe como una piscina de “pequeñas dimensiones”, pero en este contexto es relativo. El informe técnico municipal habla de una sobrecarga superior a 500 kilos por metro cuadrado. Y el Código Técnico de la Edificación toma como referencia unos 200. El problema es que bajo ese patio de luces están los garajes. El temor vecinal era que la plaza de aparcamiento dejara de ser un sitio donde aparcar para convertirse en un sitio donde nadar.
Persecución en tres actos. Primer acto: dos intentos de notificación durante septiembre, ambos fallidos. Segundo acto: el Ayuntamiento, sin saber ya a qué puerta llamar, publica el requerimiento en el BOE, en concreto el 16 de septiembre. Y llegamos al tercer acto: este tablón de anuncios que lee con devoción medio país cada mañana, no ha servido de mucho, porque la búsqueda sigue abierta. El miedo a la sanción sigue en el aire. El derecho administrativo y la comedia costumbrista dándose la mano.
UN VISTAZO A...
Lo que complica la pesquisa es que el patio no pertenece a nadie en concreto. La responsabilidad jurídica es de la comunidad. Decoesfera explica que, al no estar el espacio atribuido a un propietario, identificar a quien colocó la piscina resulta complicado. Es el crimen perfecto de la propiedad horizontal. Ya lo comentábamos aquí: cuando algo es de todos y nadie lo ha visto, nadie tiene la culpa.
Lo que dice la ley. La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal no prohíbe expresamente las piscinas. Su artículo 7.2 impide desarrollar en el inmueble actividades dañosas para la finca o peligrosas. Dicho de otro modo: si a usted le apetece un chapuzón, no tiene por qué apetecerle también al edificio. Y la densidad del agua impone que en solo 50 centímetros de profundidad ya hay 500 kilos por metro cuadrado. Por esto mismo se contempla posible sanción urbanística, con una cuantía que dependerá de las circunstancias del caso.
Final feliz (para la estructura). Mientras el propietario no aparezca, el informe municipal pide a los propios vecinos que desmonten la piscina cuanto antes. Es decir, la comunidad que presentó la queja ha pasado de denunciante a socorrista y de socorrista a encargada. Ya está desmontada, al parecer.
Si usted es el dueño, el Ayuntamiento quiere hablar con usted y ya no sabe de qué otra forma decírselo. Si no lo es, recuerde que las olas de calor tienen soluciones más ligeras: ventilador, ducha fría o, en último extremo, la piscina municipal, que esa sí tiene cimientos, aunque este verano muchas hayan terminado llenas de heces.

articles.title: What Watson Matsa discovered when he started listening to farmers
articles.text:
Don’t get Watson Matsa started on farmers and banks, as we did. By the swimming pool at Somerset Westview Hotel in Nairobi, he talks about both with the conviction of a man who has spent enough time inside a bank to know why banks don’t understand farmers.
It is a Friday evening, July 26. Around us, Nairobi is warming up for the weekend. There is coffee on one table, tea on another, and every so often someone reaches into their pocket for a cigarette. Matsa, meanwhile, is talking about soil, rainfall, and credit scores.
The founder of eSusFarm Africa wasn’t always an agriculture man. He studied economics and accounting at Rhodes University in South Africa and later worked in credit analytics at FNB. Finance was supposed to be the thing. Then an idea he encountered at university got him thinking: information unlocks capital. His problem with that idea was Africa. What happens when the information needed to unlock capital simply isn’t there?
That question eventually led him to smallholder farmers and eSusFarm Africa.
Matsa still talks like a banker—risk, underwriting, cash flows—but increasingly thinks like a farmer. Banks, he says, are built around the neatness of a salary arriving every month. Farmers earn seasonally, save for the unexpected, and wait. Perhaps, he suggests, farmers are not the problem. Banking is simply too rigid.
He misses one thing about his old life.
“The SMS that comes on the 24th of the month,” he says, laughing about what he misses most from corporate life. “The SMS saying the money has arrived—on time. A good credit score. Being able to plan trips with my family.”
Now, there is payroll to worry about, farmers to convince, and a continent’s financial assumptions to challenge.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You grew up fascinated by financial systems, not farming. How did a banker end up spending his days thinking about soil, weather, and smallholder farmers?
It goes back to when I was studying at Rhodes University. I was double-majoring in economics and accounting, and there was one book that really had me in a chokehold. It said that information unlocks capital, and that capital markets have enough information to do so.
I thought: in Africa, that’s not true. There isn’t enough information flowing fairly for capital to flow.
Initially, I was thinking about small businesses: how do we get data on them that can facilitate capital flows? I took the idea to my co-founder, who has a PhD in agricultural economics. He said, “What if this applies to agriculture? Money isn’t flowing to small farmers because there isn’t enough information.”
I asked him what data we would need. He said soil, climate, farmer-reported, and crop information. Those are some of the pillars you need when assessing risk. You can look at the soil and say: this farmer needs a certain fertiliser, so let’s finance that. You can look at the weather and determine that the farmer needs insurance.
We started mapping the data points that affect financial decisions.
I also worked at FNB in the credit analytics space as a project manager on projects aimed at improving credit scoring. That helped me understand how banks think.
Take ongoing risk management: even if I vet and qualify you for a loan, I still need to monitor you until it is repaid. That kind of ongoing risk-management system doesn’t really exist for smallholder farmers.
We took on the task of building it.
If we spoke to your younger self in South Africa, what career would he swear he’d never end up pursuing?
I always wanted to be in finance. It’s my skill set; it’s my thing.
I would advise my younger self not to pursue anything unrelated to STEM—science, technology, engineering, or mathematics. When we were growing up, the question was: how do you put food on the table? STEM was where a lot of employment was happening.
For me, mathematics could mean accounting, economics, or banking. Engineering was a good space. Technology was a good space. Science was a good space.
I still think STEM is important in Africa. We’re still trying to master how we compete in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.
You’ve lived in boardrooms and on farms. Which world has taught you more about human behaviour?
They’ve taught me different sides of human behaviour.
The boardroom taught me about governance and how to implement policies and procedures so that, when you’re doing something, you can replicate it.
The ground taught me that interpersonal relationships are more important than almost anything else. You may be a smart guy, but if you don’t know how to relate to the person opposite you and communicate in an easy, simple, and articulate way, you won’t get their buy-in.
The ground taught me how to simplify complex concepts. On one side, I’m very technical. The other side is: how do you communicate that technicality so that someone with a Grade Seven education can understand what you’re saying and the value you’re bringing?
It has made me a much better communicator. Working on the ground has also taught me empathy and how to relate to people. Those skills transfer back into the boardroom.
You often describe finance as infrastructure. What’s one lesson from banking that agriculture desperately needs, and one thing banking could learn from farmers?
One thing banking could learn from farmers is that incomes aren’t earned in the same way.
Banking tries to structure things around very rigid rules: you get paid monthly, so I’ll charge you monthly. Farming is seasonal. You receive money and then have to preserve it for a much longer period until the next tranche comes in.
Banking has been too rigid. Income flows aren’t always monthly. They can be daily, weekly or every four months. Banks need to start adapting to people’s income cycles rather than dictating them.
Farmers also understand how to use money prudently because they’re constantly preparing for eventualities. It could be a weather event or a disease outbreak. They develop a resilient mindset around preserving cash so they can survive those events.
That’s something banking can learn from farming.
People often assume farmers are poor because they lack money. Do you think the bigger problem is that financial systems have never really been designed for them?
Absolutely. The financial system was designed around salaried people—monthly earners.
But farmers and people in the informal economy can earn daily. They are micro daily earners. You may not be earning $2,000 every month, but you could be earning $20 a day.
Small farmers and small businesses are earning money, but they’re earning smaller amounts consistently.
If banks understood this better, they could tap into this class of daily earners rather than focusing almost exclusively on monthly earners.
The financial system has been designed around formal employment rather than people’s actual income potential and earning patterns.
Every founder has one meeting that changed everything. Which conversation altered the direction of eSusFarm more than any funding round ever could?
We always wanted to get into finance, but we didn’t know where to start. Was it credit? Was it insurance?
Then we had a conversation with Benny van Rooy, the former CEO of Grobank. He said, “Watson, you’ve got enough data, and I like calling you a data company. But what you need to understand is that banks can’t lend if there is no insurance.”
That conversation was the beginning of our understanding that banks come after insurance; they don’t come before.
Banks want assurance. If you cannot assure a bank of some stability in earnings, you’re going to struggle to unlock finance.
Farmers are largely an unsecured portfolio, so insurance—or assurance—becomes important. The assurance comes from data; the insurance comes from underwriting. Without those two things, banking won’t come in.
That insight changed the way we thought about penetrating the market.
Your platform combines AI, mobile money, blockchain, and insurance. How do you stop yourself from falling in love with technology instead of the problem you’re trying to solve?
For us, it has always been about not letting the small farmer fall behind.
The back end of the system can be sophisticated. It can use AI, blockchain, credit scoring and insurance. But we still make sure the delivery model can come through something as simple as USSD, so it’s accessible through a device the farmer already has.
We’ve learned that even if you’ve got complex technology in the background, you still have to deliver it simply at the last mile.
We don’t allow technology to override the mission of supporting the farmer. Technology is there to help us do that better.
If I spent a week shadowing you, what would surprise me most? Would I find you writing code, negotiating partnerships, visiting farms, or worrying about payroll?
Everything.
But you’d probably see a lot of partnership work. We have a partnership-led growth strategy. We believe in embedding our technology within existing systems.
People ask me, “Where is your app?” I tell them we don’t want to build an app. We want to be involved in what people are already using.
If you’re in Kenya and using mobile money, let me provide the solution through that ecosystem. If you’re using WhatsApp, let me provide the solution on WhatsApp.
We have MTN as a partner. We have Sanlam as an insurance partner. We also have Microsoft as a technology partner helping us scale.
Building standalone apps and systems doesn’t always make sense. I’d rather integrate our technology into existing infrastructure with a captive market than go door-to-door to acquire every user ourselves.
The second thing you’d see me worrying about is payroll. As we expand into more countries, we need larger teams, and funding in Africa remains limited.
What we’ve found is that many African investors want to invest in profitability, whereas American investors are often more willing to invest in technology for the future before profitability. They’re willing to lose money in the short term to jump the next curve.
That affects us. We have to find capital elsewhere, including grants, to help us build for that future.
When was the last time a farmer challenged an assumption you’d made and forced you to rethink the business?
We assumed farmers would willingly report information about their operations.
We built technology to collect information, and part of it depended on farmers’ self-reporting. We thought they would do it because they understood that reporting was necessary to access finance.
That was one of the biggest lessons we learned: many farmers don’t understand why they need to report. They don’t necessarily care about reporting.
We call some of them “sceptical survivors”. These are farmers between roughly 45 and 65 who have been farming for years. They’ve taken their children to school through farming. They have no appetite for a 35-year-old Watson coming to tell them to report information when there’s no clear incentive.
Why should I report? If I report, what’s the immediate benefit?
We’ve had to connect reporting directly to finance. The more information you provide, the better we can monitor and understand your risk. Then we can score that risk and potentially finance it.
We had to create an incentive structure for farmers to start reporting.
Founders often say they “empower” communities. Was there a moment when you realised the community was actually empowering you?
Yes.
We’ve profiled about 380,000 smallholder farmers across Uganda, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Eswatini. From that pool, we had about 20,000 smallholder farmers actively using our solution.
What we didn’t predict was that those 20,000 farmers would become our ambassadors in their communities.
The farmers we’d met and trained in person started onboarding thousands of others through word of mouth.
It taught us something very important about rural communities: word of mouth is incredibly powerful.
Start with a small group and make sure you do a damn good job with that group. They’ll tell the rest of the community, and other people will follow.
That’s also how the technology can scale. Don’t worry about trying to get all 380,000 people yourself. Get the 20,000 right, and they’ll help bring the rest.
You left the predictability of banking for entrepreneurship. What luxury from your corporate life do you still secretly miss?
The SMS that comes on the 24th of the month.
That SMS says the money has arrived on time. A good credit score. Being able to plan trips with my family.
I can’t plan like that now because I’m reinvesting whatever money I get into this baby. I miss the predictability of income.
What I don’t miss is the ceiling on how much I could earn.
What I love now is that there’s no ceiling. It’s an open canvas. If we work hard enough, do the right things, and execute the right strategy, the earning potential can become bigger than I could ever have imagined.
What’s the most uncomfortable truth you’ve learned about African agriculture that investors and policymakers rarely acknowledge?
They misunderstand the multiplier effect of agriculture.
We’ve analysed this and found that a single farmer who does well can create jobs throughout the value chain.
Think about a farmer buying the right seed. The seed provider may need to hire someone due to increased demand. Then there are transporters. There’s the fertiliser company. When production increases, you need more workers and perhaps tractors.
When the crop is ready to be harvested, you need people to do so. Then it needs to be packaged, transported, exported, or distributed. Eventually, it reaches shops and the end consumer.
The multiplier effect of agriculture in Africa is enormous. One successful farmer on one hectare can create jobs across the value chain.
Policymakers and investors don’t fully understand that. Not focusing on agriculture in Africa is almost a sin, given its economic multiplier effect. There are very few sectors capable of creating jobs across so many different parts of the economy.
Imagine you’re appointed Finance Minister for a day—not Agriculture Minister. What’s the first financial rule you’d change to make farming a genuinely attractive business for young Africans?
One of my dreams is actually to become AU president, so I’ve thought about these things a lot.
If I were Finance Minister, I would provide better financing solutions for young people—a combination of grants and debt—and direct that financing towards crops that can substitute imports.
If your country has a huge rice import bill, finance young people to grow rice.
If we’re importing a million tonnes of rice and want to reduce the import bill, let’s finance young farmers to produce part of what we import.
I would focus heavily on import substitution and financing young people to produce in those value chains. It would help us become more self-sustaining in areas where we currently depend heavily on imports.
What part of success worries you most: the expectations, the visibility, the responsibility, or something else entirely?
Visibility is a big one for me.
Even as an organisation, we’re an embedded solution. We like working in the background.
Too much visibility brings too many eyes and can create enemies. I try not to be too visible personally. The company can be visible, but I don’t necessarily need to be.
I think Africans are still getting used to seeing success stories from within our own communities, and sometimes success can attract jealousy. For now, I’d rather keep myself away from too much of that.
So visibility is probably the thing that worries me most.
Complete this sentence: “The biggest lie we’ve told ourselves about African agriculture is…”
That there’s more money than you can ever imagine—and that it’s easy to get.
There is money in agriculture, but it’s not what people think. It takes time. It’s not fast. Agriculture is a slow industry.
It’s different from the financial sector I come from, where you can launch a lending product and potentially acquire customers very quickly.
In agriculture, you have to go out and train people. Then people have to understand the product. Eventually, the income starts coming in.
There’s a huge amount of training and change management that have to happen before the money comes in. That means you need a much longer runway. You have to sink money into the business before you see results.
But when the volumes eventually come, they can come in huge chunks.
We’ve done case studies where farming one hectare can involve about $3,000. Multiply that across a million people, and you’re talking about a lot of money.
The quantum can be enormous. But unlocking it requires learning, training, and ecosystem development.
A lot of investors, financiers, and bankers don’t understand that. You have to invest heavily in training and change management before you see the results.
Finally, if your children asked, “What exactly were you trying to fix?” what answer would you give that has nothing to do with AI, blockchain, or fintech?
My son actually asked me this.
I told him, “I help make food. You’re eating today, aren’t you?”
He said, “Yes.”
I asked him, “Where does the food come from?”
He said, “I don’t know, Dad.”
I told him, “It comes from a farmer. If there are no farmers, you don’t have food. So I’m trying to help farmers make more food so that you can eat.”
That’s what I told my child, and it’s probably the simplest way I can explain what I’m trying to do.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Faut-il laisser son PC portable branché au secteur en permanence ? La vérité sur l'usure des batteries
articles.text:
Faut-il laisser son PC portable branché au secteur en permanence ? La vérité sur l'usure des batteries
Laisser son ordinateur portable branché toute la journée use-t-il sa batterie ? Oui et non. Ce qui fatigue les cellules, c'est de rester des heures à 100 %, et plus encore dans une machine qui chauffe. Les Mac compatibles permettent désormais de fixer une limite de charge dans les réglages. Sur PC Windows, la fonction existe souvent aussi, mais il faut la chercher dans l'utilitaire du constructeur.
Prenez un portable resté deux ans sur un bureau, branché du matin au soir à un écran externe. Il n'a quasiment jamais tourné sur batterie. Le jour où on le débranche pour une réunion, mauvaise surprise : l'autonomie a nettement baissé, et l'outil de diagnostic affiche une capacité tombée à 70 % de sa valeur d'origine. Deux ans sans servir, 30 % de perdus. Comment est-ce possible ?
Une batterie vieillit aussi au repos
Écartons une vieille peur. Un portable moderne ne "surcharge" pas sa batterie : une fois pleine, son circuit de gestion coupe la charge et le chargeur cesse d'alimenter les cellules. Ce mécanisme fonctionne très bien. Le problème se voit moins. Une batterie lithium-ion s'use de deux manières. La première, tout le monde la connaît : chaque cycle de charge et de décharge l'abîme un peu, c'est le vieillissement cyclique. La seconde est plus sournoise, puisqu'elle agit même quand la batterie ne fait rien. On parle de vieillissement calendaire, et il dépend en particulier de deux choses, le niveau de charge et la température.
À 100 %, les cellules restent proches de leur tension maximale, autour de 4,2 V pour beaucoup de batteries Li-ion (la valeur exacte dépend de leur chimie). À ce niveau, des réactions parasites se produisent plus facilement. Elles grignotent une partie du lithium disponible et dégradent les interfaces entre électrodes et électrolyte. La batterie perd de la capacité sans avoir servi. Or un ordinateur branché en permanence, sans limite de charge, passe justement l'essentiel de son temps à 100 %.
La chaleur accélère le phénomène
Deuxième facteur, la température. Une exposition prolongée à la chaleur accélère ces réactions indésirables, surtout quand la batterie est très chargée. Il n'existe pas de seuil universel : chimie des cellules, niveau de charge, durée d'exposition, tout compte. Le site Battery University donne tout de même des ordres de grandeur. Stockée un an à 40 °C en restant à 100 %, une batterie peut perdre environ 35 % de sa capacité. À 40 % de charge, la perte tombe à environ 15 %. Ces chiffres viennent d'un stockage à température constante et ne prédisent pas l'usure d'un modèle précis en usage quotidien. L'écart entre les deux reste parlant.
Dans un portable branché, les deux facteurs se cumulent vite. Processeur et carte graphique chauffent dans un boîtier compact, et une partie de cette chaleur gagne la batterie. Une session de jeu, un export vidéo, un gros calcul. Ou, plus bêtement, une machine posée sur un lit qui bouche ses aérations. La température interne grimpe, et les cellules avec. Pleine charge plus chaleur : voilà ce qui a pu user la batterie de notre exemple.
Plafonner la charge à 80 %
Pour un ordinateur qui travaille surtout sur secteur, le remède est simple : ne pas le laisser à 100 %. Plafonnée vers 80 %, la charge maintient les cellules à une tension plus basse et le vieillissement calendaire ralentit, plus encore si la machine est bien ventilée. D'après Battery University, réduire la tension de charge d'un dixième de volt par cellule peut à peu près doubler le nombre de cycles. Un ordre de grandeur, pas une promesse valable pour chaque machine. Si le portable ne quitte pratiquement jamais le bureau et que le constructeur le permet, on peut même descendre à 60 %.
Anker Nano II 65 W
Beaucoup de constructeurs proposent ce réglage sur une partie de leurs modèles. Chez Lenovo, il s'appelle mode Conservation et se trouve dans Lenovo Vantage. ASUS l'intègre à MyASUS sous le nom de Battery Care Mode, en général limité à 80 % sur les modèles récents ; certains plus anciens acceptent un plafond à 60 %. Dell, HP, Microsoft Surface, Acer et MSI ont aussi des options de limitation ou de gestion de la charge sur certains appareils, dans leur application ou dans le BIOS. Les seuils varient d'un modèle à l'autre, et il faut parfois fouiller pour les trouver. Windows 11, lui, n'a toujours pas de réglage universel. C'est dommage.
Apple a fini par bouger. macOS Tahoe 26.4, sorti le 24 mars 2026, ajoute dans les réglages de la batterie une limite de charge réglable entre 80 et 100 %, sur les MacBook à puce Apple Silicon. Le Mac s'autorise de temps en temps une charge complète pour garder une estimation fiable du niveau de batterie. Pour descendre sous 80 %, ou sur un ancien Mac Intel compatible, il reste l'application AlDente.
Quelques habitudes complètent ce réglage. Rebranchez vers 20 % plutôt que de vider régulièrement la batterie jusqu'à 0 %. Laissez les aérations libres. Avant de ranger la machine pour longtemps, laissez-la autour de 50 %. Et rien n'empêche de repasser à 100 % la veille d'un déplacement : une charge complète peut d'ailleurs recaler une jauge devenue imprécise, même si l'entretien de la batterie n'en a pas besoin.
