articles.title: School district makes dramatic U-turn on AI, banning it across all grades weeks after Google Gemini rollout
articles.text:
What just happened? Another school district has banned AI from being used in the classroom by students across all grades. While this isn't the first ban of its kind that we've seen, what's interesting is that it was introduced just weeks after the district started piloting Google Gemini for older students.
Frederick County became the latest school district to ban AI use in the classroom this week, voting 6-1 to restrict the technology from pre-K through 12th grade.
Initially, the board considered only banning AI for younger students, but eventually extended the ban through high school.
There are some instances when AI can still be used in the classroom, including lessons about the technology and accommodations for students with disabilities.
The decision marks a sharp turnaround by the district. The board had allowed middle and high school students to use Google Gemini, with teacher permission, during this school year, despite other AI platforms being blocked on school devices.
But board members expressed concern about the move. One said it was frustrating to see Gemini rolled out without any warning to parents, given that AI has been used to generate inappropriate images of students and bully others, and has generated "bad advice from a mental health standpoint."
There were also concerns about AI's impact on children, as well as teachers' inability to disable Gemini on student devices.
Scott Murphy, the district's director of curriculum and instruction, said Gemini was chosen because it was the only tool the board evaluated and found to meet the state's high standards for safety and privacy.
Justin Heid, president of the Frederick County Education Association, said that several educators are returning to traditional paper-and-pencil assignments instead of computer-based work because they are concerned students might use AI to complete their work. It's a strategy that some have been using since ChatGPT exploded in popularity three years ago.
While many parents have supported the ban, pointing out that kids can rely on AI as a crutch, others say a ban this extensive could have a negative impact on their future and leave them less prepared for college.
This isn't the first ban of its kind, though it is one of the stricter. New York City banned AI for elementary and middle school students last month, while the Los Angeles school district is also temporarily blocking access to generative AI tools on student devices across all grades.

articles.title: The Minimum Viable Manager: Building Trust, Feedback, and Alignment
articles.text:
In this podcast, Shane Hastie, Lead Editor for Culture & Methods, spoke to Matt Gjertsen, founder of Built and author of Minimum Viable Manager, about the three foundational skills every first-time manager needs, how to build trust and give effective feedback, and why human leadership skills matter even more in the age of AI.
Key Takeaways
- First principles leadership holds that every manager has three responsibilities: getting people to work together, getting them to work on the right things, and improving their work over time.
- A "minimum viable manager" needs to build the three foundational skills of building trust, setting clear expectations, and giving feedback before refining anything more advanced.
- Trust comes down to three elements: belief in someone's skills, their decisions, and the personal connection you have with them, and new managers tend to over-invest in proving their own skills while neglecting connection.
- Good feedback starts by teaching a team to ask for feedback well, then layering in reinforcing feedback before redirecting feedback, always focused on observable behaviour rather than assumed motives.
- When deciding what to develop next, apply a theory-of-constraints approach: find the one bottleneck holding the team back — trust, decision-making, or skill — and focus there before moving on.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Shane Hastie: Good day folks. This is Shane Hastie for the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Matt Gjertsen. Matt, welcome. Thanks for taking the time to talk to us.
Matt Gjertsen: Absolutely, Shane. I'm really excited to chat with you. So glad, thank you for taking the time as well.
Introductions [01:13]
Shane Hastie: My normal starting point with this is who's Matt?
Matt Gjertsen: I am the founder of a company called Built. Our mission is to train the next generation of technical leaders how to build teams capable of solving the world's hardest problems. I took kind of an interesting path to get here. I was always into the sciences. So, my undergrad was in physics at the Air Force Academy, but then I went a completely different direction for graduate school and got a degree in public relations after that. But then the first half of my professional life, I was an instructor pilot in the US Air Force. And so, I spent a decade plus flying all over the Pacific and all over the world training and teaching air crews how to do all sorts of things. I was always a space nut. So, when I left active duty, I wanted to get closer into the space world. So, I networked my way into SpaceX.
I ended up leading the training development team at SpaceX for about four and a half years where I got to do a little bit of everything, to be honest with you. For one point, for about a year and a half, I think I onboarded every employee in the company, which was pretty amazing. So, I got to work with just some of the most brilliant engineers in the world, which was really incredible. Left there for another startup and then started built about five years ago now where we now work with all kinds of startup companies, startup technology companies of all shapes and sizes. But the focus really is on technical contributors because when I was at SpaceX and all the places I've been at since then, I really saw that jump from being a great engineer to becoming a manager for the first time. It creates such a bottleneck for so many organizations because we just don't do a good job of giving them a roadmap.
That's why I started Build, that's why I wrote Minimum Viable Manager, which is my brand new book. My goal is to provide that roadmap to people.
Why Hasn't the IC-to-Manager Problem Been Solved? [03:06]
Shane Hastie: But this technical contributor to manager problem, it's something we've recognized as an industry and certainly on the Engineering Culture podcast, we've explored it many times. Why haven't we solved that problem yet?
Matt Gjertsen: Yes, it's interesting. I mean, I talk with a lot of people, a lot of leaders, and Casey Handmer, who's the founder of Terraform Industries, I love how he says, "This has been a problem since before the pyramids." Right? I think in many ways, if you look back at the history of humanity, our greatest strength has always been our ability to get large groups of people to work together. And so, like any superhero, our greatest strength is also our greatest weakness. It is the defining feature of us and that is the defining challenge. And I honestly think a lot of it just has to do with there's so much complexity and nuance to it. What works in one situation isn't going to work in another situation. And it could be the people that are involved, it could be the stage of their life that they are in, it could be the organization that they are in. It's something that I think is fundamental.
I mean, as a perfect example, Amazon is famous for their meeting memos where before a meeting you have to write a memo about what the meeting's going to be about. And I've talked with a lot of startup organizations that are starting to scale. Who do they hire? Well, they hire people from Amazon. They hire executives from Amazon because they were really successful and they come in and they try to take the thing that worked at Amazon and have it work in this new company and it always fails because the context just is different. And so, I think that's ultimately why it's so difficult is that there's so many different varieties of it. And that's honestly why I call my book Minimum Viable Manager because I don't think there is a way to say this is what the right manager is. It's like you need to get to a point where you have enough basics to not fail so that you can iterate and learn just like we do in engineering.
You need to lay that foundation so that you can iterate because how you lead is going to be unique to you, your team and your organization.
First Principles Leadership and the Minimum Viable Manager [05:12]
Shane Hastie: So, what is that minimum viable layer?
Matt Gjertsen: I spent a lot of time thinking about this after my time at SpaceX because if there's one thing that SpaceX is known for, it's first principles engineering and first principles thinking. I wanted to spend a lot of time thinking about forget about what other leadership development programs do, forget about what anybody says. How do we scale this back to the simplest level of what it means to be a leader? And so, the whole thing starts with this idea that I call first principles leadership, which says a leader has three fundamental responsibilities, get people to work together, get them to work on the right things and improve their work over time. Those are the three responsibilities. Every skill falls into trying to fulfil one of those responsibilities. And so, to me, a minimum viable manager is the one that is doing what's the first thing you need to do in each one of those buckets.
And that's build trust on your team, set clear expectations and give feedback. So, a minimum viable manager, in order to make sure you have that secure foundation, you need to be able to build trust with your team, set expectations and give feedback. If you can do that, then I honestly think you're probably going to be better than most people than the average manager that anybody's ever had, but it certainly gives you that solid foundation so then you can refine and then you can talk about things like executive presence or whatever, but that's the foundation.
Shane Hastie: Those three things are hard.
Matt Gjertsen: They are. They are. Like so many things in life. It's simple, but not easy.
Building Trust on Your Team [06:58]
Shane Hastie: So, let's dig into those. How do I build trust?
Matt Gjertsen: The way I like to think about it, and this comes from a lot of research around what are the different attributes of trust. And the way I phrase it is that trusting someone comes down to three things, the skills you have, the decisions you make and the connections you build. So, if I trust you, it means for this situation, I believe you have the skills that are required for the situation. I believe that you make good decisions and I believe that you care about me in some way, that we have some kind of connection. And so, I think in any relationship that you have, especially if you're at work and you think you're having a struggling relationship, there's somebody on your team that you don't trust or you think somebody on your team doesn't trust you, it often comes down to one of those three things.
And I think the big challenge for new leaders is that we overemphasize or mis-emphasize the first one, the skills, right? We come in and we're trying to prove our worth because our worth came from our ability to solve problems as an individual contributor. And so, we want to solve every problem. And in reality, that's just showing people that we don't have confidence in ourselves because that individual competence of solving problems isn't the skill anymore when you are a manager. So, we misemphasize that first one. And then that last one, that building connection, especially for technical people. And everybody's different. No everybody needs the same kind of connection, but I'll never forget a leadership development course I was in years ago where the facilitator had kind of this mic drop moment where he asked everybody in the room who has kids and a bunch of people raised their hand and said, "Okay, if you have kids, how many of you would say that your kids are more important than work?"
And of course, everybody said their kids were more important than work. And I said, "Okay, so how many of you with kids would say kids are the most important thing in your life?" And everybody kept their hand raised. So, I said, okay, everybody put your hand up. Then he asked everybody, okay, so you're all managers. How many of your direct reports have kids? And a bunch of people raised their hand. Said, okay, so for everybody with your hand raised, how many of you can tell me the name of their kids? And every single hand went down. None of them did. And said, okay, so let me get this straight. We're sitting here, you're asking people to come to work, you're asking them to work late, to give their most, to really be committed, and you don't know the first thing about the most important thing in their life.
Why would they trust you? So, we say it is hard, but if we think about it for things like that, it's just like, oh, let me keep track of my kids' names. If they don't have kids, what's their pet's name? What do they enjoy doing on the weekend? Do I know the first thing about them as a person? And this truly isn't going to be true for everybody, but I think for most people, if you can get some of those basics, it really goes a long way to building trust and connection.
Shane Hastie: Yes. I wonder how many of our audience are listening to this and feeling a little bit uncomfortable right now. Do I know the name of those kids?
Matt Gjertsen: Yes. And as powerful as that can be, it is also important to recognize that, and again, this goes back to your question of why is this so hard, is what builds trust with one person will break trust with another person, right? There are people who don't want to share that. And so, you have to be careful about how you get to know... every person on your team is going to be different. How you get to know them is going to be different. The questions that you ask them is going to be different. And so, it's starting simply of showing the faintest caring about what they're doing outside of work. What'd you do this weekend? What's the last movie that you saw? What kind of books do you like to read? Do you ever read books? Starting with stuff like that, and that kind of gets the ball rolling a little bit towards having those other conversations.
Giving Feedback Well [10:49]
Shane Hastie: The other one that is, in my experience and with people I talk to is a tough one, is feedback. How do we give feedback well?
Matt Gjertsen: The first thing that I'll say before giving feedback well is I think giving feedback well starts by asking for feedback well. So, many courses on feedback just start with, this is how you give feedback. But if you don't have a culture where feedback is a norm, it's going to be a struggle to do it. And so, I always start by teaching people, look, you can't just sit with your team and be like, "Hey, do you have any feedback for me?" Because when you ask that, nobody has any answers and it's a struggle for two reasons. The first is that it's asking, do you have any feedback for me? It's putting it on them. If they say anything, they're the ones saying that there's a problem or whatever. And then the second part is that it's, "Do you have any feedback for me?" It's completely wide open and just leaves this and creates like a blank page syndrome like authors have.
And so, I start by teaching people, you have to ask for feedback in a way that is both specific and assumes there is feedback. So, what is one thing I could have done better in our team meeting today to keep us on track? It narrows the scope of what you're asking them to think of and you're asking in a way where you're saying what is one thing? So, when they say one thing, you can't blame them, you ask them for that one thing. I think that's the first thing is I would say is making it clear that feedback is a normal thing, that you want feedback. And then giving feedback, when you get to the stage of giving feedback, I think there's a lot of techniques. There's like SBI for situation behavior impact. There's coin, context, observation impact and next steps. There's lots of them that are out there, but ultimately what it comes down to is you need to make sure you are giving feedback in a way where you're giving feedback on a behavior, on an action, on something that can be seen without attributing any emotions to it, right?
The classic one is, and maybe this wouldn't be feedback, but you're thinking in your head, "Oh, this person's really lazy," or, "Oh, I just don't think you care enough about the work we're doing." And you have no idea. If somebody shows up too late to work, you have no idea if it's because they don't care or because they got a flat tire. And if they got a flat tire and you say they don't care, their arms go up, they're defensive, they're pushing back. And so, you always give feedback only on those tangible things that you see. If you want to find motivations, you can ask about it, but you can never assume those motivations. And so, it's being really specific. And then the last thing I'll say on this since I know I've been going for a little while is, especially if you're new, so I like to put this in three phases.
If you're a new manager or you want to get better at feedback or make more of a feedback culture on your team, for a month, do nothing but practice asking for feedback. Just ask for feedback from everybody. Start doing it in all your one-on-ones and your team meetings. Just make that normal. Do that for a month. And then for a month, give nothing but what I call reinforcing feedback. So, you're giving that same specific feedback, but on the things you want them to continue doing. And honestly, these are the ones where we're most likely to just say good job, but if you say good job, nobody knows what you're talking about. And so, be really clear of this was the thing I saw that I thought was good, please keep doing it and do that for a month so everybody knows, "Oh, they're noticing me."
And then and only then do you start bringing in the redirecting feedback where you're asking people to change their behaviour. And through all that, it stacks on itself. So, you have to keep asking for feedback, you have to keep giving the reinforcing feedback, and then you start giving the redirecting feedback.
Managing People Who Used to Be Your Peers [14:46]
Shane Hastie: One of the tough things that we often face is I get promoted to a team leader in the team that I've been working in. So, I was a peer, I've been a peer, and now I'm their manager.
Matt Gjertsen: Yes.
Shane Hastie: This shifts, this gets to be uncomfortable.
Matt Gjertsen: It's really funny that you asked me that because I just recorded a video on this yesterday and it's something that honestly, it's not something that I'm as much of an expert in. And I think it's because of my background in the military where this was so normal. It was just like, "Look, there's rules, there's ranks. It's just a thing." And because there's such a rigid structure to it didn't come up as a problem that often, I feel like. So, I had to spend some time just the last couple days thinking about this. And I think there's two extremes that people can sometimes go to. The one extreme is to ignore it and pretend nothing is happening. You stay friends, you keep having lunch every day, you keep doing things on the weekends. Oh, it's fine. Everything's fine. And that will cause one of two things to happen.
Either you are actually favouring them and you're doing things to where you're actually giving them more resources or giving them the decisions or you're actually overtly favouring them and that's clearly bad or you are not, but everyone thinks you are because people will just assume. And then the other extreme is you completely kind of break away and in that case you lose a friend. And so, as I was thinking about it the other day, without tons of nuance and tons of details, the best thing to do that I think often gets missed is to just deal with the elephant in the room. As soon as you can, you need to sit down with the other person. There might be several of them, but especially if you have a close friend, one in particular that you need to sit down and just like, "Hey, look, this is the situation and this is what I'm thinking, this is what's going on."
I think this is an excellent time for people to talk to HR, not to necessarily set rules, but just as somebody to bounce ideas off of and be like, "Hey, what are the company policies? Is this okay? Is this not okay? What have you seen work before?" It's a great time to just have that conversation with them before anything happens. I know people don't like to go up to HR unless they get told to go to HR, but the average HR business partner that I know wants to have these kinds of conversations with their people. And so, you can start there, have the one-on-one of this just is a thing, we're going to have to make some changes. And that I think is the first thing that gets missed is just clearly addressing the elephant in the room.
Developing Others While Developing Yourself [17:31]
Shane Hastie: Developing others, helping others get better over time. I also need to develop myself. How do I do those in parallel?
Matt Gjertsen: Carefully. I mean, yes, you're developing others. Yes, we always have to develop ourselves and there's many different avenues. I think this is going to be highly dependent on your organization of what kind of support they give. But I think the thing that I think is most important with this, with any kind of development is I like to use the theory of constraints, which largely comes from the manufacturing world where there's a thousand things that are happening in a manufacturing line, but at any given time, there's exactly one thing that is holding back that whole manufacturing line. There's one thing that's the constraint. There's one process. There's one step that's the constraint. And if we can fix that, we can fix everything. And so, rather than thinking about, I need to make myself a better leader, you should be thinking about what is the one thing that's holding me back right now?
And so, as an example, to fit into those three buckets, the things that I like to ask is where am I spending most of my time? Am I spending my time dealing with employee issues where they're all talking behind each other's back or people are coming to me with problems or I'm having to resolve personality disagreements with people? Or am I having to spend all of my time making decisions? Everybody comes to me to figure out the solution or make the call, take the risk, figure out the next step, or am I spending all of my time fixing mistakes that people are making or redoing work that other people are doing? That's an example of, well, if it's the first one, then your constraint is trust on your team and you need to start focusing on how do I build a cohesive team where people can work together and talk to one another?
If it's the middle one, people aren't making their own decisions, well then I would think about are you providing enough clarity? Are you providing enough information where they can make those decisions and think about are we setting expectations appropriately so that people know what's next and know what to do? Or if it's the last one, well, there's a skill problem on the team and I need to focus on coaching people and raising their skills. That I think is the key to any kind of development, especially everybody's super busy. Every manager that I know still has individual contributor work that they have to do. And so, they're trying to balance it all and you're stepping into this new role. And so, I think the key is to think about doing things one at a time. It's not about making myself a better leader. It's what do I think is the skill that's holding me and my team back right now?
Okay, I'm going to improve that skill. And that might take a quarter, that might take a year and that's okay. You're going to make more progress that way than doing what honestly I did when I first became a leader.
If you look over on my right side, it's just this whole bookshelf filled with books. I was the nightmare manager where I'm a new manager, I don't know what I'm doing. So, I'm tearing through all these books and every other week, I'm coming into my team being like, "So, I just read this book. I want to try this new thing." It's the worst way to do it. So, focus on one thing at a time. And honestly, this is going back to my coaching background beyond being an instructor pilot. I used to coach people how to run marathons and I think it's amazing what you can do with a singular focus.
And so, if you pick three books and three podcasts and they're all on the same topic, they're all on decision making or all on delegation or all on feedback, the speed with which you can improve your performance is quite amazing if you focus on one thing at a time.
Shane Hastie: The deliberate practice and feedback.
Matt Gjertsen: Yes.
Why Human Skills Matter More in the Age of AI [21:26]
Shane Hastie: It's impossible today to talk about what's happening in organizations and teams without touching on the AI thing.
Matt Gjertsen: Yes. Before this conversation, I was looking back at all your past episodes. It's just like AI, AI. And it makes sense. If you're in software and you're not talking about AI, I don't know what you're talking about.
Shane Hastie: I'm going to assert that in the world of AI, the human stuff becomes even more important. How do we dig into that?
Matt Gjertsen: Yes, I agree with you. And from my perspective, I'll bring in some insight from at least what I'm seeing. As the head of Built, I'm selling, right? I'm out there talking to companies. I'm out there trying to bring on new clients. And I'll tell you, for the last at least 18 months, there was a big period there where I think we were thinking about are we going to need people anymore? There was a lot of de-investment, disinvestment in the people skills, the leadership skills. Everybody was pushing it off. And we've, in my opinion, turned the corner in all of the conversations, in the conversation, the core AI conversation, the AI conversation on what the impact is going to be for our society. And I'm seeing it in my business in that people are suddenly realizing, "Oh, we are still going to have people around. We are still going to need people managers."
And I would a hundred percent agree with you. I think it becomes all the more important. And the example that I always come back to is Elon Musk's explanation of what a company is. One of the ways he describes a company is through a vector sum, right? Every person in an organization is a vector. A vector is a magnitude and a direction, right? And so, the magnitude is how much skill and ability they have, and the direction is what they're pointing it at. So, every individual has their vector and an organization is just a sum of all those vectors, right? So, if you want to improve your organization, you have two options, right? You can increase the magnitude of the vectors or you can more tightly align those vectors so they're all pointing in the same direction. And especially that last part, that alignment is one of the key pillars of what it means to be a leader.
That's that center point of making sure people are working on the right things. And so, I think it's inarguable that in the age of AI, everyone is going to be getting more effective, more powerful. Their magnitude is going to go up, which means the alignment of them becomes all the more critical, keeping people going in the right direction. If you have somebody go rogue at the wrong time, I mean, whole databases will get wiped out as we've seen with agents. You got to keep that alignment. It's not just important with agents, it's important with people.
Alignment: What Separates Good Leaders From Great Ones [24:29]
Shane Hastie: I love that metaphor and it makes such a lot of sense. That alignment though, that's really, really hard.
Matt Gjertsen: It is hard, but it's the reason why leaders like Elon Musk or Steve Jobs or Jensen Huang are who they are. I don't think it can be argued, it could certainly be argued, but in my opinion, the key thing that makes them so effective is their startling ability to drive alignment amongst their people to present that long-term clear north star is one of the biggest differentiating factors of good leaders to great leaders, I would say. And it'll be really interesting to see what happens with Apple and their change in leadership of who is leading them now and the kind of north star that they will be able to provide. It's going to be an interesting case study and exactly that. So, the one more thing, I was thinking about this after I started playing around with AI a lot recently. I do not know how to code myself, but I'm always looking for ways to make my workshops more effective and practice is one of the most important things.
And so, I started using Claude Code to build a bunch of online apps that can be used to practice some of the things that I'm teaching in my workshops. And as I was doing that and reflecting on the book, I think the key thing that's going to hold back AI and going to hold back implementation of AI is that what AI really does is it makes every person a manager. These skills that we've worked so hard and had such difficulty training just like 10% of our employee population, everyone needs that now to be effective because every AI tool has different skills and abilities and can do different things well and less well. And so, just like that first pillar, it's maybe not building trust, but it's getting to know them, know their skills, know their weaknesses, know how to use them. The alignment piece we just talked about, getting your agents to work on the right things, setting clear expectations is incredibly important.
And then figuring out how to create feedback loops, whether that's building skills or getting different agents to review each other's work. All of these things fundamentally come back to the same thing that managers have been trying to do with people. And so, really the only difference is that maybe the agents aren't going to talk back to you in the same way or you don't have to worry about them giving you some strange look when you say something, but the fundamental skills are the same. And so, I could imagine a world where becoming a manager actually becomes easier because you're having to practice these skills so much, you just need to add a layer of, "Oh, well now I'm doing it with people, which is important," but historically I don't think we've had as much practice of setting expectations for others as an individual contributor. And now you need to with the AI.
Teaching Individuals to Take Advantage of AI [27:24]
Shane Hastie: Which goes back to our education but not educating individual contributors to think like that.
Matt Gjertsen: A friend of mine has a talk that she proposed or a panel that she proposed to South by Southwest that she was asking people to vote on. And it was something like why in a time with so many potentials and so many tools and more is possible than ever, do so many people feel uncertain and limited and they don't know what to do? And I think at least a part of it is because we've never had systems, broad scale systems in place, either at the company level or the culture level to teach people how to take advantage of a lot of these tools. And I'm not even talking about the technical ability, but just the way you think about what is possible, it's going to be a challenge. There's a lot to do, but the companies that invest in it, the companies that figure it out, I think are going to be the ones that succeed.
Deciding Whether the Management Path Is Right for You [28:26]
Shane Hastie: Coming close to the end, but what's the one important question I haven't asked you?
Matt Gjertsen: That's a good question. The question that I often get is where can I start? What's the single most important thing for people to do, especially for technical people to do? And one of the things that I think is really important, even though we already just said even individual contributors are going to have to develop these manager skills, I think it's really important to recognize, especially if you've lived your whole life wanting to be an engineer, wanting to build great code or build amazing tools, is you need to realize that becoming a people manager is a wholly new path. It is a different thing. It's a whole new set of skills. And almost by definition, that means you're going to lose ability in the thing you liked to do before. There's this book called The E-Myth that's about entrepreneurship.
And one of the metaphors that it uses is just because you like to bake bread doesn't mean you should start a bakery, because running a bakery involves all kinds of other stuff that has nothing to do with baking bread. And so, I think it's really important for people to understand just the different skill sets that are going to be required, the different things you're going to be able to do and ask, "Is that a path I want to go down?" I think the best companies today are companies that are creating two paths, developmental paths for their employees where you can develop as an individual contributor and you can develop as a people manager. They're two different tracks. Sure, the people manager track might take you farther, you're not going to get to the CEO on the technical contributor track, but the best organizations do that so that people aren't doing the, "Oh, I'm going to become a manager because that's the next step. I want to get paid more. I have to become a manager."
Hopefully, the people listening aren't in that kind of position. And if you're asking yourself, you need to be honest with yourself of like, "Do I want to go work on these new skills or do I just want to keep getting better and increase my influence as a technical contributor?" And if that's the road that you want to go down, you're going to be better off finding a place where you can do that than taking the manager role. Gallup has been doing research for 20 years on how engaged people are at work, and it keeps falling every single year. And the latest research, I believe it was managers, only 20% of managers are engaged at work. And so, if the managers aren't excited about coming to work, then what are their employees thinking, right? And so, the worst thing you can do is take on a manager role just because you think that's the next step. You need to really think to yourself of like, "Is this the path that I want to go down?"
Shane Hastie: Matt, a lot of deep stuff in there. If people want to continue the conversation, where can they find you?
Matt Gjertsen: The best place is definitely LinkedIn. I am really active on LinkedIn. I love having spirited conversations about this stuff, so definitely check me out there. I'll answer any questions go as deep as anybody wants to on any of this stuff.
Shane Hastie: Thank you so much. It's been a pleasure talking to you.
Matt Gjertsen: Thank you so much. It's been great.
Mentioned:
- Matt Gjertsen on LinkedIn
- Book – Minimum Viable Manager

articles.title: Google Domains Impacted by Recent ccTLD Hijacks
articles.text:
Google has disclosed that several of its domains were affected by a recent hijack of third-party country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs).
The incident occurred last week and targeted the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone), and .as (American Samoa) ccTLDs, putting all domains with those suffixes at risk.
“During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations,” the internet giant says.
According to Google, the Certification Authorities (CAs) that issued the certificates are not to be blamed, given the nature of the attacks.
Immediately after learning of the incident, Google blocked the unauthorized certificates for its domains in Chrome and worked with the issuing CAs to revoke them.
Analysis of Certificate Transparency (CT) log data revealed that multiple other organizations, including global brands and popular online services, have been affected.
“To ensure users of those sites were kept safe as soon as possible, we proactively blocked these certificates in Chrome. Where possible, we reached out to impacted organizations to alert them to our findings and actions,” Google says.
The internet giant notes that, while it took steps to identify and block the unauthorized certificates, certain domains might still be affected.
Google encourages domain owners to monitor CT logs for all their domains, especially for those in .gh, .sl, or .as, and to publish restrictive CAA DNS records to ensure safeguards after DNS control has been restored.
“Because CAs are permitted to cache and reuse completed domain control validation (DCV) checks for subsequent issuance, restoring a restrictive CAA policy, especially one that restricts issuance to specific authorized accounts and validation methods, prevents an attacker from using cached validation state to mint new certificates after a hijack ends,” Google notes.

articles.title: Starfunding: 10 of Europe's biggest celebrity-backed startup deals | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Celebrity investment in startups is nothing new, but the range of businesses attracting famous backers is expanding. Beyond traditional endorsements and brand partnerships, celebrities are putting capital into companies working on artificial intelligence, digital healthcare, clean energy, biotechnology and other emerging sectors.
Some are investing directly, while others participate through venture capital firms or dedicated investment vehicles. Their involvement can bring not only funding but also international visibility, industry connections and strategic expertise.
With that in mind, we’ve put together 10 notable celebrity-backed startup deals across Europe. The figures below reflect publicly reported investment amounts, funding rounds or financing arrangements, depending on what has been disclosed. Individual contributions are identified wherever possible.
Kylian Mbappé – Alan (France): €100 million funding round
French football superstar Kylian Mbappé, a World Cup winner and Real Madrid forward, became an investor and ambassador for Paris-based health-tech company Alan in March 2026 through his investment vehicle, Coalition Capital.
Founded in 2016, Alan provides digital health insurance and healthcare services. Earlier that month, the company secured a €100 million funding round, bringing its valuation to approximately €5 billion. It subsequently raised another €480 million in June 2026.
Although Mbappé’s individual investment was not disclosed, he is collaborating with Alan on initiatives related to preventive healthcare, mental health, nutrition and physical activity.
Leonardo DiCaprio – SolarMente (Spain): €50 million financing agreement
American actor and environmental advocate Leonardo DiCaprio, known for films including Titanic, Inception and The Revenant, became an investor in Barcelona-based ClimateTech startup SolarMente in 2024.
Unfortunately for both the founders and Di Caprio’s invesmtent, the company went bankrupt in April of 2026. SolarMente helped households access solar energy through a subscription model that reduces the need for large upfront installation costs.
That has not stopped Leo however, as he has continued his investment trends since then, having this week invested an undisclosed amount in Stockholm-based Energy-as-a-Service company Elvy.
Emma Watson – FabricNano (United Kingdom): €10.5 million Series A
British actress and activist Emma Watson, internationally recognised for playing Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter film series, joined the investors in London-based BioTech startup FabricNano in 2021.
Founded in 2018, FabricNano develops cell-free biomanufacturing technology designed to make industrial production processes more efficient and reduce dependence on fossil fuel-derived materials. Its technology uses immobilised enzymes to support the production of chemicals and other materials.
Pau Gasol – Luzia (Spain): €9.5 million funding round
Spanish basketball legend Pau Gasol, a two-time NBA champion with the Los Angeles Lakers and one of Europe’s most successful basketball players, backed Madrid-based artificial intelligence startup Luzia through his investment vehicle, Gasol16 Ventures.
Luzia develops a generative AI assistant accessible through messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram, allowing users to interact with artificial intelligence without downloading a separate application.
Elton John – Audoo (United Kingdom): €4.75 million funding round
British singer-songwriter Sir Elton John, whose career spans more than five decades and includes hits such as Rocket Man and Your Song, became an investor in London-based music technology startup Audoo in 2023.
Founded in 2018, Audoo develops audio recognition technology that identifies music played in public places such as shops, restaurants and gyms. Its goal is to provide more accurate data to music rights organisations and help artists receive fairer royalty payments.
Ibai Llanos – Plesh (Spain): €3.75 million funding round
Spanish streamer and entrepreneur Ibai Llanos, known for his massive online audience, the boxing event La Velada del Año and his involvement in the Kings League, entered the FoodTech sector in October 2026.
Together with former Barcelona footballer Gerard Piqué, Llanos led a €3.75 million financing round in Barcelona-based startup Plesh, a company developing chocolate snacks without added sugar.
Snoop Dogg – Sanity Group (Germany): €3 million investment
American rapper and entrepreneur Snoop Dogg, a prominent figure in hip-hop since the 1990s, has developed a broad business portfolio that includes technology and cannabis-related ventures.
Through Casa Verde Capital, the venture capital firm he co-founded, Snoop Dogg is connected an investment in Berlin-based Sanity Group in November 2021.
Founded in 2018, Sanity Group develops products and businesses in medical cannabis and consumer health, combining pharmaceutical expertise with regulated healthcare distribution.
Novak Djokovic – waterdrop (Austria): Seven-figure investment
Serbian tennis champion Novak Djokovic, one of the most successful players in the history of the sport.
In 2023, he became an investor and brand ambassador for Vienna-based startup waterdrop. Founded in 2016, waterdrop develops compact hydration cubes that dissolve in water.
Djokovic made a significant seven-figure investment, according to reports from January 2023. Although the exact figure was not disclosed, his personal commitment represents one of the clearer examples of an individually attributed celebrity investment in a European startup.
Diogo Dalot – Bioniq (United Kingdom): Over €1 million investment
Portuguese professional footballer Diogo Dalot, who plays for Manchester United and the Portuguese national team, joined London-based HealthTech startup Bioniq as an investor in March 2025.
Founded in 2019, Bioniq creates personalised nutritional supplements using blood biomarker data and AI-driven analysis to develop formulations tailored to individual needs.
Dalot contributed over €1 million to the company, joining fellow Portuguese footballer Cristiano Ronaldo, who had invested in Bioniq the previous year.
David Beckham – Guild Esports (United Kingdom): €272k investment
English football icon David Beckham, a former Manchester United and Real Madrid player and one of the world’s most commercially recognisable athletes, entered competitive gaming by investing in London-based Guild Esports in 2020.
Founded in 2019, Guild Esports was established to build professional gaming teams, develop esports talent and compete in international tournaments across major video game titles.
In June 2020, Beckham invested through his business DB Ventures, acquiring shares in the company ahead of its listing on the London Stock Exchange later that year.
Summary
While the amounts and structures vary considerably, the involvement of globally recognised figures can give young companies access to networks, visibility and opportunities that extend beyond traditional startup financing. At the same time, the deals highlight an important distinction: a celebrity’s participation in a multimillion-euro funding round does not necessarily mean that the celebrity invested the full amount personally.
As more athletes, entertainers and creators establish investment vehicles of their own, celebrity-backed startups are likely to remain a visible part of Europe’s innovation landscape.

articles.title: Apple reduz pedidos de componentes do iPhone 18 Pro
articles.text:
A Apple pediu a alguns fornecedores que reduzam a produção de componentes dos iPhone 18 Pro e iPhone 18 Pro Max diante de sinais de enfraquecimento da demanda. A informação foi publicada pelo Nikkei Asia nesta sexta-feira (9), que atribuiu o movimento à alta dos preços dos chips de memória e aos aumentos nos valores dos aparelhos.
Segundo o veículo, a empresa adotou uma postura mais cautelosa em relação aos envios desde o início de setembro. Os pedidos de componentes para outubro foram reduzidos em pelo menos 15% em comparação com os volumes solicitados originalmente, de acordo com pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto ouvidas pelo jornal.
A Reuters informou que não conseguiu verificar imediatamente o relato. A Apple também não respondeu de imediato a um pedido de comentário enviado pela agência.
A pressão sobre os custos de componentes está relacionada à procura por chips avançados e memória para abastecer centros de dados voltados à inteligência artificial. Empresas de tecnologia têm disputado a capacidade de fabricação desses componentes, o que contribui para a escassez e a elevação dos preços. O cenário pode reduzir os mercados globais de computadores pessoais e smartphones neste ano.
Em junho, a Apple aumentou os preços de iPads e MacBooks e afirmou que já não conseguia absorver os custos crescentes de chips de memória e armazenamento, impulsionados pela expansão da infraestrutura de data centers de inteligência artificial. O Nikkei Asia também apontou que a procura por dispositivos ficou mais fraca entre o fim de agosto e outubro, mas observou que a mudança pode estar relacionada ao novo calendário de lançamentos da fabricante.
A Apple apresentou a nova geração de seus smartphones de ponta no mês passado, junto com o aparelho dobrável Duo. O iPhone 18 Pro começa em R$ 11.999, enquanto o iPhone 18 Pro Max parte de R$ 12.999.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.
Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.
Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?
I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.
How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?
I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.
I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.
The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?
Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.
The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.
It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?
I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.
Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.
There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.
So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?
It’s definitely very early.

articles.title: Gobiernos evalúan regular los lentes inteligentes RayBan Meta ante preocupaciones por grabaciones
articles.text:
Gobiernos de distintos continentes evalúan imponer límites al uso de las gafas inteligentes, dispositivos que incorporan cámara y micrófono y que se popularizaron a partir del lanzamiento de las Ray-Ban de Meta. La preocupación central de tribunales, ministerios y asociaciones empresariales radica en que estos accesorios permitan fotografiar, filmar o grabar audio de personas sin consentimiento previo.
La discusión no se limita a un país ni a un organismo. Gobiernos nacionales, cortes de justicia, autoridades educativas y cámaras empresariales analizan en paralelo si corresponde prohibir el uso de estos lentes o restringirlo a determinados espacios, como juzgados, escuelas, salas de cine o lugares de reunión pública.
Qué países ya restringen el uso de gafas inteligentes con cámara
En Reino Unido, los tribunales de Inglaterra y Gales ya prohibieron el ingreso con las gafas inteligentes de Meta, en línea con las restricciones que existían previamente sobre la captura de imágenes y videos dentro de las salas judiciales.
La medida se suma a la decisión de los operadores de cines británicos, que según informó en agosto la Asociación de Cines del Reino Unido (UK Cinema Association) comenzaron a aplicar políticas propias para prohibir o limitar el uso de estos dispositivos durante las funciones.
En Estados Unidos, el Sistema Judicial Unificado de Nueva York dispuso la prohibición de las gafas inteligentes en todas sus instalaciones a partir del 20 de julio de 2026.
La norma alcanza tanto a modelos graduados como no graduados, además de cualquier accesorio para la cabeza que incluya cámaras, micrófonos u otra tecnología con capacidad de grabar video o audio. Quienes lleguen a un tribunal con estos lentes deberán entregarlos al personal de seguridad antes de ingresar.
Noruega avanza en una dirección similar pero con un alcance más amplio. El gobierno noruego anunció que prepara una prohibición temporal del uso de gafas con inteligencia artificial en espacios de reunión pública habitual, entre ellos parques, playas, museos, centros comerciales y eventos masivos.
Oslo, la capital del país, ya había prohibido en agosto de 2026 el uso de este tipo de dispositivos dentro de las escuelas.
Las gafas inteligentes con cámara, como las Ray-Ban de Meta, permiten grabar video, capturar fotografías y registrar audio de manera discreta mientras se usan como anteojos comunes. Esa capacidad de grabación encubierta es justamente lo que llevó a tribunales, gobiernos y empresas en varios países a prohibir o restringir su uso en espacios donde se protege la privacidad o se regula estrictamente la captación de imágenes.
Qué evalúan Australia y la Unión Europea sobre la privacidad
En Australia, el gobierno federal informó en septiembre de este año que estudia prohibir el uso de gafas inteligentes con cámara en los centros de trabajo gubernamentales, a raíz de preocupaciones vinculadas con la privacidad y la seguridad.
La ministra de Función Pública, Katy Gallagher, pidió asesoramiento formal a la Comisión de Función Pública del país para determinar si corresponde una prohibición y qué excepciones podrían contemplarse en caso de aplicarse.
En el plano europeo, la discusión se trasladó a los organismos reguladores de protección de datos y a varios legisladores del bloque. El Comité Europeo de Protección de Datos encargó un informe destinado a evaluar la aceptabilidad social de las gafas inteligentes, un paso que busca establecer criterios comunes antes de avanzar hacia una eventual regulación.
Dentro del Parlamento Europeo, la eurodiputada Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová instó a la Comisión Europea a considerar medidas específicas sobre esta tecnología. Hasta el momento, la Comisión no presentó ningún proyecto de legislación particular orientado a las gafas inteligentes, por lo que el debate permanece abierto entre los organismos comunitarios.

articles.title: Samsung pone el freno a la fabricación de móviles: “No hay beneficio, aunque vendamos”
articles.text:
Samsung está preparando un recorte en la producción de móviles para el último trimestre del año. Aunque la demanda de producto es estable, los componentes son cada vez más caros de conseguir para los fabricantes. La inteligencia artificial se ha convertido en el gran comprador de chips de memoria, dejando a Samsung y otros fabricantes con las migajas.
De acuerdo con MoneyToday, Samsung ha pedido a sus proveedores que reduzcan entre 20% y 30% el suministro para el cierre de 2026. Esto afectará la última parte del año, que regularmente es floja porque los compradores esperan a que la compañía presente sus nuevos móviles durante enero o febrero. Según los analistas, Samsung esperaba cerrar con ventas de 270 millones de dispositivos, pero ahora la cifra se quedaría en poco más de 200 millones.
Los recortes parecen algo inevitable en una industria que libra una batalla con la IA por conseguir componentes. Según la firma TrendForce, la memoria LPDDR5X de 12 GB se vendió en unos 130 euros durante el segundo trimestre del año, lo que representa un aumento del 175% respecto al 2025. “Debido al aumento de los precios de la memoria y los semiconductores, los smartphones de Samsung actualmente no generan ningún beneficio al venderse”, mencionó una fuente del sector.
Menos móviles y más caros: la triste realidad de Samsung
Mientras la producción se recorta, el precio sube. Samsung ha encarecido casi todas sus líneas de móviles y el último en sufrir la medida fue el Galaxy S26. Hace unos días, la compañía confirmó que uno de sus terminales más populares costará 100 euros más del precio original con el que se lanzó a comienzos de este año. La medida llega a menos de una semana de que se implementara en Corea del Sur y ya se resiente en países como España y México.
El Galaxy S26 base se lanzó con un precio de 999 euros, pero podía conseguirse por apenas 899 en la web de Samsung. Hoy aparece con un precio de lista de 1.098,99 euros, y si bien Samsung mantiene un descuento en su tienda oficial, el coste sigue siendo elevado. El único que se ha salvado de este incremento es el Galaxy S26 FE, que conserva sus 799 euros en la versión 128 GB, 899 en la de 256 GB y 1.099 en la de 512 GB.
La crisis de memoria también se ha cargado a los Galaxy A. Los terminales de gama media como el Galaxy A57, A37 y A27 subieron entre 40 y 50 euros. El más afectado de todos es el Galaxy A17 5G, que se posicionaba como una opción asequible para competirle a Xiaomi y otros fabricantes chinos, pero que ahora ya cuesta más de 200 euros.
Si estás pensando en cambiar de móvil, lo más recomendable es comprar un modelo del año pasado. Mientras la memoria siga cara, los precios seguirán subiendo y cada vez habrá menos unidades disponibles. Este fenómeno golpeará con fuerza al Galaxy S27, que superará los 1.000 euros cuando se lance a comienzos del 2027.

articles.title: Why identity needs a heartbeat, not a checkpoint
articles.text:
Think about what you had to do the last time you needed to prove your identity.
Did you present your ID? Snap a selfie? Pass a liveness check? In most cases of enterprise security, that’s all it takes to pass through. From that point, many systems effectively assume that the person who was verified remains the person controlling the session.
But that’s increasingly not the case.
Identity checks haven’t suddenly stopped working. Rather, fraudsters and criminals have learned to move around them.
VP of Corporate Affairs at AU10TIX.
The fraud moved past the checkpoint
The modern fraud playbook does not necessarily need to defeat the biometric check at the front door. Session-hijacking malware can take over after a legitimate login. Remote-access tools can turn a verified customer’s device into an attacker’s terminal. Fraud operations can even recruit real people to complete onboarding legitimately before handing the authenticated session to somebody else or to automated systems.
At the moment of verification, the identification document, the face and the live person could all be real. The checkpoint was not necessarily defeated – it was made irrelevant because it didn’t establish that the same person it verified remained in control five minutes later. I call this scenario the “tollbooth mentality.” It’s the belief that passing verification at login means a business can trust whatever happens afterward.
Identity is a heartbeat
The alternative is to treat identity as a continuous signal, a living, breathing thing – a heartbeat that should remain recognizably human and consistent throughout the session.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The raw material already exists. Typing cadence, navigation patterns, device and network telemetry and characteristics of how somebody interacts with a device can help establish a behavioral baseline at onboarding.
Those signals can then be compared with activity throughout the session. If somebody typing at a normal speed suddenly appears to generate thousands of keystrokes per minute, something has changed. If the natural movement of a handheld device suddenly becomes perfectly static, in a way more consistent with an emulator, that should affect the level of trust assigned to the session.
The question needs to shift from “did we verify this person?” to “does what we are seeing now remain consistent with the person and device we originally trusted?”
When that heartbeat changes materially, the system can increase the risk score, request additional verification or, in a high-confidence case, terminate the session.
Who is moving, and who is bleeding
The industries moving fastest are unsurprisingly those where fraud can translate almost immediately into financial loss.
Fintechs, crypto exchanges and neobanks have strong incentives to adopt continuous, risk-based session monitoring. They have also learned that adding more friction at the front door can punish legitimate customers without creating an equivalent obstacle for automated attackers.
A human has limited patience for another password, one-time code or identity challenge. Automated systems do not get frustrated. They can repeat processes at scale.
Businesses therefore cannot simply out-friction machines.
Sectors still anchored to one-time checks (particularly where knowledge-based authentication remains part of the security model) face a different challenge. In an environment where vast quantities of personal information have been compromised, static questions and credentials provide diminishing assurance.
A four-part framework for continuous trust
Just as the heart has four main parts, so too does the framework for treating identity as a heartbeat, not a timestamp.
Enterprise security experiences should be strong yet seamless, preventing disruption for low-risk customers while triggering proportionate intervention for anomalous behavior. For organizations looking to make that transition, the operational framework includes four parts:
- Baseline at onboarding. The identity check at the front door becomes the calibration event. Capture the behavioral and device baseline when identity assurance is highest.
- Monitor passively. Continuous does not have to mean intrusive. You can evaluate relevant behavioral and device signals in the background without repeatedly interrupting the customer to request more data. Identify the signals necessary to assess whether a session remains trustworthy.
- Escalate proportionally. Customer experience cannot go out the window in the name of security. Tighten thresholds for small anomalies. Trigger session termination for hard ones. This way, you’ll increasingly avoid insulting valid customers by asking for more proof that they are who they say they are.
- Hold the evidence. An evidentiary trail of risk signals and interventions can support investigations, audits and regulatory scrutiny. Ultimately, organizations must use this evidence to prove not only that a user passed verification, but that trust was maintained afterward.
As fraud moves beyond the capabilities of authentication, organizations must know not only who entered, but whether the digital heartbeat on the other side of the door still belongs to that person.

articles.title: Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
articles.text:
CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that’ll support the older, more affordable type of memory.
Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.
On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support “upcoming” processors built on Intel’s LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new LGA 1700 chips “expected to launch in early 2027.”
Intel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This backtrack stems from LGA 1700’s cross-compatibility with both kinds of RAM — an advantage over its successor that’s recently become much more important. Intel’s strategy may be to offer users the choice of a new CPU that doesn’t require them to switch to new, and very expensive, DDR5 memory, too. AMD is doing something similar: in August, Gigabyte also announced a new series of motherboards for AMD’s last-gen, DDR4-compatible AM4 platform to go along with the 10th-anniversary relaunch of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU.
DDR4 started hitting the market in 2014 and has since been succeeded by the much faster DDR5. Under normal circumstances, buying new hardware to use technology that’s over a decade old would probably be a bad investment. But the RAM shortage is changing the math, with DDR4 RAM seemingly feeling the sting of price hikes much less than DDR5.
I recently saw the price disparity first-hand while shopping around for new RAM after a DDR4 kit abruptly died on me. Right now, a DDR5 32GB Corsair Vengeance RAM kit costs $620, while the corresponding DDR4 kit costs $260. Even though it’s more than 32GB of DDR4 RAM typically cost back in mid-2025, that’s more than double the price for DDR5! Of course, DDR5 has significant advantages, like higher speeds and better power efficiency. But those perks might not be worth the current price of admission.
It could be years before prices drop again, a reality that’s starting to really sink in with the official return of older sockets and chipsets. But at least it’s a good time to hang onto your DDR4 RAM.

articles.title: Micromania ouvre les précommandes du display Cyberpunk TCG, le jeu de cartes qui a affolé Kickstarter
articles.text:
Lancée en mars 2026, la campagne Kickstarter de Cyberpunk TCG a atteint son objectif de financement (100 000 dollars, environ 85 000 €) en cinq minutes. Le jeu est conçu par le studio WeirdCo, en partenariat avec CD Projekt Red, le studio derrière Cyberpunk 2077. Les contributeurs ont reçu leurs cartes en septembre. Cette campagne a battu des records. Elle s’est terminée avec 28,35 millions de dollars (environ 24 millions d’euros) promis par 50 773 contributeurs. Kickstarter la présente comme le jeu le plus financé de l’histoire de la plateforme.
Le premier set, baptisé Welcome to Night City, arrive maintenant dans le commerce, avec des avant-premières en boutique le 30 octobre puis une sortie officielle le 6 novembre 2026.
Micromania prend déjà les précommandes du display de 24 boosters en version française, affiché à 139,99 €. Ce montant correspond au tarif de lancement. L’offre est limitée à un exemplaire par client et réservée aux détenteurs de la MégaCarte.
C’est quoi, Cyberpunk TCG ?
Cyberpunk TCG oppose deux joueurs, et une partie dure environ un quart d’heure. Chaque joueur recrute des alliés, les équipe et gêne son adversaire pour réussir ses missions dans Night City. Les personnages viennent de Cyberpunk 2077 et de la série animée Cyberpunk: Edgerunners.
Le display Welcome to Night City vendu par Micromania contient 24 boosters, chacun renfermant 12 cartes en français, soit 288 cartes au total. Le contenu de chaque paquet est aléatoire. Le display vise les joueurs qui veulent beaucoup de cartes dès le lancement pour monter un deck, et les collectionneurs qui cherchent les cartes rares du premier set.
Le set Welcome to Night City propose six niveaux de rareté, des cartes communes aux versions les plus difficiles à obtenir. Les collectionneurs pourront notamment tenter de mettre la main sur des Epic Rares et des Secret Rares, mais aussi sur les Iconic Rares, qui comptent parmi les cartes les plus convoitées. Ces Iconic Rares sont des versions à illustration alternative de cartes du set. Le contenu des boosters étant aléatoire, acheter un display de 24 paquets ne garantit pas d’obtenir une carte précise, même avec 288 cartes à ouvrir.
Chaque booster contient 7 cartes communes, 3 peu communes et au moins 2 cartes rares ou mieux. Sur un display, cela garantit donc au moins 48 cartes rares ou plus.
Investir dans le display Cyberpunk TCG vaut-il le coup ?
Proposé à 139,99 €, le display de 24 boosters revient à environ 5,83 € par booster, pour un total de 288 cartes. Ce tarif correspond au prix de lancement annoncé et ne constitue donc pas nécessairement une promotion. La précommande permet avant tout de réserver sa boîte en amont de la sortie, prévue le 6 novembre 2026. Micromania limite par ailleurs les achats à un display par client, une restriction à prendre en compte si vous souhaitez ouvrir plusieurs boîtes. Plus de 50 000 personnes ont soutenu le jeu sur Kickstarter, et le display pourrait vite se retrouver en rupture de stock.
Si vous souhaitez simplement découvrir Cyberpunk TCG sans investir une fortune, les boosters constituent une porte d’entrée plus accessible qu’un display complet, et sont vendus 5,99 €. En revanche, les joueuses et les joueurs qui veulent construire leur propre deck et les collectionneurs qui cherchent à obtenir des cartes rares pourront davantage apprécier les 24 boosters réunis dans cette boîte.
Pour apprendre à jouer, la gamme compte aussi deux decks de démarrage prêts à l’emploi, The Heist et Embracing Power au prix de 34,90 €. Ils sont disponibles en précommande chez plusieurs boutiques spécialisées.
