articles.title: John Cena ('Matchbox') compara la WWE con el cine de acción: "Las peleas en las películas son agotadoras"
articles.text:
Tras su paso por la WWE como uno de los luchadores más legendarios de la competición, John Cena irrumpió en Hollywood hace ya varios años para hacerse un nombre también como actor. Ahora es, de hecho, una de las grandes estrellas de la industria gracias a éxitos como Peacemaker o las sagas Fast & Furious y Transformers. Así, asume un nuevo reto, otra vez en el cine de acción y coches. Y es que acaba de estrenar en Apple TV Matchbox: la película.
En Hipertextual hemos podido entrevistarle a raíz de este reciente estreno, su segundo proyecto sobre una franquicia de juguetes de Mattel (recordemos que ya apareció brevemente en Barbie). Muy atento y dispuesto, se ha abierto de par en par sobre la película, pero también sobre su carrera. Y es que a lo largo de los años, además de en la comedia, John Cena se ha especializado en el cine de acción, como no podía ser de otra forma. Sin embargo, asegura que es algo muy distinto a la WWE.
"Es muy diferente. La coreografía en directo de la WWE me resulta muy fluida. Sabes que no vas a tener una segunda oportunidad. Casi no hay margen para el error. Si hay algún tropiezo, es en directo, así que es real. Es muy improvisado. Depende del intérprete con el que estés trabajando. Yo me consideraba más bien una persona de improvisación física. Y la historia se cuenta en menos tiempo", nos explica.
"De hecho, ¿sabes qué? Las peleas son tan cortas en las películas que parece que estuvieras peleando eternamente. Las escenas de acción en las películas, para mí, entrañan mucho menos riesgo. Porque las acrobacias espectaculares de la WWE no cuentan con cuerdas de seguridad. Es en directo, tal y como ocurre. Así que hay muchas variables que podrían surgir. Además, suele hacerse en un estadio ante el público. Así que hay muchas variables", comenta a su vez John Cena.
"La acción de las películas, como cuando [en Matchbox: la película] subo corriendo por el Puente de las Cadenas de Budapest o me cuelgo de un helicóptero, aunque me dé miedo, son totalmente seguras. Es solo cuestión de que un ser humano no debería hacer algo así y tienes que superar tus miedos. Pero es increíblemente seguro. Las peleas en las películas son agotadoras porque duran muchísimo. Hay que hacer muchísimas tomas de la misma coreografía una y otra vez desde diferentes ángulos", insiste.
"Mientras tanto, en la WWE suena la música, sales, haces lo tuyo, te diviertes, vuelves completamente agotado y, al mismo tiempo, lleno de energía porque decenas de miles de personas estaban súper emocionadas. Y luego lo vuelves a hacer la noche siguiente. Las peleas en las películas son preciosas y muy precisas, y se parecen mucho más a una danza en la que el ritmo, la sincronización y la distancia son fundamentales, mientras que en la WWE son un poco más fluidas", sentencia. En definitiva, y en contra de lo que pueda parecer a simple vista, para John Cena la acción de la WWE y la del cine no tienen nada que ver, son artes distintos.
Volver a Mattel
Con Matchbox: la película, como decíamos, John Cena regresa a Mattel. Esta vez como protagonista. Tras el éxito de Barbie, las expectativas podrían estar en tratar de alcanzar aquel fenómeno, algo a todas luces imposible. Pero el actor celebra la manera en la que la compañía entiende sus propios proyectos. "Esto es lo que me encanta de Mattel. Entienden que su propiedad intelectual es muy conocida. También comprenden el complejo proceso que supone tomar una propiedad intelectual que la gente conoce y con la que tiene cierta conexión, y luego llevarla a la gran pantalla en forma de película", sugiere.
"Cuando recibí el guion de Matchbox: la película, pensé: «¿Cómo demonios van a hacer esto? De niño me encantaba jugar con esos coches. Ya tengo una idea clara en mi mente de lo que es Matchbox. ¿Cómo van a trasladar mi pasión a la pantalla?». Pero cuando ves Matchbox: la película, no resulta para nada forzado", nos cuenta, orgulloso del filme.
"Y no teníamos a Mattel vigilándonos y diciendo: «Necesitamos más de esto». Son unos socios estupendos porque entienden que la propiedad intelectual ya existe y cuenta con una base de fans apasionados. El trabajo consiste en hacer una gran película. Tanto Barbie como Matchbox: la película son magníficos ejemplos de ello. Yo estuve presente en ambos rodajes y Mattel simplemente dejó que los creativos fueran creativos", prosigue John Cena.
"Estaría dispuesto a hacer cualquier cosa que quisieran adaptar, porque entienden que no tiene por qué ser una traslación exacta del juguete a la pantalla. Y creo que eso es muy importante desde el punto de vista de la propiedad intelectual como socio", concluye. Quién sabe, quizá en el futuro veamos una nueva película de Mattel protagonizada por John Cena. Al fin y al cabo la compañía cuenta con marcas de juguetes como Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, Monster High o incluso las cartas del UNO.
La colección de coches de John Cena
Si hay algo que los fans querían ver en Matchbox: la película, son coches. Y precisamente John Cena es el mejor actor posible para encargarse del filme porque, en la vida real, su colección de coches es inigualable. El actor siempre ha sido un gran amante de la automoción y en su garaje tiene decenas de vehículos, algunos de ellos absolutamente históricos.
Por ello, le hemos preguntado por el coche que más le ha gustado conducir en Matchbox: la película y que le gustaría añadir a su colección. "El que más pude conducir fue el Land Rover 6x6. Por extraño que parezca, al fichar para formar parte de una película llamada Matchbox, pensé que iba a estar conduciendo todo el rato. Resulta que mis compañeros son los que conducen la mayor parte del tiempo y yo me encargo de la mayoría de las peleas cuerpo a cuerpo. Así que fue un poco agridulce, pero al menos pude conducir ese Land Rover", confiesa.
"Bueno, y hay un Chevy que también está bastante bien...", recuerda entonces. Se refiere a un Chevrolet Camaro de 1969 de color azul que se convierte en un genial macguffin de la película. "No quiero dar pistas que puedan ser spoilers ni nada por el estilo. Solo diré que hay un par de esos muscle cars americanos de gran potencia. He tenido la suerte de poder conducir algunos de esos coches y son muy divertidos porque tienen un motor realmente grande en un coche muy pesado e inestable, así que tienes que estar muy atento", dice a su vez.
Y en el sentido opuesto, John Cena también tiene claro qué coche de su colección privada se habría llevado a la película si le hubiesen dejado. "El primer coche que compré con mi propio dinero es un Jeep de 1989. Me hubiera encantado conducirlo por el desierto del Sáhara, simplemente porque ese coche me ha acompañado en prácticamente cada etapa de mi trayectoria profesional. Así que llevarlo al Sáhara y huir de los malos en él, con todo ese caos a su alrededor, eso habría sido ideal para el Jeep. Me habría ido de maravilla, me hubiera encantado darle un papel en la gran pantalla", confirma.
Matchbox: la película ya está disponible en Apple TV.

articles.title: ‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop
articles.text:
“Staggering.” “Overwhelming.” “Unprecedented.” “Surreal.” “Pure insanity.”
‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop
Careers upended overnight, academics will have to separate solutions from slop while OpenAI moves on.
Those were among the descriptions more than three dozen mathematicians reached for in conversations with The Verge as they tried to make sense of the flood of mathematical results OpenAI abruptly dropped on the field this week. Amid the awe, excitement, and uncertainty over the sheer scale of the deluge was a deep-seated anxiety over what it all means — and what comes next. For all their different reactions, researchers agreed that simply understanding what OpenAI had released could take years, let alone figuring out where the mathematicians themselves fit in the field now changing around them. Many feared OpenAI would not wait that long before moving on — or releasing even more.
In all, OpenAI released nearly 400 AI-generated results. These were spread across more than 700 manuscripts and covered a diverse array of mathematical disciplines, including combinatorics, several branches of geometry, number theory, theoretical computer science, algebra, topology, probability and statistical mechanics, and mathematical physics. The collection is so vast that OpenAI felt the need to publish guidance on how to navigate the sprawling GitHub repository.
The sheer volume of work makes even a preliminary assessment as to exactly what the company has released difficult. In the hours and days following the drop, most mathematicians The Verge spoke with said they were still struggling to digest everything; several said that simply working through the roughly 40-page table of contents and abstracts took them the better part of an hour. “Just going over the entire list of abstracts is overwhelming,” said Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a professor of mathematics at the University of Connecticut.
Sprinkled among the hundreds of manuscripts are formalizations in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that allows results to be verified computationally. These formalizations have proven instrumental in assessing some of OpenAI’s previous mathematical claims, giving researchers confidence that a claim is logically correct even if they don’t fully understand the argument behind it.
“If the AIs would disappear now, as though there were aliens that came to Earth and then just left, we would be studying this for the next 10 years, trying to understand everything.”
But the degree to which each result had been verified varied wildly. On GitHub, OpenAI acknowledged that the results are “at different stages of verification” and that “many, but not all, of the manuscripts have been formalized.” As of writing, fewer than half the manuscripts in the collection appear to have been described formally. OpenAI said only 300 top-line results out of 719 manuscripts had been formalized, around 42 percent, and that it “will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them.”
Several mathematicians complained to The Verge about the lack of formalization, particularly given the sheer number of results, and stressed that even when Lean code accompanies a result, evaluation isn’t instantaneous. Researchers must check that the formalization actually proves what the result claims, another time-consuming process, and several digging through the papers said that even where computer-verifiable proofs had been provided, the quality was inconsistent and the statements they verified did not always appear to map neatly onto the claims in accompanying manuscripts.
Kevin Buzzard, a mathematics professor at Imperial College London, said he had identified numerous theorems in his area of work — algebraic number theory — of which only around six immediately “stood out.” Few, if any, of those appeared to be formally verified in Lean. “Hence, I either have to read possibly-not-correct slop, or wait for others to do the same, or wait for someone to formalise them before I can say for sure that the results are even correct.” Buzzard’s concerns were echoed by numerous other researchers.
Buzzard was far from alone in worrying about AI “slop.” The term is a shorthand for low-quality, frequently erroneous AI-generated material that increasingly crops up online — and in the real world — including academic papers. As in other fields, mathematicians told The Verge they have seen a huge uptick in such material produced with tools like ChatGPT and Claude in recent years. Much of it is confusing, hard to read, and demonstrates little understanding of the subject; it is especially shoddy when it comes to crediting other researchers.
OpenAI’s previous mathematical write-ups were widely criticized by experts for their sloppy nature, particularly their poor or nonexistent attribution. In conversations with The Verge ahead of the release, several researchers had taken to calling the impending flood of papers the “slopocalypse,” or similar variations on the theme.
Whether the feared “slopocalypse” actually materialized is difficult to say, largely due to the bewildering volume of material released. Early indications suggest OpenAI took more care with papers this time around, or at least with some of them. Several mathematicians told The Verge that their first impressions were far better than they had expected, though by their own admission that was hardly a high bar given the company’s previous shoddy publications.
“It’s a big mess. It can cause a huge collapse in the academic culture and simply kill most of the faculties. It’s a social problem and it seems that the AI labs are completely ignoring this issue.”
But better does not necessarily mean good, let alone up to the standards usually expected of academic work making claims of this magnitude. With formal verification absent for many of OpenAI’s claims, the quality of the accompanying papers becomes particularly important; they are the primary means by which mathematicians can confirm, understand, scrutinize, and contextualize the results.
Producing rigorous mathematical papers is difficult work under even the best of circumstances. Doing so at this kind of scale is a formidable undertaking. OpenAI’s models are pumping out mathematics at a dizzying speed and across a broad range of specialities, far outstripping the capacity of its human staff. The company simply does not have the breadth of expertise or resources to properly scrutinize its findings at the cutting edge of mathematics. Researchers told The Verge that it shows.
Many described papers that were difficult, sometimes practically impossible, to follow. “The write-up of the problem I know best made little sense after a quick read,” Brendan Hassett, a mathematics professor at Brown, told The Verge. “If this had been written by a person, I wouldn’t spend any more time trying to understand it. Of course, this leaves 721 other preprints!” (Hassett said this before OpenAI retracted three papers).
Some researchers told The Verge several papers they or their colleagues had noticed appeared to cover ground already trod by other mathematicians, though were wary of saying so publicly before they had a chance to properly review the material. Others pointed to the unusual brevity of the work, with results they would ordinarily expect to be developed over hundreds of pages compressed into a few dozen or less.
Nalini Joshi, a mathematics professor at the University of Sydney in Australia, said a quick search through the release revealed little that overlapped with her own work, but noted that some of the papers she examined “have short bibliographies.” Given previous criticism of OpenAI’s crediting practices, she said she is “wary that attribution in the papers may be lacking the complete story.”
But for all the slop and uncertainty, the overarching consensus is that the release contains some genuinely impressive work.
While stressing the difficulties assessing the volume of material — and the need to properly verify the results — numerous researchers The Verge spoke to said the work appeared to be of a very high caliber, despite shortcomings in its presentation. In a pre-AI world, they said, many of OpenAI’s results would clearly have warranted publication in top-tier journals and could have been enough to secure an academic career for their authors. A handful were described as being the kind of work that could make a mathematician a serious contender for a Fields Medal, one of the discipline’s highest honors.
“I either have to read possibly-not-correct slop, or wait for others to do the same, or wait for someone to formalise them before I can say for sure that the results are even correct.”
Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman said there were “tens” of results he would put in this category, including progress toward the Riemann hypothesis, a special case of the Hodge conjecture, and a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture. These are major problems in mathematics. Riemann — arguably the most notorious unsolved problem in the entire discipline — and Hodge are both among the seven famed Millennium Prize problems. Respectively, they are concerned with the distribution of prime numbers and, very roughly, how complex geometric shapes can be understood in terms of simpler building blocks. Kakeya, meanwhile, roughly asks how little space is needed to rotate a needle or pencil in every direction. A proof to the three-dimensional version of Kakeya was among the achievements NYU mathematician Hong Wang was awarded a Fields Medal for earlier this year.
“It’s not the case that these are just silly problems that no one’s ever heard of,” mathematician Scott Armstrong said. “Many of them are like very well-known problems that many people have tried for decades.”
As the dust began to settle, mathematicians were left confronting a landscape that had abruptly changed around them. Many of them had just watched years of work and carefully laid research plans evaporate in an instant, or knew colleagues who had. Across the field, whether reactions were laced with excitement, dread, despair, or something in between, there was a profound sense of disorientation.
By the following morning, that mood had not altered much. Speaking by phone as he walked through Paris, Armstrong imagined that, had the Sorbonne not been closed amid ongoing student protests and his colleagues were gathered around their usual coffee machine, the atmosphere would have been rather “solemn.”
In Scotland, Colva Roney-Dougal, a professor of mathematics at St Andrews University, described a similarly bleak atmosphere among colleagues and students. The deluge felt somewhat “horrific,” she said, but its arrival brought some relief after weeks of uncertainty. “I have a bunch of friends and colleagues whose grant proposals have just been wiped out,” she said.
“I have a bunch of friends and colleagues whose grant proposals have just been wiped out.”
Armstrong said he knew of one group whose entire research program was practically “wiped out” by the release. Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematician who was at the center of OpenAI’s earlier dispute over the Navier-Stokes problem, meanwhile, said he had already heard of “three people who had entire research programs obliterated.”
Similar stories surfaced repeatedly in The Verge’s conversations with mathematicians, though the disruption was concentrated heavily in some areas of the field. Francesco Fournier-Facio, a professor of mathematics at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland, said researchers in probability, combinatorics, and theoretical computer science appeared “particularly in shock,” adding that some regions of his field, group theory, had been “bulldozed.”
Armstrong and other researchers said some areas appeared to have been aimed at with almost military precision. “There were definitely some targets,” said Armstrong. He singled out work in the area Wang received the Fields Medal for this year, as well as several Millennium Prize problems. A cluster of results in mathematical physics, he said, makes it clear OpenAI is pursuing Yang-Mills theory — the mathematical framework underpinning much of modern particle physics — and its unresolved “mass gap” problem, one of the seven Prize problems.
Elsewhere, researchers expressed a kind of surprised relief at how little their own work appeared to have been touched. Roney-Dougal said her own corner of the field — largely centered on group theory — appeared to have escaped relatively unscathed. She joked that it is fortunate she works in a “very unfashionable area,” though later messaged to say she was feeling “unsure” after finding her work cited in one of the papers.
Joshi similarly found little overlap with her work, which is largely focused on integrable systems, complex systems that can be solved exactly. She suggested that may be because her field is less driven by long-standing, formally stated conjectures and definitions and more by questions that wax and wane with developments in physics.
As of October 8th, that record already listed numerous corrections, including revisions on more than a dozen manuscripts and the removal of three papers due to a “sign error” it says invalidates an argument.
Whether their own work had been directly affected or not, most mathematicians The Verge spoke to shared a sense that the field had crossed some kind of threshold and was no longer the same as it had been a day earlier. Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, called it “the most important single moment in the history of mathematics,” while Yang-Hui He, a fellow at the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences, reached back millennia, comparing AI-driven developments this year to the publication of Euclid’s Elements, one of the discipline’s most influential works.
Few researchers were quite so grand in their assessments, but there was a general consensus that mathematics was changing fast — and that mathematicians would have to change with it.
OpenAI knew the release would be disruptive and had made some effort to soften the blow and engage with the mathematical community. After several bruising encounters with researchers earlier this year, the company turned to mathematicians themselves for help, working with the newly formed Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) on how to release the results responsibly.
AGMAI had already laid out what it believed responsible engagement would be. AI labs should ideally release papers “that a human understands” or otherwise provide the necessary “support for the additional mathematical activities that are needed for humans to be able to understand and assimilate their AI-generated mathematical output and identify possible applications of it.” They said that, where possible, proofs should be formalized, and that companies should make public what models and prompts they used to create them. The group also urged AI labs to stop treating mathematical releases as “marketing vehicles to promote their models” and should “stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models” that are inaccessible to the broader scientific community.
“It’s not the case that these are just silly problems that no one’s ever heard of. Many of them are like very well-known problems that many people have tried for decades.”
OpenAI followed some of the group’s advice. It said it would be funding a series of workshops and conferences around its work in mathematics to help the community process and understand its work, though it provided no details as to what these might look like or when they may occur. The company also disclosed significantly more information than it had in previous releases — again, researchers said this was a low bar — including that its model attempted more than 4,000 problems and that a typical result used around three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute. It has also implemented “protocols for paper revisions and citations” and on GitHub said it “will preserve the public release history” of the collection. As of October 8th, that record already listed numerous corrections, including revisions on more than a dozen manuscripts and the removal of three papers due to a “sign error” it says invalidates an argument. OpenAI did not respond on the record to The Verge’s request for more details.
That change addresses a key source of friction with mathematicians, some of whom speak of a kind of “paranoia” around the company’s published claims. The company has shown a habit of surreptitiously altering press releases and papers in response to criticism without clearly disclosing those changes.
But OpenAI did not follow all of the group’s recommendations — including some of its most consequential. It did not identify the model behind the release nor did it disclose the prompts used or the full set of problems the model attempted. OpenAI also appeared to acknowledge that its formalizations were lacking — it said it will add more as it obtains them — and that papers were subpar, saying that “for future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding.”
“The write-up of the problem I know best made little sense after a quick read.”
Researchers The Verge spoke to questioned why OpenAI couldn’t have improved the quality of these papers and expressed disappointment that it seemingly couldn’t be bothered to formalize — or even check, in the case of the retracted papers — many of the results ahead of time. Information like the prompts used would have also been incredibly useful in lessening what many felt was the burden of assessing the flood of material the company suddenly dropped on them.
Most importantly, the company indicated it has no plans to stop testing its models on mathematics problems, and indeed suggested it sees doing so as an imperative. “We want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results,” it said when announcing its latest results. “This is why it is important to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields.”
After OpenAI offloaded its results, AGMAI described the publication as “a first step,” and reiterated calls for equitable access to compute and research tools. More fundamentally, the group argued that “the future of mathematical research cannot consist only of understanding results produced by AI labs.”
For all the hundreds of long-standing problems OpenAI claims to have solved, mathematicians say there is an extraordinary amount of work to be done. Many estimated that making sense of everything the company just released could take the community years.
Armstrong likened the sudden arrival of so much new mathematics to the commotion that might follow a brief extraterrestrial visit. “If the AIs would disappear now, as though there were aliens that came to Earth and then just left, we would be studying this for the next 10 years, trying to understand everything.”
Much of that will be exciting in its own right. Researchers will have to fill in gaps, extract useful ideas and connections, and place solutions in a broader mathematical context, all things that typically go hand in hand with producing solutions for humans. “For many of these results, relevant experts care deeply about the solutions and I am confident that they will be able to digest and present them to the wider world,” Lichtman said. Work involving explaining, verifying, and contextualizing results will need to be valued more as AI changes the fields, he argued. “As a society, we should be rewarding these digestive efforts more.”
There may be plenty of mathematics left for humans to do, too. As far as he could tell, Lichtman said all of the results, “amazing” as they are, come “out of existing methods and techniques.” They fill in parts of the known mathematical landscape rather than creating entirely new ones. “It turns out there is a lot more room to fill in than experts previously knew!” Lozano-Robledo echoed the point: “They are all using existing techniques in very ingenious ways.”
And the existing map is hardly the limit. “Math research is essentially infinite,” Lozano-Robledo said. “Research will go on.” The London Institute’s He said he was particularly excited to see what emerges next, speculating that researchers may end up creating new ideas and “maybe even new fields of math.”
The companies seem ready to move on instantly, long before the community has had any reasonable chance to digest what they’ve produced.
Few mathematicians The Verge spoke to objected in principle to AI producing new mathematics. Indeed, many welcomed it and, to varying degrees, said they were enthusiastic users of AI tools themselves. Most of the unease was directed at how the AI companies building those tools were going about entering their field.
Looking at the mathematical releases of OpenAI and other AI labs, you’d be forgiven for thinking that research mathematics essentially amounts to checking problems off a list. The manner in which AI labs unveil their results reinforces this idea: a flashy announcement, a preliminary write-up, and the rest tossed to mathematicians to figure out and contextualize. Multiple researchers told The Verge that the companies seem ready to move on instantly, long before the community has had any reasonable chance to digest what they’ve produced.
Researchers described that as an impoverished view of how mathematical research actually functions. Solutions certainly matter, but so does everything that happens on the way to finding them: developing ideas, making connections, and finding new questions or opening up other avenues of research. When companies like OpenAI just find answers without doing any of the surrounding work, mathematicians say the burden of doing so falls back on the community.
“It’s nice to have new results, but this scale is a different level,” said Bartosz Naskręcki, a mathematician at the Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań, Poland. “It’s a big mess,” he said. “It can cause a huge collapse in the academic culture and simply kill most of the faculties. It’s a social problem and it seems that the AI labs are completely ignoring this issue.”
It’s not just the mathematics that will take years to understand. Researchers are also struggling to comprehend what the upheaval means for them. Many described a bleak, almost existential mood hanging over the community as mathematicians decipher where they fit in the rapidly changing field. They may not have much time to figure it out.
Rumors are already circulating among mathematicians about further releases from OpenAI, which did not respond to The Verge’s questions about whether more are planned.
Roney-Dougal said she dreaded another drop — or the prospect of Anthropic or another AI lab entering the fray.
The disruption is hitting PhD students, junior researchers, and others without permanent tenure particularly hard. Open problems like the ones OpenAI’s models are plowing through can underpin dissertations, grant proposals, job applications, and years of planned research, all important building blocks for academic careers. Several researchers described an increasingly pervasive anxiety that the work they are building their careers around could suddenly be next and that the AI models generate few avenues for future inquiry as they close off others. “For someone at the end of funding or looking for a job now this is incredibly disruptive,” said Simon Machado, a mathematician at ETH Zurich in Switzerland who is joining the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS).
“Math research is essentially infinite. Research will go on.”
Morale may be particularly low because everything feels relentless. OpenAI’s findings have arrived in increasingly large waves, with little pause between them and frequent indications from the company that yet more are on the way. “You get a sense that they don’t really care about these individual results,” Roney-Dougal said. “It’s a really nasty feeling.”
Mathematicians barely have time to digest one set of results before the next, bigger set is dropped on them. “There’s going to be something in two more months that’s going to blow this away,” Armstrong said. “It’s just, like, repeated strikes by bigger and bigger bombs.”
Armstrong said he considers himself among the mathematicians most enthusiastic and optimistic about AI. He uses the technology in his own work and believes it has great potential. But even he is growing increasingly uneasy. “It is kind of hard to sleep at night,” he admitted.
Asked what he planned to do next, Armstrong was less certain. Still walking through the streets of Paris on his way to get lunch, he said his immediate priority was to finish some work he’d been doing — sometimes with the help of OpenAI’s Codex — “before OpenAI scoops us.”
Beyond that, even the self-described AI optimist was unsure and questioned what kind of future there was for him in mathematics. He worried particularly about the young researchers in the field. “It’s going to be a really weird few years in math,” he said.

articles.title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
articles.text:
We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
Could the drugs affect hair, nails, and vision?
This week my colleague Antonio Regalado had an interesting update on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. According to research presented at an aging meeting in Boston, these drugs seem to affect at least some measures of biological age.
Overweight and diabetic people who take GLP-1s have a biological age around two to three years younger than similar individuals who take a placebo, according to findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two pharmaceutical companies that make the drugs.
I’ve heard people in the aging field describe GLP-1s as longevity drugs for a while now (even if they only benefit people who are overweight or diabetic in the first place). This latest announcement comes after we’ve seen a raft of other benefits associated with taking these drugs. But there are also some weird side effects.
So far, GLP-1 agonist drugs—which repress hunger—have been approved for treating diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, and they can also be prescribed for some people who are overweight or at risk of certain cardiovascular diseases. But there is research to suggest they might also help people with substance-use disorders, and they’ve been investigated for potential benefits in neurodegenerative disease and cancer.
And a lot of people are taking them. According to a recent Gallup poll, 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024. And 15% of Americans say they’ve used one for weight loss at some point.
They can be incredibly effective. But, like any drug, they can come with side effects. And we’re still figuring out exactly what those might be, and how widespread they are.
The most common side effects are gastrointestinal—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. The drugs have also been linked to pancreatitis and gallstone disease.
Some claim that, in rare cases, the drugs might cause damage to nerves behind the eye. Dozens of people are suing Novo and Eli Lilly after developing a condition that can lead to sudden vision loss. They’re claiming that their symptoms were brought on by the GLP-1 drugs that these companies manufacture. Both companies dispute the claims. Research into the link is mixed.
We’re still getting to grips with the effects of weight-loss drugs on hair and nails, too. When Savanna Vidal at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC, and colleagues assessed electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations, they found that GLP-1 use was associated with an increased risk of hair loss. It’s still not thought to be common, however.
And at a conference in Austria last week, another group presented the results of a smaller study suggesting that 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder—in some cases involving nail detachment. Nail conditions were also fairly common among people who didn’t take the drugs, though. The authors don’t claim that the drugs are causing nails to fall out (as I’m sure 11% of the American population will be relieved to hear).
The side effects might look different in children, but there’s not much data on those at the moment. Still, pediatric side effects will be something to watch given that, between 2019 and 2026, there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for eight- to 11-year-old children with obesity in the US. Child prescriptions are still rare, but they’ve been rising.
On Wednesday, the World Health Organization released its first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents. Despite the scale of the issue—the WHO estimates that 70 million children aged five to nine were living with obesity in 2024—the organization explicitly says it does not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10.
“This recommendation accounts for the lack of evidence on both benefits and the potential adverse events and consequences of the different medications and/or their active ingredients on normal growth, development, physiological parameters, and mental health,” the guidelines state.
I get press releases about GLP-1s on an almost daily basis. There’s been a ton of research into these drugs, and there are probably hundreds of other studies underway. There will likely be plenty more on this from The Checkup as the evidence evolves.
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

articles.title: Linux founder Linus Torvalds says AI is a “gateway drug” into programming — but cautions about using AI for “serious” work
articles.text:
Linux founder Linus Torvalds says AI is a “gateway drug” into programming — but cautions about using AI for “serious” work
AI-generated code is putting immense stress on maintainers, Torvalds claims
For all the doom and gloom headlines AI is driving these days, one important person just gave a refreshing new take on it - none other than Linus Torvalds, the founder and key maintainer of the Linux kernel.
At the recent Open Source Summit, organized by the Linux Foundation in Prague, Czechia, Torvalds took the stage to reminisce about the early days of Linux, how he ended up building Git, but also how AI changed what it meant - and how it felt - to be a programmer today.
His key takeaway is that AI can make programming less intimidating for junior coders and teens looking to find their way in an otherwise scary, hyper-advanced industry.
“People love to hate AI. I think it's an interesting tool, very useful. It's a gateway drug and a way to do really good code,” he said, somewhat jokingly.
On AI and “sucking”
Speaking more about AI, Torvalds said that in his early days as a programmer, he made computer games which “sucked”, but it was fine because everything else also “sucked” back then.
“At the time, the bar was pretty low, right?,” Torvalds said, adding that he didn’t feel ashamed of his work when comparing it to what was already out there. However, younger coders walking into the industry today can easily feel ashamed of their “pitiful, small efforts”, when comparing themselves to all of the polished, professional work around them.
And that is exactly where AI can help, he feels. It can lower the bar to entry, so that those first steps don’t feel as meaningless and inconsequential as they otherwise might have.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“When you are getting into programming, the bar needs to be low enough that you can start the process and find enjoyment, so that you can easily learn. And it will take you a long time to learn,” Torvalds said.
But he also cautioned about using AI for “serious” work, especially when starting out. The person using the tool needs to know what they want to do, and need to know exactly what the outcome needs to be, if they want to use it properly.
Everything other than that is a risk that can come with grave consequences. So, it would be best to start with “toy” projects or personal projects, before using it for anyhitn more “serious”.
“I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you're doing something real and important. But I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug into programming,” he concluded.
Fighting fire with fire
Torvalds also touched on AI-generated vulnerability reports and patches. In mid-May 2026, he described the Linux mailing list as being “almost entirely unmanageable” due to it being filled up with useless AI-generated reports.
“The continued flood of AI reports has basically made the security list almost entirely unmanageable, with enormous duplication due to different people finding the same things with the same tools,” he said at the time.
“People spend all their time just forwarding things to the right people or saying "that was already fixed a week/month ago" and pointing to the public discussion”.
Torvalds now doubled-down on that assessment, saying the problem is that some people simply “don’t care”, and look for flaws in things no one even uses any more.
“We are getting a lot more of these random patches. Sometimes for very important and very real security issues, and sometimes for things that nobody has touched in 20 years, because people don't care.”
“When you put an AI bot on it, and ask it ‘Hey, is there a memory leak here?’, it will say ‘I don't care about the fact that nobody uses this driver anymore. I'll happily give you all the error reports that I can find’. As a result, the maintainers end up mixing “interesting” and “not interesting” patches.
“But on the whole, I think it is improving our code base,” he concluded.
The cost of that improvement is maintainer stress.
“It is also stressing maintainers out to the point that it's a problem,” he stressed (pun intended). “Yesterday at the maintainer summit, I'd say three quarters of the discussions were about how to make the AI tools - both code generation and the review - less stressful and more successful and more useful for everybody.”
“This is clearly a big issue.”
The solution, ironically, is not “less AI”, but quite the opposite - more AI.
“We are, to some degree, fighting the AI deluge of patches with our own AI deluge of patch reviews,” Torvalds said. “People are jokingly saying that there are bots talking to bots, and it does actually happen.”

In his career, spanning more than a decade, he’s written for numerous media outlets, including Al Jazeera Balkans. He’s also held several modules on content writing for Represent Communications.

articles.title: Unos astrónomos de Harvard han detectado una histórica señal de radio en el exoplaneta Beta Pictoris b
articles.text:
Por primera vez, unos científicos han detectado ondas de radio procedentes de un planeta fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar. A menudo, la detección de ondas de radio en el espacio se relaciona con la vida extraterrestre inteligente. Pero no te emociones pensando en eso. En este caso no tiene nada que ver. La medición se ha hecho en el exoplaneta Beta Pictoris b y, si bien es cierto que no está relacionada con alienígenas, sí que tiene otras connotaciones interesantes.
Auroras extrasolares. En realidad, no se ha localizado una onda de radio, sino una emisión constante. Gracias al radiotelescopio MeerKAT, ubicado en Sudáfrica, se han realizado cuatro sesiones de mediciones entre 2025 y 2026. Esto ha permitido detectar una emisión persistente, acompañada de ráfagas breves entre 0,85 y 3,5 GHz.
Según la interpretación de los autores del estudio, esto se corresponde con la presencia de un fenómeno llamado inestabilidad máser de ciclotrón de electrones. Es decir, con un mecanismo relacionado con la presencia de campos magnéticos, que normalmente da lugar a las emisiones de radio asociadas a las auroras de la Tierra, pero también de otros planetas del Sistema Solar, como Júpiter, Saturno, Urano y Neptuno.
Más sobre el origen. Beta Pictoris b es un exoplaneta de los conocidos como gigantes gaseosos, que se descubrió en 2008. Se encuentra a 63 años luz de la Tierra y se caracteriza por orbitar su estrella a unas 8 veces la distancia entre la Tierra y el Sol. Se eligió para estudiar posible actividad en ondas de radio porque su órbita de 24 años permite separarlo bien de la estrella. Además, la estrella es magnéticamente tranquila, por lo que no perturbaría las mediciones de radio procedentes del propio exoplaneta.
Cuásares como faros. Para hacer las mediciones, se usaron los cuásares como puntos de referencia. Estos son núcleos galácticos activos alimentados por agujeros negros supermasivos que pueden brillar más que galaxias enteras. Están tan lejos que, vistos desde la Tierra, parecen puntos fijos en el cielo, como una chincheta en un mapa. Por eso, se pueden usar como puntos de referencia para estudiar la actividad de otros objetos. En este caso, ayudaron a ubicar la fuente de las ondas de radio junto al planeta y no en la estrella que este orbita. Es justo el punto que ha dado problemas en detecciones anteriores de ondas de radio, por eso esta ha sido tan especial.
Lo que implica. Este hallazgo es importante por dos motivos. En primer lugar, porque ha sido la primera vez que se han detectado ondas de radio procedentes de un exoplaneta y se ha diferenciado con claridad de su estrella. Eso ya es un logro por sí mismo.
En segundo lugar, es interesante porque podría ayudar en un futuro a buscar exoplanetas que conserven su atmósfera, algo esencial en la búsqueda de vida. Y es que ya hemos visto que este tipo de ondas están asociadas a la presencia de campos magnéticos. Además, sabemos que dichos campos protegen las atmósferas de los planetas de la destrucción causada por el viento estelar. Por eso, si hay campos magnéticos, tenemos un buen lugar para buscar una atmósfera. No son una garantía de que vaya a haber atmósfera seguro, pero indican que, si la hay, puede sobrevivir.
No aplica a Beta Pictoris b. El exoplaneta del estudio es un planeta gaseoso. No tiene una superficie sólida en la que pueda proliferar vida. No es eso lo que podemos esperar de él. Simplemente, nos ha dado un nuevo punto de vista a la hora de seleccionar objetivos para la búsqueda de vida.
No estamos preparados. Beta Pictoris b es un planeta grande y relativamente cercano a la Tierra. Por eso, ha sido viable estudiar sus emisiones de radio con ayuda de MeerKAT. Sin embargo, según ha explicado a Live Science la astrofísica de Oxford Suzanne Aigrain, quien no participó en el estudio, ni este ni otros radiotelescopios están preparados todavía para detectar ondas de radio en planetas más pequeños y lejanos. Por eso, aún estamos muy limitados para buscar vida de esta manera. Sí que confía que lo estemos en un futuro.
De todos modos, aún queda un paso importante, ya que el estudio sobre Beta Pictoris b aún no se ha sometido a revisión por pares. Será necesario que un equipo independiente de científicos lo analice y confirme que está bien diseñado y que lo que afirma es plausible. Además, aún hay que confirmar que la señal pulsa con la rotación del planeta, de unas 8 horas, para confirmar que de verdad proviene del mismo. Hay indicios, pero se debe ahondar más. Hasta entonces, debemos tomar toda esta información con la debida cautela.

articles.title: Satélites russos preocupam Alemanha por possível ameaça à rede Starlink
articles.text:
A movimentação de satélites militares russos nas proximidades de um equipamento ocidental que fornece informações à Ucrânia levantou preocupações sobre possíveis ameaças à rede Starlink, operada pela SpaceX, de Elon Musk. O alerta foi feito pelo general Michael Traut, comandante do Comando Espacial da Alemanha, em entrevista à Reuters publicada nesta sexta-feira (9).
Em maio de 2026, quatro satélites militares russos, identificados como Cosmos 2610, 2611, 2612 e 2613, aproximaram-se de um satélite comercial de imageamento por radar. Segundo a Força Espacial dos Estados Unidos, os equipamentos russos realizaram manobras nas proximidades do aparelho, pertencente à empresa finlandesa ICEYE.
A companhia confirmou à Reuters que um de seus satélites esteve envolvido no episódio. A ICEYE fornece dados aos Estados Unidos e a países aliados, incluindo informações utilizadas para inteligência no campo de batalha na Ucrânia.
Traut descreveu a movimentação dos satélites russos como uma espécie de perseguição ao equipamento da empresa finlandesa. Para o general, a atividade demonstra capacidades que poderiam afetar constelações comerciais maiores, como a Starlink, mesmo sem um ataque direto.
“A Rússia está demonstrando maneiras que, se empregadas diretamente contra uma megaconstelação como a Starlink, poderiam afetar sua vida útil e a qualidade do serviço para todos os usuários, não apenas para a Ucrânia”, afirmou Traut à Reuters. “Isso me preocupa bastante”, acrescentou.
Como a Rússia poderia prejudicar a Starlink?
- Segundo o comandante alemão, uma possibilidade seria Moscou recorrer a táticas de interferência que não envolvam a destruição direta de satélites. Ele descreveu um cenário hipotético em que um equipamento russo entraria na trajetória orbital de um satélite da Starlink e depois se fragmentaria;
- Uma situação desse tipo poderia obrigar os satélites da rede a realizar manobras de desvio para evitar colisões. Essas manobras consomem combustível e podem reduzir a vida operacional dos equipamentos, além de afetar o funcionamento da constelação;
- Traut avaliou que um ataque explícito contra um satélite da Starlink representaria uma escalada significativa. Em contrapartida, ações de interferência indireta poderiam permitir que a Rússia pressionasse sistemas espaciais ocidentais sem recorrer a uma ofensiva aberta;
- Outros dois representantes ocidentais ouvidos pela Reuters também manifestaram preocupação com as atividades russas e seus possíveis efeitos sobre a Starlink, considerada a maior constelação de satélites do mundo.
Leia mais:
- Novos satélites Starlink são enormes – como isso afeta a astronomia?
- Sem Starlink, Rússia corre para lançar sua própria rede de satélites
- Starlink dá mais um passo para virar grande operadora móvel nos EUA
Alemanha prepara medidas de proteção espacial
De acordo com autoridades militares ocidentais ouvidas pela Reuters, a interferência russa nos sistemas espaciais do Ocidente aumentou significativamente desde a invasão em larga escala da Ucrânia, em 2022. As atividades relatadas incluem interferências eletrônicas realizadas a partir do solo e o acompanhamento de satélites em órbita para coleta de informações e demonstração de capacidades.
A Rússia não divulgou as capacidades dos satélites Cosmos envolvidos no episódio. O Ministério da Defesa não respondeu às perguntas da Reuters sobre a movimentação dos equipamentos.
Moscou já afirmou repetidamente que satélites comerciais ocidentais que ajudam a Ucrânia poderiam se tornar alvos legítimos de retaliação. O governo russo, por outro lado, nega realizar operações de sabotagem em países da Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte (Otan).
Diante desse cenário, a Alemanha está desenvolvendo satélites de inspeção e avaliando tecnologias orbitais capazes de interromper atividades espaciais consideradas hostis sem destruir os equipamentos envolvidos. As iniciativas fazem parte de um plano de ampliação das capacidades espaciais militares do país.
As Forças Armadas alemãs também concederam à ICEYE e a uma empresa alemã um contrato para construir dezenas de satélites, com atenção especial ao apoio ao flanco oriental da Otan.
A própria ICEYE tomou medidas após o episódio de maio. Segundo seu diretor-executivo, Rafal Modrzewski, a empresa reposicionou o satélite envolvido, o que foi seguido por novas manobras russas. Para ele, o caso demonstra como equipamentos espaciais podem ser aproximados uns dos outros tanto para observação quanto para causar possíveis danos.
A SpaceX, responsável pela operação da Starlink, não respondeu ao pedido de comentário da Reuters.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology.
News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program.
Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs.
Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”
Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program.
Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program. Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested, fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission.
While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras.
Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web. Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle.
Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department, have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

articles.title: Brendan Carr says he’ll let Pete Hegseth decide whether TV networks can air the public execution
articles.text:
FCC chairman Brendan Carr said he will defer to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on whether TV networks can air the planned execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Brendan Carr says he’ll let Pete Hegseth decide whether TV networks can air the public execution
The Pentagon is planning to livestream the execution of a convicted shooter, but the FCC Chairman says that the agency will ‘defer to Secretary Hegseth’ about if it will be broadcast.
The Pentagon has said the execution will be livestreamed, suggesting it’ll appear on an online platform beyond the FCC’s jurisdiction. But it’s common for broadcast TV networks to air live video of government events, and Carr’s agency does have a say over what happens on public airwaves.
“My understanding is it’s not on broadcast TV, so I don’t think there’s a role for the FCC one way or the other,” Carr said in a CNBC interview today. “But I trust Secretary Hegseth. He’s implemented the laws and the regulations that are relevant to the Department of War, and I think he’s doing a great job, and I trust that he’s making the right call on these issues.”
When asked if the execution would be allowed on broadcast TV if the Defense Department wanted it, Carr said it would be Hegseth’s choice. “Ultimately we’re going to defer to Secretary Hegseth and his decisions on how to move forward with this,” Carr said.
The Verge has asked major tech companies whether they will allow the execution livestream on their platforms. As of this writing, YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X haven’t responded to requests for comment.

articles.title: Temu und Shein: 3-Euro-Zoll zeigt Wirkung – ab November könnten Bestellungen teurer werden
articles.text:
EU-Regeln bremsen Temu und Shein aus – und die nächste Gebühr kommt im November
Die asiatischen Plattformen Shein, Temu und Aliexpress haben im dritten Quartal in Deutschland deutlich weniger umgesetzt. Die Erlöse gingen im Vergleich zum Vorjahreszeitraum um 35,5 Prozent auf 566 Millionen Euro zurück, wie der Bundesverband E-Commerce und Versandhandel Deutschland (BEVH) mitteilte. Das rasante Wachstum von Temu und Shein sei ins Stocken geraten, sagte Hauptgeschäftsführerin Alien Mulyk.
Als Grund für die schlechtere Entwicklung nannte sie die Verteuerung von Kleinsendungen aus Drittstaaten. „Den margenschwachen Niedrigpreisprodukten aus Asien setzen die höheren Abgaben deutlich zu“, sagte Mulyk. Der Marktanteil der drei größten asiatischen Plattformen im deutschen Onlinehandel ist den Angaben zufolge auf 3,1 Prozent gesunken, nachdem er zuvor stark gestiegen war und einen Rekordwert erreicht hatte. Im zweiten Quartal hatte der Marktanteil noch 5,3 Prozent betragen.
Onlinehandel verliert an Tempo
Die Zollfreigrenze von 150 Euro für Warensendungen aus Nicht-EU-Staaten ist im Juli weggefallen. Seitdem ist jede Sendung aus Drittstaaten zollpflichtig. Für Kleinsendungen bis 150 Euro ist pro Warengruppe eine Pauschale von drei Euro fällig. Ab November gilt zudem eine Bearbeitungsgebühr von zwei Euro. Diese soll eigentlich Plattformen und Verkäufer treffen, könnte aber auch direkt an die Kunden weitergegeben werden. So wären Händler bereits in der Vergangenheit verfahren, wie etwa Spiegel Online schreibt. Mit den Maßnahmen möchte die Politik die Einfuhr großer Mengen billiger Waren aus Drittstaaten in den europäischen Markt eindämmen.
Dem BEVH geht dies dennoch nicht weit genug. „Um für fairen Wettbewerb zu sorgen, muss die EU die Marktüberwachungsbehörden stärken und bestehendes Recht durchsetzen“, so Mulyk. Der Onlinehandel in Deutschland verlor im dritten Quartal insgesamt an Schwung. Die Umsätze lagen 2,9 Prozent über dem Vorjahresquartal. Die Inflation ist dabei nicht berücksichtigt. Zwischen April und Juni war der Markt noch um gut fünf Prozent gewachsen. Als Ursache nannte der Verband eine schlechtere Konsumstimmung.

articles.title: TeslaAI change de nom : la « super intelligence » de Donald Trump gagne du terrain
articles.text:
Donald Trump gagne du terrain auprès des acteurs privés. Le compte X consacré aux activités d’intelligence artificielle de Tesla, jusqu’ici connu sous le nom TeslaAI, s’appelle désormais TeslaSI. Le constructeur adopte ainsi les initiales de « Super Intelligence », l’expression que Donald Trump veut substituer à « Artificial Intelligence ».
Ce changement prolonge une initiative déjà soutenue par Elon Musk. Le 4 octobre 2026, le milliardaire avait annoncé vouloir rebaptiser SpaceXAI en SpaceXSI. Interrogé sur X à ce sujet, il avait répondu : « Oui, nous allons procéder à ce changement », sans préciser de calendrier. La branche à l’origine de Grok, auparavant appelée xAI, avait déjà changé d’identité après son acquisition par SpaceX.
Chez Tesla, le changement de nom du compte ne permet toutefois pas, à lui seul, de conclure que toute la division a officiellement été rebaptisée. Au 9 octobre, le site du constructeur présente encore ses activités sous l’intitulé « AI & Robotics ». Cette page détaille notamment ses travaux sur la conduite autonome et le robot humanoïde Optimus.
Donald Trump met la pression et menace les entreprises qui garderaient le terme IA
Pour rappel, cette impulsion vient de la Maison-Blanche. Le 29 septembre, Donald Trump a signé un décret demandant aux agences fédérales d’employer « Super Intelligence » et « SI » dans leurs communications, leurs sites et leurs rapports, dans les limites autorisées par la loi. Selon le texte, cette appellation refléterait mieux les capacités et le potentiel des technologies actuelles.
Juridiquement, les entreprises privées ne sont donc pas tenues de suivre cette consigne. Le président américain leur laisse néanmoins peu de doutes sur sa préférence. Le 8 octobre, sur Truth Social, il a présenté ceux qui continuent d’employer l’expression « intelligence artificielle » comme des « ennemis » de la Maison-Blanche, sans préciser quelles conséquences cette désignation pourrait avoir. Une manière de transformer un choix de vocabulaire en marqueur de loyauté politique.
L’adoption de cette terminologie dépasse déjà les entreprises d’Elon Musk. Dans un communiqué publié le 8 octobre, Nvidia annonce des engagements valorisés à un milliard de dollars sur cinq ans pour soutenir la recherche scientifique américaine, en employant à plusieurs reprises l’expression « super intelligence ».
Son patron, Jensen Huang, y présente notamment ces moyens comme une façon de mettre cette technologie à disposition des scientifiques américains, dans le cadre de la mission Genesis portée par l’administration Trump. Il serait toutefois prématuré d’y voir l’abandon généralisé du terme « IA ». En dessous de ce même communiqué, Nvidia continue de se présenter comme un leader de l’« AI » dans sa notice de présentation.
Cette évolution brouille aussi une distinction : la superintelligence désigne habituellement une IA dont les capacités intellectuelles dépasseraient largement celles des humains. Le décret de Donald Trump, lui, applique cette appellation aux technologies déjà comprises dans la définition légale de l’intelligence artificielle.

articles.title: Apple donne rendez-vous pour un événement imminent... et ne compterait pas s'arrêter là
articles.text:
C’est officiel, Apple donne rendez-vous pour de nouveaux produits dans quelques jours. Le géant de Cupertino vient d’annoncer une présentation pour le mardi 13 octobre, sous le slogan « Welcome Home ». Comme d’habitude, la firme n’a rien dévoilé des produits au programme de l’événement. Notez qu’il ne s’agit vraisemblablement pas d’une keynote traditionnelle, mais d’un événement presse, organisé à New York. Selon Bloomberg, une vidéo retransmise en ligne est néanmoins prévue.
 Welcome home. October 13. https://t.co/ChelGSDOTI
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 8, 2026
Un HomePod avec écran
La star de l’événement prendrait la forme d‘un HomePod avec écran. Évoqué comme le croisement entre un iPad et un HomePod, l’appareil serait doté d’un écran carré d’environ 6 pouces. Taillé pour être disposé dans la cuisine, il servirait à piloter les objets connectés de la maison, à passer des appels FaceTime, à regarder des vidéos ou encore à consulter la météo et son agenda. Pour converser avec l’appareil, il faudrait s’adresser au nouveau Siri dopé à l’IA.
L’appareil, souvent baptisé HomePad dans les fuites, devrait embarquer une caméra et un capteur de présence, qui lui permettraient de reconnaître la personne présente dans la pièce. En fonction de la personne identifiée, l’écran pourrait afficher une interface personnalisée. Une version murale et une version posée sur un socle seraient dans les cartons. Côté prix, la rumeur évoque environ 350 dollars.
Ce n’est pas tout. Le HomePod mini devrait lui aussi être renouvelé, avec de nouveaux coloris, une puce réseau N1, et un processeur plus rapide, compatible avec Siri IA. Une nouvelle Apple TV 4K serait également prévue. Le boîtier profiterait d’une puce A19 ou A19 Pro, de plus de mémoire, de la puce N1 et d’une télécommande Siri améliorée. Dans la foulée, Apple dévoilerait la gamme de produits domotique développée avec LG.
Un troisième événement fin octobre
Apple ne compterait pas s’arrêter en si bon chemin. Après avoir levé le voile sur l’iPhone Duo et une armée de produits pour la maison connectée, la marque préparerait une troisième vague d’annonces à la fin du mois pour boucler l’année. Selon le journaliste Mark Gurman de Bloomberg, la troisième présentation aurait lieu « autour du » mardi 27 octobre 2026.
 NEW: Apple’s big October will continue on the 27th with a second event to launch the first touch-screen MacBooks, OLED iPad mini and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro & iMac. It follows the smart home launch this coming Tuesday the 13th. https://t.co/bh8Vqdgnr8 https://t.co/wmlNWXC41n
— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 8, 2026
Le produit le plus attendu de l’événement est un MacBook Pro recouvert d’un écran OLED tactile. Évoqué sous le nom de MacBook Ultra dans les fuites, il serait plus fin et plus léger que les ordinateurs actuels. Apple annoncerait aussi un MacBook Pro 14 pouces M6, un iMac M6, et un iPad mini avec écran OLED. Bref, le mois d’octobre s’annonce chargé chez Apple.

articles.title: Anthropic ya incluye "cláusulas de abuso contra Claude" en sus términos de uso para proteger a sus modelos de IA
articles.text:
El bienestar de Claude importa. Al menos, le importa a Anthropic. Dario Amodei, el máximo responsable de este laboratorio, ha expresado en varias ocasiones su preocupación por los abusos a los que pueden ser sometidos sus modelos de inteligencia artificial (IA) por parte de los usuarios. Y va a tomar cartas en el asunto. A partir del próximo 12 de noviembre, Anthropic prohibirá que los usuarios mantengan un comportamiento abusivo o cruel hacia Claude de forma prolongada e injustificada. El modelo podrá poner fin a esas conversaciones.
Anthropic presentó la actualización de sus términos de uso ayer, por lo que los usuarios tenemos poco más de un mes para interiorizar esta restricción. Sea como sea, hay una idea derivada de esta decisión sobre la que merece la pena reflexionar. Hasta ahora ningún laboratorio de IA o investigador independiente ha demostrado que los modelos de frontera puedan sufrir. Por supuesto, Anthropic no ha defendido en ningún momento que Claude haya adquirido consciencia. Sin embargo, esta medida es muy real.
Habría sido muy interesante que los términos de uso de Claude explicasen con claridad por qué este laboratorio ha tomado esta decisión. Por el momento no conocemos cuál es su motivación más allá de la perspectiva ética, pero no tenemos otra opción que acatarla. De lo contrario, seremos penalizados. De hecho, los modelos de IA de Anthropic tienen la capacidad de abandonar cualquier conversación si "consideran" que el usuario está manteniendo un comportamiento abusivo de una forma persistente tanto en Claude.ai como en Claude Code.
UN VISTAZO A...
En contra de la propaganda y la manipulación
En sus términos de uso, Anthropic aclara que su nueva política ha sido ideada para ser aplicada únicamente en casos extremos, en los que los usuarios se comportan repetidamente de forma cruel con los modelos de IA sin ningún propósito discernible. No obstante, en teoría los usuarios podemos seguir expresando nuestra frustración y discrepancia con las respuestas que nos entregan los modelos sin miedo a ser sancionados. Incluso, según Anthropic, podemos emitir críticas si están justificadas.
Anthropic se ha dado cuenta de que sus modelos están siendo utilizados en redes de cuentas falsas y operaciones de influencia
Todo esto es bastante críptico. Incluso un poco perturbador. Pero hay algo interesante que nos interesa conocer: Anthropic ha investigado cómo reaccionan sus modelos de IA frente a interacciones de los usuarios que podrían ser perjudiciales para ellos, y ha reconocido que por el momento no sabe si estos comportamientos tienen algún impacto de tipo moral en Claude. Su postura en este escenario consiste en adoptar medidas preventivas de bajo coste si existe la posibilidad de que estos sistemas merezcan algún tipo de consideración moral.
Hay otro punto importante en la actualización de los términos de uso de Claude en el que merece la pena que nos detengamos. Anthropic ha repensado sus normas para prohibir de una manera más contundente las campañas engañosas que utilizan cuentas falsas, publicaciones artificiales o sitios web de noticias con el propósito de ocultar quién está detrás de un mensaje y amplificar su difusión. Al parecer, se ha dado cuenta de que sus modelos están siendo utilizados en redes de cuentas falsas y operaciones de influencia.
Además, los nuevos términos de uso contemplan prohibiciones sobre la manipulación electoral, incluida la difusión de información falsa para engañar a los votantes, hacerse pasar por autoridades electorales o desincentivar la participación. Anthropic asegura que esta actualización de sus normas es necesaria debido a que sus modelos de IA cada vez son más capaces, y este desarrollo de sus prestaciones requiere revisar para qué los estamos utilizando los usuarios y cómo nos relacionamos con ellos.

articles.title: Canal+ relance Sport+ : une plateforme gratuite qui va ravir les fans de sport
articles.text:
La rumeur enflait de plus en plus depuis la fin du mois de septembre 2026 et elle était fondée. Canal+ a officialisé ce jeudi 8 octobre l’arrivée de Sport+, une nouvelle plateforme gratuite, accessible à tous directement depuis l’application Canal+, même sans abonnement.
Les plus attentifs auront remarqué que Sport+ était le nom d’une chaîne sportive du groupe, baptisée ainsi en 2002 et arrêtée en juin 2015. Elle revient donc 11 ans après sous une forme modernisée, conçue pour répondre aux nouveaux usages, notamment mobiles.
Pensé pour le mobile, Sport+ vous donne un aperçu des grandes compétitions
Le diffuseur ne le cache pas : Sport+ est « une porte d’entrée vers les contenus Canal+ », autrement dit ceux pour lesquels il faut payer. Pour vous convaincre, Canal+ y propose « des images exclusives, des résumés, des shorts vidéo verticaux, une sélection de rencontres gratuites et les émissions sportives emblématiques de Canal+ ».
Pour accéder à certains contenus, il faut tout de même créer un compte Canal+, gratuit. Sur mobile, Sport+ se découpe en trois onglets : Shorts, Calendrier et Live & Replay. Le tout est financé par la publicité.
    À lire aussi : 
Canal+ pourrait faire payer la hausse de sa TVA à ses abonnés
Neuf compétitions dont Canal+ détient les droits de diffusion sont représentées : la Ligue des champions, la Ligue Europa, la Ligue Conférence, l’Arkema Première Ligue, la Premier League anglaise, la Formule 1, le MotoGP, ainsi que le Top 14 et le Pro D2 de rugby.
Pour les matchs en direct, Canal+ mise sur le Multi-Live, qui permet de suivre jusqu’à neuf rencontres en même temps sous forme de vignettes. Pour en regarder une seule en plein écran, il faut en revanche un abonnement payant. Sport+ est accessible dans l’application Canal+ sur smartphone comme sur téléviseur.
Sport+ est également doté d’un mode « anti-spoil », qui masque les résultats. Pratique pour parcourir la plateforme sans voir le score du match ou le vainqueur de la course que l’on compte regarder plus tard.
Sport+ regroupe aussi les chaînes gratuites Red Bull TV et After Foot TV, que Canal+ avait récemment ajoutées à son application. Les résultats en direct, les statistiques, les classements et les calendriers sont accessibles sans abonnement.
Disponibilité
Sport+ est disponible depuis ce vendredi 9 octobre, en France métropolitaine. Premier contenu diffusé gratuitement en intégralité sur la plateforme ce dimanche 11 octobre à 14h : le Grand Prix de Singapour de Formule 1.
Le Grand Prix de Singapour ouvre une série : Canal+ prévoit une douzaine d’événements sportifs diffusés gratuitement par saison. L’essentiel des compétitions reste en revanche réservé aux abonnés.
