articles.title: On connait les prix de la version GTI de la très intéressante Volkswagen ID. Pol
articles.text:
Du côté de Wolfsburg, le coup d’accélérateur est mis sur la gamme des voitures électriques. Après le lancement commercial de la Volkswagen ID. Polo, c’est la version GTI qui débarque. Une déclinaison plus dynamique de la citadine électrique. Voici les prix de la nouvelle Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI.
Un tarif plutôt salé
Alors que la Volkswagen ID. Polo débute à 24 995 euros avant l’aide du bonus écologique dans sa version Trend avec une batterie de 37 kWh et une motorisation de 116 chevaux, il faut compter 41 450 euros avant déduction de la prime coup de pouce CEE pour la GTI.
La différence de prix est importante pour deux déclinaisons d’un même modèle. Toutefois, on observe aussi ces différences entre les prix de la Renault 5 E-Tech et de l’Alpine A290 vendue 39 500 euros, mais aussi de la Peugeot e-208 et de la Peugeot e-208 GTI à partir de 42 900 euros. C’est aussi le cas pour la cousine Cupra Raval qui débute à 25 995 euros et voit son prix passer à 42 000 euros avec une motorisation très proche de celle de l’ID. Polo GTI.
Une voiture finalement peu comparable
La différence de prix s’explique par une différence de fiche technique importante. La version GTI de l’ID. Polo embarque un moteur électrique de 226 chevaux et 290 Nm de couple, ce qui lui permet d’atteindre 100 km/h en 6,8 secondes. La vitesse maximale est de 190 km/h. La motorisation n’est finalement pas si différente de celle de l’ID. Polo 211 chevaux. La batterie de 52 kWh est une NMC permettant une autonomie de 431 km, ce qui est bien plus généreux que les 375 km (avec pneus Hankook) de la Peugeot e-208 GTI.
Mais c’est la partie châssis et trains roulants qui évolue franchement. Pour gérer la puissance de 226 chevaux sur le train avant, Volkswagen ajoute un blocage de différentiel électronique pensé pour éviter le patinage et le sous-virage. Elle est équipée de série de la suspension à double valve DCC (Dynamic Chassis Control), capable d’adapter le comportement des amortisseurs au mode de conduite souhaité.
Le style est aussi spécifique. Volkswagen équipe cette version ID. Polo GTI de jantes de 19 pouces au design dédié, mais aussi d’un kit carrosserie sur mesure comprenant une calandre avant en nid d’abeille, un aileron arrière ou encore des liserés rouges typiques des GTI. On peut noter dans l’habitacle des sièges sport avec sellerie à motif GTI, un mode d’affichage sur le compteur numérique simulant les compteurs à aiguille des anciennes GTI et enfin un mode de conduite spécifique.
Ainsi, l’ID. Polo GTI est la première voiture électrique de Volkswagen à porter la mythique appellation sportive. Elle tend à lui faire honneur, d’autant plus que Volkswagen fête cette année les 50 ans de la première Golf GTI.

articles.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026
A recap of the latest Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from September 2026
At AWS, we believe the fastest path to enterprise AI is giving builders real choice at every layer: model, runtime, and tooling. That belief shapes how we invest across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands. Amazon Bedrock continues expanding access to leading frontier models so you can build and scale AI applications securely. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the managed infrastructure to build, connect, and deploy enterprise agents using any framework or model. Strands gives you an open source toolkit to build agents and run anywhere.
As AI models become more capable and model choice expands, the industry conversations are shifting. Model performance is no longer the only question. Customers now weigh cost against benefit for their specific use case, and those decisions matter when delegating work to agents in production. AI agents are already moving into workflows that require them to reason over enterprise knowledge, operate across long-horizon tasks, and act in systems where security, accuracy, and governance matter. The focus is now shifting beyond the model itself to the broader system around it, including the context agents can access, the actions they can take, and how enterprise data is governed and protected.
In September, updates across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands strengthened those foundations. New capabilities expanded model choice, made agent operations more efficient and measurable, and created more direct ways to connect AI applications with current business information.
Run faster agents and evaluate what matters
Build agents optimized for OpenAI models. Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents, powered by OpenAI, is now available in public preview, helping you build production-ready AI agents without sacrificing enterprise security. You can now use OpenAI models while keeping data within AWS, reuse existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and maintain full auditability through AWS CloudTrail. Durable sessions and built-in human approval workflows help reduce development overhead and mitigate risk.
Agents now start faster with less infrastructure overhead. The latest AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, has more efficient memory management and lower cold start latency for serverless agents, so you pay for actual usage rather than the peak memory. You can run agents faster at lower cost with pay-as-you-go pricing and no need to pre-provision capacity. Sessions scale to zero when idle and run in hardware-isolated environments.
Lower your token cost with frontier performance. Strands harness is a new open source agent harness that matches popular harnesses on accuracy while using 28 percent fewer tokens. You can spin up a production-ready agent in a single line of Python or TypeScript, with built-in context management, prompt caching, and memory, then deploy it anywhere.
Let your models make big decisions safely, locally. Strands Decider 2B is a small, open source, 2B-parameter decision model that picks between predefined options (instead of generating text), delivering answers in ~115ms locally. It’s optimized for agentic AI tasks like tool selection, routing, and guardrails, with all code, data, and weights available on GitHub and Hugging Face.
Find the right model for each workload
Choose from a broader set of OpenAI models for your everyday work. OpenAI’s Astra, Sol, and Luna models are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, with options for demanding projects, recurring complex work, and high-volume tasks.
GPT-6 Astra is the flagship model for your most ambitious work, bringing deeper reasoning to complex decisions, document analysis, and software development with up to 1 million input tokens. It brings stronger reasoning and more precise judgment to complex business decisions, operates across software and files, and delivers professional-quality output aligned with organizational voice, templates, and standards. GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast adds a premium speed tier for GPT-6 Astra, built for workloads where speed matters most. It delivers up to 6x faster inference in the API, with up to 300 tokens per second.
Sol brings near-Astra intelligence to coding, computer use, and professional workloads that run frequently. Both GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Sol are available on Amazon Bedrock. GPT 6.1 Luna is designed for high-volume tasks such as extraction, summarization, classification, and routing. Together, they help you balance intelligence, latency, and cost across workloads.
Take on long-running coding and research with Claude. Model choices for Claude now include the latest versions to advance your coding and scientific work. Claude Fable 5.1 expands options for coding, scientific research, and enterprise workflows. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for agentic coding, knowledge work, and long-running tasks. It uses adaptive thinking to gauge how much reasoning a task needs and an effort parameter to set an upper bound on reasoning depth. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a smarter, more efficient Sonnet suited to focused coding and knowledge work, delivering 30 percent lower cost per task at 30 percent faster speed than Claude Sonnet 5.
Reason through complexity with a broader model portfolio. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. According to Moonshot AI, Kimi K3 is its most capable model and the first open model to reach 2.8 trillion parameters. With a 1-million-token context window, native vision, and built-in prompt caching, it helps you build smarter apps 2.5x faster at lower cost than previous versions.
xAI’s frontier models Grok 4.6 and Grok 4.7 offer a 500K token context window and support configurable reasoning effort and self-verification for more reliable long-running tasks.
Together, these additions give you more flexibility when matching models to your requirements such as context length, latency, throughput, and cost.
Get more control over your enterprise AI agents
Keep agent knowledge current. With new automatic sync scheduling in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can now configure daily, weekly, and monthly refresh options for all native data-source connectors. As a result, your enterprise AI agents retrieve the latest information. The user-managed setup for SharePoint, OneDrive, and Confluence reduces reliance on admin-managed service accounts when you already have the access you need.
Connect more enterprise sources without maintaining custom ingestion pipelines. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports ServiceNow, Confluence Data Center, Salesforce, and Zendesk as native connectors to handle data crawling, metadata extraction, and incremental sync automatically. These connectors reduce the amount of custom ingestion code you need to build and maintain support content, internal documentation, and operational knowledge.
Get started
Explore Amazon Bedrock, deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI, or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK.
Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation.

articles.title: Cyberpunk 2077 : un film live est en route avec déjà un gros point positif
articles.text:
Confirmée simultanément par Deadline et Variety ce 8 octobre 2026, l’information a été rapidement validée par Michał Nowakowski, co-PDG du studio polonais : la machine est lancée, et Hollywood compte bien traire la vache jusqu’à la dernière goutte de chrome. Un film Cyberpunk 2077 arrive.
Un producteur de Transformers aux commandes de Cyberpunk 2077
Aux manettes de cette adaptation live-action de Cyberpunk 2077, on retrouve Lorenzo di Bonaventura, le producteur historique derrière la saga Transformers. Habitué aux grosses productions hollywoodiennes, autant dire qu’il sait comment emballer des explosions à 200 millions de dollars et faire briller du métal tordu à l’écran. C’est très positif et les premiers retours sur le sujet sont encourageants.
Si CD Projekt Red fait partie de la boucle pour garder un œil sur le lore et éviter un massacre pur et simple, aucun réalisateur, scénariste ou casting n’a encore été officialisé. La question qui brûle déjà les lèvres des 40 millions d’acheteurs du jeu vidéo : Keanu Reeves rempilera-t-il dans le rôle de Johnny Silverhand, ou le rôle sera-t-il recasté pour lancer une toute nouvelle trame dans les bas-fonds de Night City ?
Hollywood ne sait plus quoi inventer et pille dans les jeux vidéo
Cette adaptation de Paramount n’a rien d’un hasard créatif : c’est un pur calcul d’épicier. Après les cartons au box-office et en streaming de The Last of Us, Fallout, Mario ou Minecraft, les studios de cinéma ont définitivement acté que les bandes dessinées ne suffisaient plus. Les jeux vidéo sont devenus le nouvel eldorado des dirigeants d’Hollywood, qui rachètent les droits à tour de bras (même pour des projets aussi improbables qu’un film Arc Raiders).
Pour Paramount, fraîchement restructuré et fusionné, réussir le portage de Cyberpunk 2077 est un test majeur. Transformer une expérience immersive à la première personne portée sur la violence crue, les néons, la nudité et les implants cybernétiques en une superproduction rentable sans édulcorer l’essence même du titre : voilà le vrai défi. Rendez-vous dans les salles quand la poussière de Night City sera retombée.

articles.title: Diese gefährliche Malware ist auf bestimmten Smartphones schon vorinstalliert
articles.text:
Midnight Mimosa: Diese Malware ist auf günstigen Smartphones bereits vorinstalliert
Die meisten von uns denken beim Begriff Malware wahrscheinlich daran, dass man aufpassen muss, sich eine solche nicht auf seinem Smartphone einzufangen. Doch es gibt auch andere, noch schwieriger zu verhindernde, Szenarien: dass die Malware bereits auf dem eigenen Gerät vorinstalliert ist.
Forscher:innen haben eine Malware-Kampagne aufgedeckt, die auf preiswerte Android-Smartphones abzielt. Das bedeutet: Die betroffenen Geräte sind bereits kompromittiert, noch bevor man sie überhaupt nutzen kann.
Bedrohung besteht bereits, wenn das Gerät noch gar nicht eingeschaltet wurde
Bitdefender, ein Anbieter von Cybersicherheits- und Antivirensoftware, berichtete in seinem Blog über die Entdeckung einer bösartigen Masche namens „Midnight Mimosa“. Diese Malware ist in der Firmware des Geräts vorinstalliert – und das bedeutet, dass die Bedrohung selbst dann schon besteht, wenn das Gerät noch gar nicht eingeschaltet wurde. Erschwerend hinzu kommt, dass sich die perfide Malware nicht wie eine gewöhnliche Android-App deinstallieren lässt. „Man wird sie also nicht mehr los“, schreibt Android Police dazu.
Midnight Mimosa nutzt eine System-App, die fest in die Firmware des Smartphones integriert ist und ihr so Zugriff auf Systemebene verschafft. Zu diesen erweiterten Berechtigungen gehören beispielsweise die Kontrolle über die Installation und Deinstallation von Apps und sogar die Vergabe von Berechtigungen.
Die Malware kann die Google-Play-Store-App vorübergehend deaktivieren
Die Bitdefender-Forscher:innen entdeckten 32 getarnte Apps, die mit dieser betrügerischen Aktion in Verbindung standen. Diese Apps werden für Werbe- und Klickbetrug eingesetzt und generieren gefälschte Impressions, ohne dass die Nutzer:innen davon wissen oder ihre Zustimmung gegeben haben.
Das betrügerische Konzept dahinter ist ausgeklügelter, als man zunächst vermuten würde: Die Malware kann die Google-Play-Store-App vorübergehend deaktivieren, während sie bestimmte Schadfunktionen ausführt. Sobald diese Funktionen aktiv sind, wird der Play-Store wieder freigeschaltet. Dieses Ein- und Ausschalten des Play-Stores hilft, die Erkennung durch Google Play Protect während der Installation zu umgehen.
Midnight Mimosa wurde auf preiswerten Android-Geräten verschiedener Marken festgestellt, die auf Mediatek-Plattformen basieren. Obwohl es sich dabei meist um weniger bekannte Modelle handelt, sind Smartphones in mehr als 150 Ländern betroffen. 7,3 Prozent der so infizierten Geräte wurden in Deutschland entdeckt, damit liegt Deutschland auf Platz fünf der betroffenen Länder. Am stärksten betroffen sind Mexiko (13 Prozent) und Frankreich (12,5 Prozent).
Weitere Apps kommunizieren mit derselben Infrastruktur wie Midnight Mimosa
Bei einigen Geräten handelt es sich um gefälschte Klone von Premium-Modellen wie dem Galaxy S24 Ultra oder S26 Ultra. Echte Samsung-Smartphones seien demnach nicht betroffen. Die vollständige Liste der gefährdeten Geräte ist noch nicht bekannt, doch die Forscher:innen haben eine Reihe preiswerter Android-Smartphones genannt, die Teil der Malware-Kampagne waren. Diese lauten beispielsweise Kingkong X, S200 X, S25 Ultra oder Nitro A65.
Die Untersuchung förderte zudem 13 Apps aus Googles Play-Store zutage, die mit derselben Infrastruktur kommunizieren wie Midnight Mimosa. Das bedeutet, dass die Bedrohung weiter verbreitet ist als nur auf den bereits infizierten Geräten.
Sollten ihr zu den Unglücklichen gehören, die von dieser Sicherheitsbedrohung betroffen sind, könnt ihr laut Android Police kaum etwas tun, um sie zu entfernen. Am besten sei es, das Gerät komplett auszutauschen.

articles.title: Los drones ucranianos están consiguiendo lo que años de transición energética no lograron: que los rusos se lancen a la compra de coches eléctricos
articles.text:
Rusia lleva años intentando impulsar el coche eléctrico con subvenciones, ventajas fiscales y nuevas estaciones de carga. Sin embargo, el mayor acelerador de esa transición ha llegado desde el cielo y tiene forma de dron ucraniano. Los ataques contra las refinerías rusas están provocando una escasez de gasolina que ha dejado colas interminables en las gasolineras y ha disparado la demanda de vehículos eléctricos, especialmente de fabricación china. Quién lo iba a decir: Ucrania está consiguiendo con sus ataques algo que años de políticas energéticas rusas apenas habían logrado.
La guerra ha llegado a las gasolineras. Lo hemos ido contando. Desde finales de junio, Ucrania ha intensificado sus ataques con drones contra instalaciones petroleras rusas, afectando al suministro de combustible en distintas regiones del país. Las consecuencias se han trasladado directamente a la vida cotidiana de los conductores, que han llegado a esperar varias horas para llenar el depósito.
Según Gdebenz, una plataforma que recopila información sobre la disponibilidad de carburante, en estos momentos únicamente el 46% de las gasolineras rusas vende combustible. La proporción descendía al 27% en Nizhni Nóvgorod y se situaba en el 53% en Moscú, donde durante algunos episodios de julio y agosto apenas una de cada cuatro estaciones disponía de existencias.
El país del petróleo descubre el coche eléctrico. Recordaba esta semana el New York Times que Rusia figura entre los grandes productores mundiales de petróleo, una posición que durante décadas contribuyó a mantener relativamente barata la gasolina y redujo los incentivos para electrificar su parque automovilístico. Las enormes distancias entre ciudades, las temperaturas extremas y la escasez de cargadores también dificultaron la expansión de estos vehículos.
Ahora, la crisis de suministro está alterando las prioridades de los compradores. Según el Ministerio de Industria y Comercio ruso, las ventas de vehículos eléctricos e híbridos pasaron de 43.000 unidades entre enero y agosto de 2025 a más de 83.000 durante el mismo periodo de 2026, un incremento cercano al 93%.
Los drones han conseguido acelerar la transición. El cambio resulta todavía más llamativo al observar la cuota de mercado de los vehículos capaces de circular sin consumir gasolina. Según la consultora rusa Avtostat, los eléctricos puros y los híbridos enchufables representaban aproximadamente el 5% de las ventas de automóviles a comienzos de 2026.
A finales de septiembre, esa proporción había alcanzado el 11,5%, más del doble en apenas nueve meses. La cifra supera ligeramente la cuota estadounidense citada en el reportaje, aunque continúa muy lejos del 45% registrado en China. El dato refleja hasta qué punto la disponibilidad de combustible puede influir en las decisiones de compra en un país históricamente vinculado al petróleo.
Un mercado inesperado. El gran beneficiado de esta transformación está siendo el automóvil chino, que ya había ganado terreno en Rusia tras la retirada de numerosos fabricantes occidentales, japoneses y surcoreanos a raíz de la invasión de Ucrania. En un gran complejo comercial situado al noroeste de Moscú, más de 25 de sus 40 concesionarios corresponden ahora a marcas chinas.
UN VISTAZO A...
La demanda ha llegado a vaciar los inventarios de algunos establecimientos, mientras disminuye la oferta de eléctricos de segunda mano. Sergei Tselikov, uno de los principales analistas del sector automovilístico ruso, compró en julio un GWM Ora 03 GT después de recorrer cinco gasolineras sin encontrar la gasolina que necesitaba. Pocos días después, el precio del modelo había aumentado unos 2.000 dólares.
El Gobierno intenta apagar una crisis de combustible. Ante las dificultades de abastecimiento, las autoridades rusas han autorizado la comercialización de carburantes de calidad inferior para ampliar la oferta disponible. La medida ha generado nuevas preocupaciones entre algunos propietarios de vehículos y talleres mecánicos, que relacionan determinadas averías con el combustible utilizado.
Un responsable de un taller especializado en Volvo en Moscú aseguró en el NYT que haber recibido 15 automóviles con filtros de partículas diésel obstruidos durante apenas dos semanas de agosto. La escasez también está modificando los hábitos de movilidad: algunos ciudadanos recurren al transporte público, las bicicletas eléctricas, los patinetes o las conversiones de sus vehículos para funcionar con gas natural.
El problema ahora está en los enchufes. Rusia comenzó a impulsar con mayor intensidad la infraestructura eléctrica en 2022, mediante subvenciones para cargadores rápidos y conexiones a la red, y en 2023 introdujo nuevas exigencias para incorporar instalaciones de recarga en edificios de nueva construcción. El número de puntos públicos ha pasado de menos de 1.500 en 2022 a más de 8.000 en 2026, una expansión considerable que todavía resulta insuficiente en determinadas zonas.
Punkt E, uno de los principales operadores del país, asegura que la demanda en sus estaciones se ha duplicado durante las últimas semanas y que ya se forman colas para cargar los vehículos. La compañía ha decidido acelerar la construcción de otros 100 puntos, aunque los permisos y los plazos de instalación impiden responder inmediatamente al crecimiento del mercado.
Una transición energética impulsada por la necesidad. Los eléctricos siguen siendo caros para buena parte de los consumidores rusos y su autonomía, especialmente durante los inviernos más duros, continúa planteando dificultades. Los híbridos podrían beneficiarse especialmente de esta situación, al ofrecer una alternativa más flexible en un país con una infraestructura de recarga todavía desigual.
El Gobierno ya había introducido incentivos como exenciones fiscales, aparcamiento gratuito en grandes ciudades y ventajas en autopistas de peaje, con resultados relativamente modestos durante años. La ofensiva ucraniana contra las refinerías ha añadido un incentivo mucho más inmediato: la incertidumbre de encontrar gasolina. Y ha terminado convirtiendo una campaña militar contra la infraestructura energética rusa en un inesperado motor de electrificación de sus carreteras.

articles.title: GMKtec EVO-X3 Mini-PC Review Looking at a 128GB AMD Local AI Box
articles.text:
Calling AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ chips well-received in the mini-PC market is probably an understatement. The high-performance Zen 5 chips have proven particularly adept in this market thanks to a combination of CPU and iGPU performance, plus high memory capacity and bandwidth from LPDDR5X. Especially in this era of AI development, software developers looking to test and run inference locally have been quick to snap up the mini-PCs.
One result of this popularity is that AMD’s many mini-PC partners have been addressing a market large enough (and with margins big enough) to justify working through multiple generations of mini-PC designs within the Ryzen AI Max family’s lifecycle. A prime example is GMtec, one of the industry’s better-known mini-PC vendors. Last year the company released its first Ryzen AI Max+ box with the EVO-X2, and this year they are back again with a new and very different Ryzen AI Max+ mini-PC design that they are dubbing the EVO-X3.
| GMKtec EVO-X3 Key Specs (As Configured) |  | 
| Processors | AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 16C/32T (5.1GHz) | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 Pro | 
| Memory | 128GB LPDDR5X-8000, Soldered | 
| Drive Bays | 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Lexar NQ790 4TB) 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Empty) | 
| GPU | Radeon 8060S Graphics (40 CUs) | 
| PSU | 230W External PSU | 
| Form Factor | Mini-PC | 
| Dimensions | 353 x 186 x 41 mm (13.9 x 7.3 x 1.6 in) | 
| Weight | 2.3kg (5.07 lbs) | 
| Wireless | Wi-Fi 7 (2×2) + Bluetooth 5.4 (MT7925) | 
| Color | Gray & Neon Green | 
| Ports | Front: 1x USB-A 5Gbps, 1x USB-A 480Mbps, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack Rear: 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x USB-C 40Gbps, 1x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x 2.5GbE LAN (RJ45, RTL8125BG), 1x OCuLink (Gen4 x4) | 
The EVO-X3 stands out in a crowded mini-PC market for a few reasons. First and foremost, the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 SoC at the heart of the system delivers its AI performance and enables it to tap into 128GB of LPDDR5X memory for its iGPU. The second, and far more unique reason is its connectivity. GMKtec has outfitted the system with an OCuLink port, making it a rare Ryzen AI Max system with external PCIe connectivity, and it surpasses even Thunderbolt 4 systems in available bandwidth.
Surprisingly, GMKtec is aiming the EVO-X3 at a pretty broad customer base, even pitching the OCuLink port as a gaming feature for use with an eGPU. In practice, though, it is hard to imagine the system being used as anything other than a productivity desktop, especially since GMKtec even preloads the system with AI development software. That is okay, because the Ryzen AI Max platform has proven well suited for that role.
If you wanted to find the GMKtec EVO-X3 online, here is an Amazon Affiliate link.
GMKtec EVO-X3 External hardware Overview
One of the most notable design aspects of the previous iteration, the EVO-X2 mini-PC, was that the system operates upright, a pretty big distinction from the more classic wide-and-low desktop mini-PC form factors. For the EVO-X3, GMKtec seems to have doubled down on this design strategy even more, resulting in a mini-PC that can only be described as a metal monolith. The stange form factor makes more sense once we get inside.
The metal, by the way, is a notable change from the EVO-X2, which notably (and noticeably) featured a plastic chassis. On the other hand, this EVO-X3 is fully metal. The overall monolithic design is even more clearly meant to stand, especially with the (required) base attached.
The tall, slim profile does mean that there is very little to the front of the system, though. For the purposes of our article layout (and your browser window), we have laid the mini-PC flat, which goes to show just how thin the 41mm PC is. Despite packing in a high-performance processor, it is not much thicker than a desktop replacement-class workstation laptop.
This view also underscores the limited I/O connectivity on the front of the PC, however. Aside from the 3.5mm combo audio jack, GMKtec has placed only two USB-A ports on the front of the system, and only one is a fast 5Gbps USB 3.x port. The second USB-A port is an even slower USB 2.x port, and there is no front-panel USB Type-C connectivity. The system supports plenty of I/O bandwidth, as we will see, but just not in the front.
Meanwhile, towards the other end of the system, we find a rather striking neon green power button sitting within the grey metal chassis.
Speaking of aesthetics, the EVO-X3’s standing design is not just a style choice for GMKtec. Both the left and right sizes feature significant ventilation. Meanwhile, if there is any doubt about what the primary market is for this system, the “AI workstation” labeling etched into the left side of the case should remove all doubt.
Shifting to the rear of the system, we find much better ventilation with clearly visible heatsinks. More importantly, this is also where the rest of the system’s I/O lives, including its unusual OCuLink port.
Starting there, GMKtec has opted to route four of the Ryzen SoC’s PCIe lanes to an OCuLink port for directly attaching a device to the system. This port can technically connect any device, but the most common use for OCuLink these days is attaching a dock for an external GPU, making it possible to add a high-end video card (or other accelerator) to the system. The OCuLink specification itself tops out at PCIe Gen4 x4 (or ~64Gbps), so it is not comparable to the amount of bandwidth a full-fledged PCIe slot can offer. With the Ryzen AI Max chips offering only 16 PCIe lanes to begin with (all PCIe Gen4), GMKtec can realistically offer only 4 lanes, since they need the other lanes for other features.
In any case, the drawback to OCuLink as an external port is the same here as it always was: it is not a hot-plug-capable port. That is why GMKtec has put a very explicit sticker here warning users not to plug (or unplug) an OCuLink cable while the system is operating. On that note, credit to the engineer who had the foresight here to put the OCuLink port to the left of the DC power jack, isolating it from the hotplug-capable USB ports.
The thin profile of the EVO-X3 means that GMKtec is relying on an external power supply here. At 230 Watts, they technically could have gotten away with a USB-C power supply, but barrel jack units are still a common fixture here.
Next is the system’s sole USB-C port. A native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, this is a full 40Gbps USB4 port that also supports DP Alt Mode to double as a display output for the system. In fact, this is the only way to get DisplayPort video out of the X3, as there is also no dedicated DisplayPort output on the system. Otherwise, given GMKtec’s focus on external I/O bandwidth with the X3, it is somewhat surprising to see that they did not include a second 40Gbps USB-C port, as the Ryzen SoC provides for two ports.
To the right, we have the system’s sole dedicated display output: an HDMI 2.1 port. Another native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, there is little reason not to include it here.
Moving down the line, we find another USB Type-A port. The second (and final) USB port on the rear of the system is a 10Gbps port. Including the earlier Type-C port, this gives the X3 a total of 4 USB ports, which is serviceable, but it falls short compared to most other Ryzen AI Max mini-PCs that offer a few more ports. In practice, it means the OCuLink port and USB-C port are doing a lot of heavy lifting as far as I/O goes, as there simply are not a lot of ports otherwise for plugging in peripherals after you add a mouse and keyboard. There is again a reason for this that we will see inside.
Finally, we have the system’s dedicated Ethernet jack. This is a 2.5GbE port backed by Realtek’s RTL8125BG controller. This is a common enough sight across PCs these days, but for a recently-released Ryzen AI Max system, it is a shame that GMKtec did not use one of Realtek’s newer 10GbE chips, which have become readily available (and relatively cheap) this year. Not including 10GbE is quickly becoming a missed opportunity for AI development-focused PC.
Shifting perspectives once again, here is a shot of what is on top of the X3 when the system is standing. Matching the colorful neon green accent of the power button we saw earlier, the solid green top gives the system a distinct two-tone color scheme. And perhaps a smidge of irony for the Ryzen-powered system, since it is much closer to NVIDIA’s shade of green than AMD’s.
In any case, the top features another airflow vent as well. So, like virtually every other side of the system, it needs to be kept clear for cooling purposes. This also serves as the one significant non-metallic portion of the system for cleanly routing the wireless radio antennas.
Last but not least, here is a look at the bottom of the system. Normally hidden by the system’s base, this is where GMKtec has placed the product stickers, as well as the means to access the system’s internals.
Looking at the base itself, interestingly, GMKtec has opted to etch the full system information into the base, including its power specifications and regulatory trademarks. This ensures that the information is visible without dismantling the system, but it means that the base is an integral part of the system for more than just holding up the monolithic mini-PC.
The base relies on a pair of screws to secure it to the bottom of the mini-PC’s chassis. GMKtec has also taken care to include rubber feet on the base to prevent slippage. Unfortunately, these feet are not built into the base, and in fact have to be removed to access the screws that hold the base on. Which means this is not a design that is meant to be opened more than a couple of times, as it will wear out the adhesive on the feet.
Now that we have taken a look at the outside of the EVO-X3, let us dig into the guts of the system.
Unfortunate that they did not give y’all the 495 SKU. The 395 is pretty well understood.

articles.title: Google Pixel 10 Exploits Earned Hackers $560,000 at Pwn2Own
articles.text:
Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 has come to an end, and participants earned more than $1.2 million for exploits targeting phones, printers, smart speakers, smart home hubs, a wellness device, AI infrastructure and coding tools, and cloud databases.
The highest rewards were paid out for Google Pixel 10 exploits, which were demonstrated by three teams. They collectively earned more than $560,000 for their work.
The Ikotas Labs team earned the full $300,000 payout by chaining multiple bugs to remotely hack a Pixel phone.
Tim Becker and Yves Bieri received $150,000 for their Pixel exploit — they did not get the full payout because their exploit involved a previously known flaw.
The third Pixel hack was demonstrated by Dimitrios Valsamaras and Ken Gannon, who earned $112,500 for an exploit that chained a zero-day with a previously known vulnerability.
Last year, Valsamaras and Gannon earned $50,000 for hacking a Samsung Galaxy S25 device. They later showed how they exploited vulnerabilities in Samsung software, including the virtual assistant Bixby, to hack mobile devices.
In addition to the Pixel exploits, a significant reward, $50,000, was earned by a researcher for a Sonos Era 300 smart speaker hack.
Rewards of $40,000 were paid out for several exploits, including ones targeting Oracle Autonomous AI Database, OpenAI Codex, Nvidia’s Dynamo AI inference framework, the LiteLLM AI gateway, and the Philips Hue Bridge Pro smart lighting hub.
Researchers received roughly $30,000 for exploits targeting the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Home Assistant Green smart home hub.
Pwn2Own participants earned $20,000 for hacking Lexmark and Brother printers, and the Garmin Index BPM blood pressure monitor.
Rewards ranging from $4,250 to $17,500 were paid out for exploits involving Sonos Era, Galaxy S26, LiteLLM, Philips Hue Bridge Pro, Lexmark CX532adwe, Oracle Autonomous AI Database, Home Assistant Green, Chroma, Garmin Index BPM, and Canon imageFORCE 1643F.
Affected vendors will be provided with the full details of all exploits.
No one targeted the iPhone 17 and WhatsApp, both of which had a maximum prize of $300,000.
Related: TP-Link Faces State Lawsuits and New Scrutiny Over ISP Router Flaws
Related: Android’s October 2026 Updates Patch 25 Vulnerabilities
Related: Google Narrows Open Source Bug Bounty Amid Wave of Invalid Automated Reports

articles.title: Microsoft quer transformar o Windows em um sistema operacional de IA
articles.text:
A Microsoft quer transformar o Windows 11 em uma plataforma capaz de executar agentes de inteligência artificial para realizar tarefas pelos usuários. A estratégia combina processamento local e serviços em nuvem para adaptar o sistema a uma nova forma de usar computadores.
Apresentada em um evento sobre Windows e dispositivos Surface, a proposta também busca atrair desenvolvedores e criadores. Mas as demonstrações ainda deixaram dúvidas sobre os benefícios para quem usa o computador em atividades cotidianas.
Menos nuvem, mais processamento local
A chamada inteligência híbrida permite combinar modelos de IA instalados no computador com serviços em nuvem. A ideia é executar determinadas tarefas localmente e reduzir gastos com processamento externo.
Durante o evento, a Microsoft mostrou o GitHub Copilot realizando tarefas de programação no próprio dispositivo. Também apresentou modelos que podem rodar localmente, agentes como OpenClaw, Hermes e Perplexity e uma integração mais profunda do Copilot ao Windows.
O CEO da empresa, Satya Nadella, destacou a mudança de perspectiva. “Acho que hoje é o dia em que começaremos a falar e pensar no ecossistema de fronteira com contornos talvez um pouco diferentes”, comentou.
As demonstrações, porém, não convenceram plenamente. Faltaram exemplos concretos de como os modelos locais podem ajudar quem não desenvolve sistemas de IA. Por enquanto, a Microsoft parece concentrar esforços em conquistar justamente esse público especializado.
Surface Laptop Ultra mira desenvolvedores
Para atrair profissionais que precisam executar modelos grandes, a empresa apresentou o Surface Laptop Ultra, equipado com chips Nvidia RTX Spark. O computador pode rodar localmente modelos com mais de 120 bilhões de parâmetros.
Nós o desenvolvemos para desenvolvedores e criadores que exigem o máximo de desempenho e desejam portabilidade com acabamento excepcional.
Pavan Davuluri, executivo responsável pelo Windows, durante evento.
O preço limita o alcance da máquina. O Surface Laptop Ultra começa em US$ 2.599 (cerca de R$ 13.515), enquanto alguns computadores com RTX Spark podem chegar a US$ 6.999 (aproximadamente R$ 36.395). Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo e MSI também oferecem equipamentos com essa plataforma.
Para quem trabalha intensamente com IA, o investimento pode compensar se reduzir significativamente os gastos com processamento em nuvem. Para o consumidor comum, é mais difícil justificar esse custo sem vantagens práticas claras.
Windows ainda precisa provar o valor da IA
Uma novidade potencialmente mais útil para o público geral é a reformulação da Busca do Windows 11. A interface foi redesenhada para exibir resultados diretamente na tela e funcionar de maneira semelhante a um iniciador de aplicativos.
Leia mais:
- Microsoft lança novo notebook Surface com foco em IA e alto desempenho
- Governo Trump trava pedidos de green card patrocinados por big techs
- Agência dos EUA poderá testar computador quântico da Microsoft sem depender da empresa para isso
A experiência anterior da Microsoft com IA ajuda a explicar a cautela. Os PCs Copilot+, lançados dois anos antes, deram destaque às NPUs, chips que aceleram tarefas de inteligência artificial. Até agora, porém, poucas ferramentas de fotografia, vídeo e produtividade aproveitam esses recursos. O Recall, apresentado como um dos grandes destaques da plataforma, perdeu relevância após preocupações com privacidade e atrasos no lançamento.
Os computadores com RTX Spark podem ter mais sucesso entre desenvolvedores e criadores, que têm motivos concretos para executar modelos localmente. Para chegar a um público maior, será necessário levar essas capacidades a máquinas mais acessíveis.
A Microsoft também enfrenta uma mudança que vai além do hardware. Agentes executados na nuvem, em máquinas virtuais Linux, podem ampliar a compatibilidade com aplicativos desse sistema. A empresa quer preservar a posição do Windows em um cenário no qual a maneira de usar computadores está mudando. Para isso, precisará mostrar que os agentes de IA oferecem vantagens reais, e não apenas computadores mais caros para especialistas.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
articles.text:
Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change once you turn down the lights and turn up the brightness on the e-reader.
Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
Reddit users are reporting shadows and visible LEDs around screen edge of new Kindles.
In some cases, users see shadows around the edges of the screen, or even visible LED strips. The issue appears to affect both the plastic and aluminum models in all colors. Some minor glowing around the edges might be a byproduct of the combination of front lighting and a flush screen. But Reddit users say images shared there show something more dramatic that appears to be a defect.
Good e-Reader says that Amazon is aware of the issue and has confirmed that a manufacturing issue may have led to defects in the current batch of Kindles. When contacted by The Verge, Amazon spokesperson Katie Condon said, “In certain, highly specific conditions, such as using dark mode at a higher brightness settings in a dark environment, customers may see a subtle glow on the edge of the display on devices with colored bezels. This can be mitigated by adjusting the front light to a lower level.”
Update October 9th, 2026: Added statement from Amazon.

articles.title: SenseHuman AI is building an AI-powered hardhat that watches your back | BetaKit
articles.text:
On a busy construction site, it can feel like you need eyes in the back of your head to avoid accidents. SenseHuman AI wants to provide you with those “eyes.”
The Edmonton-based startup has developed a hardhat imbued with AI machine vision, giving the wearer 360 degrees of worksite surveillance. The company has already had traction, signing customers and completing pilots. Now, co-founder and CEO Adil Muhammad says they need to meet demand.
“We want to scale up manufacturing … and we’re trying to get the attention of investors so we can scale.”
Adil Muhammad, SenseHuman
Originally from Pakistan, Muhammad founded SenseHuman AI last year alongside three co-founders: Gavin Mei, Vicente Gonzalez, and Gaang Lee. A graduate of the University of Alberta (U of A), Muhammad completed his master’s degree in civil engineering and spent time working in the U of A’s IHT Lab researching ways AI can be integrated into construction site safety. But it wasn’t his education that served as the lightbulb moment for Muhammad, but rather a video game.
“If you’ve ever played Call of Duty, there’s this minimap on the bottom of the screen. If something comes at you from the back, you see it on the minimap,” Muhammad said. “I thought, why not use the same thing with a worker?”
SenseHuman’s hardware doesn’t actually create a minimap. In fact, there are no screens at all. Instead, it uses four cameras and machine-vision software to create a 360-degree field of vision. If that software detects an imminent risk—like, say, a trench, ledge, or tripping hazard—it sends a vibrating signal through the hardhat in the direction of the danger. SenseHuman can even custom build the helmets to factor job site rules—like standing three metres from a piece of operating machinery—into its risk assessments.
SenseHuman’s platform isn’t perfect (it can’t yet reliably predict falling objects from above, and it can’t stop every accident on a job site from happening), but the company is focused on preventing the minor injuries that make up the lion’s share of job site incidents.
RELATED: From sawdust to seed round: ConstructionClock grows from Winnipeg
“I was reading a lot of incident reports from the Workers’ Compensation Board, and talking to different companies,” Muhammad said. “Every year you see news articles—and many more that go unreported—about accidents that lead to minor injuries. These are the main incidents that are happening, and these guys have the most pain in the industry.”
The Association of Workers’ Compensation Boards of Canada (AWCBC), a nonprofit body representing Canada’s workers’ compensation boards, reports that in 2024 there were more than 320,000 lost time claims, meaning an injury was serious enough that a worker could not be at work. Among that number, jobs in the trades, transportation, and equipment operators were far and away the most common.
Financial incentives
Beyond the potential safety benefits, there’s value for employers, too. Muhammad said SenseHuman’s cameras can create video footage—which excludes audio recording due to privacy concerns—that it claims has already been used by its pilot partner to investigate an accident.
WorkSafeBC, the BC provincial counterpart to the AWCBC, in its own report last May said that the construction industry had around 38,000 accepted claims, with nearly 5,800 of those involving falls and nearly 7,000 involving equipment or vehicular collisions. WorkSafeBC estimates total costs from those claims tallied at more than $1.3 billion.
While most workers’ compensation claims are paid by the province, companies still incur costs, either from subsequent investigations or fines levied against them after an accident. In Alberta, penalties can run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Momentum and bottlenecks
Since launching last October, SenseHuman has had remarkable traction. In January, it received $250,000 CAD in pre-seed funding from OpenCircle Contractors Association, a non-profit construction industry association, alongside an additional undisclosed investor. It later sold its first five units to OpenCircle and has 12 smart helmets active in the field today.
SenseHuman has also completed several pilot programs, including Edmonton Unlimited’s Built World Venture Pilot program, where the company partnered with Sherwood Park, Alta.-based industrial contractor The Bartlett Group. It has used the feedback from those relationships to further tailor its product to industry needs.
“Right now, the main issue is that we have a lot of interest from companies, but we don’t have capacity to build more units,” Muhammad said. “We want to scale up manufacturing … and we’re trying to get the attention of investors so we can scale.”
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of SenseHuman AI.

articles.title: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
articles.text:
Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges.” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments.
The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations.
To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks.
One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance.
The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall—has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms.
No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency.
The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program, developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society.
Topics covered
The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment.
The topics are:
- Fundamental principles of design and functionality.
- Practical insights into advanced architectures.
- Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment.
- Emerging trends and evolving architectures.
- Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT).
The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems.
It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments.
The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments.
By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.
AI-generated avatars explain concepts
The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action.
A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect.
In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments.
By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.
The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material.
Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions.
Modeling expert reasoning through dialogue
The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance.
Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development.
The program goes further by interrupting the dialogue at key moments and inviting the learner to step in. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team.
A new standard for advanced engineering education
By merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. It captures the complexity of real‑world problem‑solving, humanizes the learning experience, and challenges participants to think like the engineers who are defining the future of AI hardware. It is not simply a new course; it is a new way of learning.
For individual access, visit the IEEE Learning Network.
For customized organizational options, contact a content specialist to discuss volume pricing.

articles.title: Multa récord de 750.000 euros por la rifa que realizó TheGrefg de su coche de lujo sin tener los permisos necesarios
articles.text: Consumo no señala al infractor, pero los datos coinciden con este sorteo organizado por TheGrefg en 2024. El Ministerio de Consumo ha multado con 750.000 euros a EBR Management SLU, la empresa que puso en marcha la rifa de un coche de lujo impulsada por un youtuber español residente en Andorra . La compañía ha cometido una infracción administrativa considerada muy grave según la Ley de Regulación del Juego (LRJ), al no pedir permiso para organizar dicho sorteo. Se trata de la sanción conocida más alta en España por la acción de un influencer , cuyo nombre no ha revelado el departamento de Pablo Bustinduy, pero los datos coinciden con un sorteo organizado por TheGrefg , alias del murciano David Cánovas, quien precisamente usó esa empresa en las bases legales de su rifa . EL PAÍS ha intentado recoger la versión de Cánovas —que suma casi 20 millones de suscriptores en YouTube— sin éxito. articles.title: Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
articles.text:
Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
Following last week’s release of Clef and Clef-flash, Cloudflare’s open-weight decision models, we decided to bring forth more gifts. Today, we’re releasing Clef-omni, which takes in audio and video input alongside text and image. We also cut the price of Clef-flash so it is now cheaper than Jev, and we made Clef faster.
Although the model game is still early for Cloudflare, innovation and iteration is in our DNA, and we apply these principles to everything we do. In fact, the story of Clef came together over the course of less than a week. We decided we wanted to do something in the decision model space on a Friday evening, trained the model over the weekend, and launched it on Thursday. Even with such a short timeline, we were able to ship performant, high-quality, open-weight models for the community — imagine what more we can do in the future.
For today, we’re excited to keep up the momentum with new additions and improvements to our Clef family of models. This is just the beginning, and we’ll continue to get better, faster, cheaper, and more innovative.
Clef-omni takes audio, video, image, and text input
Our new Clef-omni model is able to take audio, video, image, and text input. This changes the paradigm for decision models, which have been largely text-only since the debut of Jev from TypeSafe. With Clef, we supported images and video frame arrays, but Clef-omni is able to take in audio (wav or mp3) and video (mp4 or webm) alongside text and images.
Instead of setting up cascading pipelines of models that transcribe speech-to-text, or splitting audio and image channels from video, you can just call one model to make decisions across any modality. We are now one step closer to a model that is able to interact with the world as we experience it — through audio, visual, and textual communication, all in one.
Check out our developer docs for the new Clef-omni model. We also released the model open-weights on HuggingFace. For a quick start, here’s how you can send new modality inputs to Clef-omni:
curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_AUTH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "clef-omni",
    "state": "Review the installation: a photo of the unit, an audio recording of it running, and a video of the fan.",
    "images": ["data:image/png;base64,<base64-png>"],
    "audio": ["data:audio/mpeg;base64,<base64-mp3>"],
    "videos": ["data:video/mp4;base64,<base64-mp4>"],
    "questions": {
      "label_visible": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the model and serial number label visible in the photo?"},
      "sounds_normal": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the unit sound like it is running smoothly, without rattling or grinding?"},
      "fan_running": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the fan running in the video?"}
    }
  }'
Clef-omni expands our open-weight decision architecture to natively handle multimodal workflows. We built this on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct mixture-of-experts (MoE) foundation, where the model was already capable of processing text, imagery, audio, and video directly within a single pipeline. However, we adopt the primary comprehension backbone while discarding the text-to-speech output components. In production, Clef-omni executes a quick prefill pass across the complete payload, scoring all modalities and valid parameter options simultaneously.
Because we skip output token generation since Clef models are not Large Language Models (LLMs), we remove the overhead of transcribing or captioning incoming files. Media elements map straight into the unified sequence, where video and audio are synced with visual frames for joint processing. Clef-omni then pulls candidate values directly from internal embeddings using our two-stage attention routing: every valid option gathers key evidence from the input (regardless if they are buried in text snippets, visual elements, or audio streams) before field vectors cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. We add a built-in lexical grammar that preserves option semantics, so that we can deliver fast, schema-constrained scoring across every input type.
We train the model with the same techniques as we did with Clef — freezing the Qwen3 backbone, training low-rank adapters (LoRA), and applying our standard post-training approach: combining label-smoothed cross-entropy loss with Brier score calibration. The result is a model that is resilient and designed to succeed regardless of schema variations, field ordering, and prompt structures.
This brings several core upgrades to the Clef model family. Calibrated, schema-bound decisions now seamlessly handle text, images, audio, and synchronized video in a single API call. It's also fast. Text-only decisions return in about 130 ms at the median, image inputs in about 150 ms, and audio clips in a few hundred milliseconds. Even a full 21-second video clip with sound is scored in about 1.5 seconds, all in a single API call.
Our benchmarking shows strong performance across benchmarks, even with new modalities and MoE architecture.
| Benchmark | Clef-omni | Clef | Clef-flash | Jev | 
| BFCL · case exact | 98.2 | 98.47 | 98.76 | 95.75 | 
| ToolRet · nDCG@10 | 66.6 | 69.19 | 66.43 | 65.28 | 
| API-Bank · accuracy | 92.7 | 91.93 | 93.11 | 88.19 | 
| Home appliances · case exact | 69.3 | 82.95 | 97.73 | 52.27 | 
| When2Call · accuracy | 63.3 | 72.37 | 65.58 | 80.97 | 
| BANKING77 · macro-F1 | 94.8 | 94.20 | 90.93 | 79.74 | 
| CLINC150+OOS · macro-F1 | 97.7 | 97.43 | 66.77 | 89.27 | 
| BRIGHT · nDCG@10 | 42.0 | 45.91 | 39.26 | 47.52 | 
| Amazon ESCI · macro-F1 | 57.8 | 57.48 | 57.39 | 55.21 | 
| PhishNChips · accuracy | 73.2 | 79.60 | 75.05 | 62.55 | 
We also benchmarked against the TypeSafe evals to show how Clef-omni performs.
| Workflow | Metric | Clef-Omni | Clef | Clef-flash | Jev | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invoice processing | Exact actions | 60.2 | 64.7 | 57.1 | 61.8 | 
| Invoice processing | Primary action | 82.0 | 86.2 | 73.3 | 83.1 | 
| Customer service | Exact actions | 71.6 | 76.3 | 77.0 | 76.0 | 
| Security incidents | Exact actions | 61.7 | 62.9 | 61.7 | 61.7 | 
| Agent trace observability | Primary action | 65.8 | 68.5 | 69.8 | 71.6 | 
Clef-flash model is now cheaper
We heard your feedback — you want a decision model affordable enough to incorporate into any workflow. We’ve made a few optimizations and can now offer Clef-flash at cheaper prices. We want Clef to be able to make decisions that scale for you across all your agentic workflows, and now our pricing also incentivizes that.
We were able to optimize the model to the point where Clef-flash is now cheaper than Jev while still being performant and high-quality. Check out the developer docs for the most up-to-date pricing information at all times, including more detail on how image and audio modalities are converted to input tokens for pricing.
- Clef-flash – originally $0.09 per M input tokens, now $0.038 per M input tokens
- Clef – remains at $0.24 per M input tokens
- Clef-omni – launched today at $0.15 per M input tokens
However, one trade-off we have to make in order to have cheaper pricing is to cut the context window of Clef-flash. The hosted version of Clef-flash now has a context window of 24k, instead of 64k as previously advertised. The model weights on Hugging Face are untouched and were trained to support a 256k context window should you choose to self-host it.
From our usage data, we see that only 0.24% of requests exceed 24k input tokens. Based on this data, we decided to make the call to drop the context window to 24k for Clef-flash in order to price it at a more accessible entry point. Our Clef model remains at a 64k context window, and we encourage folks with larger context needs to switch to Clef instead of Clef-flash.
Clef model is now faster
Speeds are also faster for the Clef model, with new optimizations to the hosted version of Clef on Workers AI. No new model weights are released because most of the optimizations we made are at the serving infrastructure layer, not materially to the model weights or architecture. Check out our new speeds below:
| Input size | Before: median / p95 (ms) | Now: median / p95 (ms) | Median speedup | 
| ~800 tokens | 262 / 438 | 152 / 351 | 1.7× | 
| ~3,400 tokens | 616 / 777 | 305 / 531 | 2.0× | 
| ~16,000 tokens | 2,721 / 3,250 | 1,635 / 1,805 | 1.7× | 
One of the optimizations we made was to move to SGLang for serving the model. We worked with the SGLang team and made pull requests to incorporate Clef (PR #42721), which will be released in SGLang 0.5.22. You can also self-host Clef since we released the weights, and the new SGLang launch commands are available on our updated Hugging Face repo as well as the SGLang cookbooks.
How are people using Clef?
At Cloudflare, we’ve had teams experimenting with Clef as a model that can help classify over general domains. The coolest thing about watching teams adopt Clef is that the capability to do detections and classifications have moved into the model layer, where it is accessible for anyone to start incorporating decision models into their use cases. Previously, even with zero-shot classifiers, the small models may not have been powerful enough to classify across any domain without further tuning. You might have needed to stand up a specialized machine learning team to help train over your particular domain, and gather a corpus of data in order to train a better model. Now, all you need to do is call a model to instantly parse through input data with precision.
A few highlights of how teams at Cloudflare are using Clef: Our public GitHub docs repo uses Clef to instantly detect and close spam issues. EmDash, our content management system, moderates plugin libraries for phishing. Our data loss prevention team is scanning data for potential personally identifiable information (PII) like government IDs. And our threat intelligence team is using Clef to help detect malicious domains.
Give it a try!
We’re excited to bring you more from the Clef family of models, including new modalities like audio and video, as well as making the model more accessible with cheaper pricing and faster speeds. articles.title: 3 KI-Figuren, ein Konsens: Claude Skills als Sparringsteam für Selbstständige
articles.text:
3 KI-Figuren, ein Konsens: Claude Skills als Sparringsteam für Selbstständige
Bei Adrian Rohnfelder übernehmen drei KI-Figuren diese Rolle: Eine antwortet so, wie er selbst antworten würde, eine sucht die Schwachstellen in seinen Plänen, die dritte fragt nach den Menschen, die eine Entscheidung betrifft. Das Team ist ein Baustein: Rohnfelder organisiert seine ganze Arbeit rund um Claude, mit gebündeltem Wissen und festen Abläufen. Zusätzliche Werkzeuge braucht er für die drei Figuren nicht.
Warum ein KI-Sparringspartner nicht von selbst widerspricht
Einfach einen Chatbot nach einer Zweitmeinung zu fragen, reicht nicht. Sprachmodelle reden ihren Nutzer:innen gern nach dem Mund, in der Forschung heißt das Sycophancy. Wie ausgeprägt das ist, hat ein Team der Stanford University im Fachmagazin Science gezeigt. Elf führende Modelle bestätigten das Verhalten ihrer Nutzer:innen im Schnitt 49 Prozent häufiger als Menschen. Schon nach einer Unterhaltung fühlten sich die Testpersonen stärker im Recht. Die zustimmenden Antworten hielten sie trotzdem für vertrauenswürdiger.
Ein selbst gebauter Kritiker löst das Problem nicht automatisch. Rohnfelders erste Version wiederholte denselben Einwand, egal was er ihr erklärte. „Beim achten Mal habe ich gesagt: So kommen wir nicht weiter.“
Damit alle drei Figuren in jedem Chat bereitstehen, hat er sie als Claude-Skills angelegt: gespeicherte Anleitungen, die Claude abruft, sobald eine Aufgabe sie verlangt. Rohnfelder kann jede Figur einzeln ansprechen oder alle drei untereinander diskutieren lassen. Dann widersprechen sie sich, räumen Punkte ein und legen ihm am Ende eine gemeinsame Empfehlung vor, samt der Fragen, die offen bleiben. Das System läuft im Claude-Pro-Abo, das er ohnehin nutzt. Die Pflege kostet ihn höchstens ein bis zwei Stunden pro Woche.
Claude-Skills als Beispiel: Was einen KI-Kritiker brauchbar macht
Entscheidend sind die Regeln, nach denen die Figuren widersprechen. Ein Kritiker, der immer etwas findet, wird überhört. Einer, der zu schnell nachgibt, bringt nichts.
Was du in dieser Blaupause bekommst
In diesem t3n PRO Use Case liest du, wie sich ein Solo-Selbstständiger mit Claude Skills ein KI-Sparringsteam aus drei Figuren gebaut hat:
- Einblick in Aufbau und Pflege: Interview-Methode, Datenbasis, Diskussionsverfahren
- Im Detail: die Axiome des Kritikers und sein festes Format für Einwände
